questions.q: What is the minimum age to be issued a New York real estate salesperson license?
questions.explanation: A salesperson applicant must be at least 18. Age 20 is the minimum for a broker license—don't swap the two.

questions.q: How many hours of approved qualifying education must a new, non-exempt salesperson applicant complete?
options: 75 hours
77 hours
90 hours
152 hours
questions.explanation: The current salesperson qualifying course is 77 hours. 75 hours was the old course (now needing a 2-hour supplement), and 152 hours is the broker requirement.

questions.q: A New York real estate salesperson license is issued for a term of:
options: 1 year
3 years
2 years
4 years
questions.explanation: NY real estate licenses run for two-year terms and must be renewed every two years. A passed state exam result is also valid for two years.

questions.q: To renew, a salesperson must complete 22.5 hours of continuing education. How do the required topic components (fair housing, agency, ethics, implicit bias, etc.) relate to that total?
options: They are added on top of the 22.5 hours as extra time
They are optional electives that can replace the 22.5 hours
They apply only to brokers, not to salespersons
They are counted within the 22.5 hours, not added on top
questions.explanation: The required components (fair housing 3h, agency 1h/2h first term, ethics 2.5h, recent legal matters 1h, cultural competency 2h, implicit bias 2h) fit inside the 22.5-hour total. They do not increase it.
questions.citation: NY RPL § 441 (continuing education); DOS licensing requirements

questions.q: During a salesperson's FIRST license term, how many continuing-education hours must cover agency?
options: 1 hour
3 hours
2 hours
4 hours
questions.explanation: The agency component is 2 hours in the first salesperson term and 1 hour in later terms. Both count toward the 22.5-hour total.
questions.citation: NY RPL § 441 (continuing education); DOS licensing requirements

questions.q: After a closing, a grateful buyer hands salesperson Maria a $500 check payable to her personally as thanks for her work on the deal. What should Maria do?
options: Decline it; only her sponsoring broker may pay her for licensed work
Keep it, since a voluntary gift from a customer falls outside license law
Keep it, as long as she reports it to the IRS as taxable personal income
Keep it, if it is less than her share of the commission on the sale
questions.explanation: A salesperson may not accept compensation for licensed services from anyone other than the broker they are associated with. A payment for the deal is compensation even if it's called a gift.

questions.q: Broker Dan deposits a buyer's $10,000 earnest money check into his firm's general operating account 'just until closing.' This is:
options: Conversion, because the money was spent on business expenses
Permitted, as long as none of the entrusted funds are actually spent
Permitted, because the commission will be earned at closing
Commingling, because client funds were mixed with the broker's own
questions.explanation: Putting entrusted client money in the broker's own operating account is commingling, even if none of it is spent. Conversion is actually using the money for an unauthorized purpose.

questions.q: A broker withdraws a buyer's deposit from the escrow account to pay office rent, planning to put it back after closing. This is best described as:
options: Commingling—mixing two clients' deposits in a single account
Conversion—using another person's money for the broker's own purposes
Acceptable, because the coming commission will exceed the amount taken
An advance on commission, allowed if the broker documents it
questions.explanation: Using entrusted funds for the broker's own expenses is conversion. Planning to repay it or expecting a commission does not make the deposit the broker's money.

questions.q: Under current DOS rules, a broker who receives entrusted client funds (such as a down payment) must deposit them in a separate special account within:
options: One business day
Three business days
Ten business days
Thirty days
questions.explanation: Entrusted client funds must go into a separate, federally insured special account within three business days. They must be kept safe until then.

questions.q: A seller tells a broker: 'I need $400,000 from this sale. Sell it for whatever you can and keep everything above that as your fee.' The broker should:
options: Accept, as long as the arrangement is put in writing
Accept, if the seller is first told the property's estimated market value
Accept, but only if the property is vacant land
Decline, because net listings are prohibited in New York
questions.explanation: In a net listing, the broker keeps everything above the seller's minimum. New York prohibits them. This is not the same as a negotiated commission rate combined with an estimate of the seller's net proceeds.

questions.q: Which task may an unlicensed assistant in a brokerage office lawfully perform?
options: Scheduling appointments for licensees with buyers and sellers
Showing a listed home when no licensee is available
Answering a buyer's questions about acceptable offer terms
Cold-calling homeowners to solicit new listings
questions.explanation: Unlicensed assistants may do clerical work such as scheduling, typing, and assembling documents. Showing property, negotiating, and soliciting brokerage business all require a license.
questions.citation: DOS guidelines on unlicensed assistants; NY RPL Article 12-A

questions.q: How may a broker lawfully pay an unlicensed assistant who performs only clerical tasks?
options: A percentage of every commission the office earns each month
A bonus for each listing that sells
An hourly wage or salary not tied to closed transactions
A referral fee for each buyer who closes
questions.explanation: Clerical staff may be paid hourly or by salary for clerical work. Pay tied to completed transactions is compensation for licensed activity and requires a license.
questions.citation: DOS guidelines on unlicensed assistants; NY RPL § 442

questions.q: A broker offers his unlicensed neighbor $1,000 for every buyer the neighbor refers who closes on a home. This arrangement is:
options: Legal if it is disclosed in writing to the buyer before closing
Legal because the neighbor does no negotiating or showing
Legal if it is paid as a personal gift after the closing
An illegal fee split (kickback) with an unlicensed person
questions.explanation: A broker may not share any part of a commission with an unlicensed person for helping bring about a transaction, and a referral fee counts. Disclosing it or calling it a gift does not make it legal.

questions.q: Under DOS regulations, a broker may receive compensation from more than one party in the same transaction only when:
options: The total does not exceed a typical commission
The broker discloses it after the closing
All parties have full knowledge of it and consent
The amount appears on the closing statement
questions.explanation: The broker must make clear which party it is acting for. It may take compensation from more than one party only with the full knowledge and consent of all parties. Disclosure after the fact does not satisfy the rule.

questions.q: While performing licensed real estate activities, a salesperson must:
options: Carry the original license certificate at all times
Carry the DOS-issued pocket card and show it on request
Wear a visible DOS-issued photo badge
Carry a copy of the sponsoring broker's license
questions.explanation: Brokers, associate brokers, and salespersons must carry their DOS pocket card and show it when asked. Carrying the license certificate itself is not what the rule requires.
questions.citation: NY RPL Article 12-A; DOS licensing rules

questions.q: A broker classifies all of her associated salespersons as independent contractors. Which statement is correct?
options: She must still supervise their licensed activity regularly and consistently
Independent contractors need no broker supervision at all under license law
Each salesperson may run advertising without broker approval
The salespersons may accept fees directly from customers
questions.explanation: Tax or employment status does not affect license law. The broker must still provide regular, frequent, and consistent supervision, including of advertising and funds.

questions.q: A salesperson posts an online ad for one of her firm's listings that shows only her name and personal cell number. What is the main problem?
options: It fails to identify the sponsoring brokerage
It must also list the seller's name and phone
Salespersons may never advertise listed property
It must state the commission rate being offered
questions.explanation: Ads must identify the brokerage and be approved by the broker. A personal cell number does not replace the required brokerage identification, and leaving the brokerage out makes it a blind ad.

questions.q: After notice and a hearing, DOS finds that a licensee committed misconduct. Which of these is NOT a sanction DOS can impose administratively?
options: Revocation of the license
Suspension of the license
An administrative fine
Imprisonment of the licensee
questions.explanation: DOS may reprimand, fine, suspend, or revoke a license. Jail can only come from a criminal court, which is a separate proceeding.

questions.q: A salesperson licensed in New Jersey moves to New York and wants to practice. Based on current DOS information, which statement is correct?
options: NJ licensees may practice in NY for one year before needing a NY license
NJ licensees need only complete 22.5 hours of NY CE
DOS reports no current reciprocity agreements, so NY requirements apply
An out-of-state license substitutes for a sponsoring NY broker
questions.explanation: DOS currently reports no reciprocity agreements with other states, so the applicant must meet New York's licensing requirements. Older textbook reciprocity lists are out of date.

questions.q: A salesperson leaves Broker A to join Broker B. Before the change of association is processed, a former client asks her to show a home. She should:
options: Show it under Broker A's name, since she recently worked there
Not perform licensed activity until the new association is complete
Show it under Broker B's name, since the paperwork is pending
Show it on her own, since her license itself has not expired or lapsed
questions.explanation: A salesperson may act only through a sponsoring broker, so no licensed work is allowed in the gap between brokers. A commission she already earned at Broker A is a separate contract issue.
questions.citation: NY RPL Article 12-A; DOS change-of-association rules

questions.q: A salesperson's license expired last month. Which statement is correct?
options: She may keep practicing for 90 days while her renewal is pending
She may keep practicing if her CE hours are already complete
She must retake the state exam before she is allowed to renew
She may not practice until renewed; there is no grace period
questions.explanation: An expired license does not allow any practice. DOS allows renewal within two years after expiration without retaking the exam, but the licensee cannot work until renewed.

questions.q: Which best describes an associate real estate broker?
options: A person qualified as a broker who works under a sponsoring broker
A salesperson with more than two years of experience at one firm
A broker who owns and runs an independent branch of the firm
An unlicensed office manager who supervises the firm's agents
questions.explanation: An associate broker meets the broker qualifications but chooses to work under another broker's supervision and name. The title does not create an independent business.

questions.q: Without being told to by the seller, a seller's agent declines to tell a buyer the lowest price the seller would accept. Which fiduciary duty is the agent fulfilling?
options: Accounting
Obedience
Confidentiality
Reasonable care
questions.explanation: Keeping the client's bargaining position private is confidentiality. Because the seller gave no instruction, obedience is not the duty involved.

questions.q: A listing agent promptly deposits a buyer's earnest money and keeps exact records of it. Which fiduciary duty does this best reflect?
options: Accounting
Loyalty
Disclosure
Obedience
questions.explanation: Accounting means safeguarding, recording, and accounting for money and property entrusted to the agent. Mishandling deposits violates both this duty and the escrow rules.

questions.q: A seller tells her listing agent not to show the house to any family with children. The agent should:
options: Comply, because the duty of obedience is owed to the seller
Comply, but only if the seller puts the instruction in writing
Comply, because the seller may choose who enters her own home
Refuse, because obedience covers only lawful instructions
questions.explanation: Obedience applies only to lawful instructions. Excluding families with children is familial-status discrimination, so the agent must refuse.
questions.citation: Federal Fair Housing Act, 42 U.S.C. § 3604; NY Executive Law § 296

questions.q: A seller's agent is working with an unrepresented buyer (a customer). What does the agent owe that buyer?
options: Undivided loyalty and confidentiality of the buyer's position
Honest, fair dealing and disclosure of known material facts
The same full fiduciary duties owed to the seller
Only the information the seller authorizes
questions.explanation: Fiduciary duties go to the client (the seller). A customer is still owed honesty, fair dealing, and disclosure of known facts that materially affect the property's value or desirability.

questions.q: A seller tells his agent to keep quiet about a known basement leak that floods every spring. A buyer customer asks whether there are water problems. The agent should:
options: Disclose the leak; confidentiality never covers hiding known defects
Stay silent, because the duty of confidentiality is owed to the seller
Say there are no problems, since the buyer is only a customer, not a client
Refer the buyer to the seller's attorney and say nothing further
questions.explanation: Confidentiality protects the client's bargaining position. It never allows hiding a known material defect or making a false statement. An instruction to conceal is unlawful and must be refused.

questions.q: A buyer's agent will be paid through a split of the listing broker's fee, which comes from the seller's proceeds. Whom does the buyer's agent represent?
options: The seller, because the seller's proceeds fund the commission
Both parties, as an automatic dual agent sharing one fee
The buyer, because who pays does not decide who is represented
Neither party, acting only as a neutral transaction facilitator
questions.explanation: Representation depends on the agency relationship, not on who pays. Sharing a commission does not, by itself, create agency with the seller.

questions.q: A buyer signs the acknowledgment on the New York agency disclosure form. By doing so, the buyer has:
options: Entered a binding buyer-agency agreement with the broker
Acknowledged receiving the disclosure, not hired the broker
Agreed to pay the broker's commission if a purchase closes
Automatically consented to any dual agency that may arise
questions.explanation: The form states 'THIS IS NOT A CONTRACT.' Signing confirms only that the buyer received it. A representation agreement is a separate document.

questions.q: When must a listing agent give the agency disclosure form to the seller of a single-family home?
options: At the first open house held for the property
When the first written offer arrives from a buyer
At or before the closing, with the other documents
Before entering into the listing agreement
questions.explanation: A seller's agent must give the seller the disclosure before the listing agreement is signed. A buyer's agent must give it to the buyer before a buyer-agency agreement.

questions.q: A seller's agent meets a prospective buyer at an open house and starts discussing the buyer's budget and housing needs. When must the agent give this buyer the disclosure form?
options: Before the buyer makes a written offer
Only if the buyer asks for it
After the buyer signs a purchase contract
At this first substantive contact
questions.explanation: The disclosure goes to the other party at the first substantive contact. A casual greeting doesn't count, but discussing the buyer's finances and needs does.

questions.q: Which transaction is NOT covered by the RPL § 443 agency disclosure requirement?
options: Sale of an owner-occupied two-family house
Sale of a vacant, unimproved building lot
Sale of a condominium unit in a high-rise
Sale of a cooperative apartment's shares
questions.explanation: Section 443 covers 1-4 family residential property and condo/co-op units. It does not cover unimproved land. The agent's general agency and honesty duties still apply.

questions.q: A licensee is helping a landlord rent out a residential apartment. Which agency disclosure form applies?
options: DOS-1736, the buyer and seller disclosure form
DOS-2156, the fair housing notice
DOS-1735, the landlord and tenant disclosure form
The Property Condition Disclosure Statement
questions.explanation: DOS-1735 covers landlord/tenant relationships and DOS-1736 covers buyers and sellers. The fair housing notice and the PCDS are separate documents and do not replace the agency disclosure.

questions.q: A buyer refuses to sign the acknowledgment on the agency disclosure form. The licensee should:
options: Make a written declaration of the refusal and keep it at least three years
Stop working with the buyer, since the form must be signed to proceed
Tell the broker verbally about the refusal; no written record is needed
Sign the buyer's name with the buyer's verbal permission and continue
questions.explanation: A refusal does not cancel the disclosure duty. The licensee prepares a written declaration of the facts (under oath or affirmation) and keeps it, like signed acknowledgments, for at least three years.

questions.q: A New York broker may act as a dual agent in a sale only if:
options: The broker tells the buyer about the dual role orally
Both the buyer and the seller give informed written consent
The seller consents, since the seller pays the commission
Both clients are handled within the broker's own office
questions.explanation: Dual agency requires informed consent in writing from both principals. Each side gives up the right to undivided loyalty, so oral or one-sided consent is not enough.

questions.q: Can a buyer or seller consent to dual agency before a specific dual-agency situation arises?
options: No, consent is valid only after a specific property is chosen
No, dual agency is prohibited in New York sales
Yes, but only by telling the broker orally
Yes, advance informed consent can be given on the disclosure form
questions.explanation: The DOS form has checkboxes for advance informed consent to dual agency, with or without designated sales agents. The agent should still explain the arrangement when it actually happens.

questions.q: With informed written consent, a dual-agent broker designates Salesperson A for the buyer and Salesperson B for the seller. Which statement is correct?
options: The broker remains a dual agent; neither designee gives undivided loyalty
The broker stops being a dual agent once the sales agents are designated
Each designated agent gives full undivided loyalty to his or her client
The designated agents must be associated with different brokerages
questions.explanation: Designated sales agents advocate for their assigned clients, but the broker is still a dual agent. The NY form says designated agents cannot provide undivided loyalty. Some other states treat this differently, but New York does not.

questions.q: Salesperson Kim of ABC Realty has a buyer-agency agreement with Lee. Lee wants to buy a house listed by another ABC Realty salesperson. What is ABC Realty's position?
options: There is no conflict, because different salespersons handle each side
Kim may continue as Lee's agent with no further consent
ABC would be a dual agent and needs both parties' informed written consent
The listing salesperson automatically becomes Lee's agent
questions.explanation: The agency relationship is with the brokerage, not the individual salesperson. A firm representing both sides is a dual agent no matter which associates handle each side, so written informed consent is required.

questions.q: Without either party's written consent, a listing salesperson secretly advises the buyer on how low to offer. Which statement is correct?
options: It is allowed if the seller ends up accepting the buyer's offer anyway
It is allowed because the buyer is only a customer, not a client
It is undisclosed dual agency, which a successful closing does not cure
It is designated agency, which requires no written consent from either party
questions.explanation: Acting for both sides without informed written consent is undisclosed dual agency and a breach of loyalty to the seller. It can lead to DOS discipline and loss of the commission even if the sale closes.

questions.q: A listing agent engages a broker's agent from a different firm to help find a buyer. If the broker's agent misrepresents the property, who has liability for the broker's agent's acts, according to the NY disclosure form?
options: The listing agent who directs the broker's agent
The seller, because the broker's agent works for the seller
The buyer, because the buyer relied on the statement
No one, because broker's agents owe no duties
questions.explanation: The form says the seller cannot direct a broker's agent and has no vicarious liability for its acts. The listing agent who engages and directs the broker's agent carries that liability.

questions.q: How does a seller's subagent differ from a broker's agent?
options: A subagent represents the buyer; a broker's agent represents the seller
Only a subagent's acts can make the seller vicariously liable
A subagent must belong to the listing firm; a broker's agent need not
They are the same role, described under two interchangeable names
questions.explanation: A subagent is the seller's agent through the listing broker, so the seller can be vicariously liable for its acts. A broker's agent answers to the engaging agent, and the seller has no vicarious liability for it.

questions.q: Which event terminates a listing agency relationship by operation of law?
options: The listing being entered into the MLS
A buyer's agent showing the property
The seller hiring an attorney for closing
The death of the seller-principal
questions.explanation: Death or incapacity of the principal (or destruction of the property) ends the agency by operation of law. The other events are ordinary parts of a transaction.

questions.q: A listing expires without a sale. A buyer then asks the former listing agent what the seller's bottom-line price was. The agent should:
options: Disclose it, since all agency duties ended with the listing
Keep it confidential, because that duty survives the agency's end
Disclose it only if the buyer signs a buyer-agency agreement
Disclose it if the seller has not relisted the property
questions.explanation: Confidentiality continues after the agency ends. The former agent may not use or reveal the ex-client's confidential bargaining information.

questions.q: A seller's agent helps an unrepresented buyer fill in an offer form and describes the home's features. Does this, by itself, make the agent the buyer's agent?
options: Yes; helping fill in the offer form creates buyer agency
Yes; the agent automatically becomes a dual agent at that point
No; helping a customer does not by itself create buyer agency
No; but the agent must stop assisting the buyer immediately
questions.explanation: A seller's agent may give an unrepresented buyer factual help and stay the seller's agent. To avoid accidentally creating agency, the agent should explain their role and not coach the buyer's negotiating strategy.

questions.q: Which New York deed gives the grantee the greatest protection, containing covenants of seisin, quiet enjoyment, against encumbrances, further assurances, and warranty of title?
options: Full covenant and warranty deed
Bargain and sale deed with covenant against grantor's acts
Quitclaim deed
Referee's deed
questions.explanation: The full covenant and warranty deed carries all five statutory covenants and is the strongest deed for a grantee. A bargain and sale deed with covenants only promises the grantor did nothing to encumber the property.

questions.q: In a typical New York residential sale, the seller's deed states only that the grantor has not done anything to encumber the property. Which deed is this?
options: Full covenant and warranty deed
Bargain and sale deed without covenant against grantor's acts
Bargain and sale deed with covenant against grantor's acts
Quitclaim deed
questions.explanation: The bargain and sale deed with covenant against grantor's acts implies the grantor holds title and promises only that the grantor has not encumbered it. It is the deed most commonly used in NY residential closings, but it gives no warranty against defects created by earlier owners.

questions.q: A title search shows a former owner's nephew may have a claim to a parcel. To clear the cloud, the nephew is asked to sign a deed giving up whatever interest he may have, with no warranties at all. Which deed fits?
options: Full covenant and warranty deed
Quitclaim deed
Executor's deed
Bargain and sale deed with covenants
questions.explanation: A quitclaim conveys only whatever interest the grantor actually has, if any, and makes no promises about title. That is why it is used to remove clouds on title; it does not guarantee clear title.

questions.q: After a court-ordered mortgage foreclosure sale, the deed to the successful bidder is signed by an officer appointed by the court. What type of deed is it?
options: Executor's deed
Quitclaim deed
Full covenant and warranty deed
Referee's deed
questions.explanation: In NY, foreclosure and partition sales are conducted by a court-appointed referee, who conveys by a referee's deed. The referee does not personally warrant title.

questions.q: A homeowner dies leaving a will that names her brother to settle the estate. The brother sells the house to a buyer. What type of deed will he most likely use?
options: Executor's deed
Referee's deed
Administrator's quitclaim deed
Full covenant and warranty deed
questions.explanation: The person named in a will to handle the estate is the executor, who conveys estate real property by an executor's deed. An administrator is appointed by the court only when there is no will (or no executor able to serve).
questions.citation: NY RPL § 258 (statutory forms of deeds); NY EPTL

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT required for a deed to be valid in New York?
options: The grantor's signature
An adequate legal description
The grantee's signature
Delivery and acceptance
questions.explanation: A conveyance of real property must be in writing and subscribed by the grantor; the grantee normally does not sign. The grantee must, however, accept the delivered deed.

questions.q: A seller signs and delivers a deed to a buyer, but the deed is never acknowledged before a notary. What is its status?
options: Void, because acknowledgment is required for a deed to be valid
Valid between the parties, but it cannot be recorded until acknowledged
Valid and fully recordable as it stands, without any acknowledgment
Voidable at the option of the grantee only, until it is notarized
questions.explanation: Acknowledgment is a requirement for recording, not for validity. An unacknowledged deed can transfer title between the parties but cannot be recorded, so it gives no constructive notice.

questions.q: A mother signs a deed conveying her house to her son, then locks it in her own safe-deposit box and keeps the only key. The son finds the deed after her death. When did title pass to the son?
options: At the moment the mother signed and dated the deed
Automatically at the moment of the mother's death
When the son recorded the deed in the county clerk's office after finding it
Never through that deed, because it was never delivered
questions.explanation: A deed transfers title only when it is delivered with present intent to pass title and accepted. Signing and keeping control of the deed is not delivery, and recording cannot cure a failure of delivery.
questions.citation: Common-law delivery and acceptance requirement; NY RPL Article 8

questions.q: What is the main legal effect of recording a deed with the county clerk?
options: It gives constructive notice of the grantee's interest to the world
It makes an otherwise invalid or undelivered deed valid
It is the legal act that transfers title to the grantee
It guarantees that the title is free of all defects, liens, and claims
questions.explanation: Recording protects the grantee by giving constructive notice to later purchasers and lenders. Title passes on delivery and acceptance; recording does not validate a defective deed or guarantee title.

questions.q: An owner sells a lot to Ana, who does not record. The owner then sells the same lot to Ben, who pays value, knows nothing of Ana's deed, and records first. Who prevails under New York's recording act?
options: Ana, because her deed was delivered and accepted first
Ana and Ben, who become tenants in common of the lot
Ben, as a good-faith purchaser for value who recorded first
Ana, because a deed is valid between parties without recording
questions.explanation: NY is a race-notice state: an unrecorded conveyance is void against a later good-faith purchaser for value whose deed is recorded first. Ana's remedy is against the seller.

questions.q: Under New York's recording act, a later buyer who records first will NOT defeat an earlier unrecorded deed if the later buyer:
options: Financed the purchase with a mortgage
Knew of the earlier conveyance when buying
Received a bargain and sale deed
Closed without ordering a survey of the parcel
questions.explanation: Recording-act protection goes only to purchasers in good faith for value. A buyer with actual knowledge of the prior deed is not in good faith, even if that buyer records first.

questions.q: A buyer finances a purchase and the lender requires a lender's (mortgagee's) title policy. Which statement is accurate?
options: The lender's policy protects both the lender and the buyer for the full price
Every lender requires the buyer to also purchase a separate owner's policy
The owner's policy must be renewed and repaid each year to stay in force
The lender's policy protects only the lender; an owner's policy protects the buyer
questions.explanation: A lender's policy insures the lender's lien, and its coverage generally declines as the loan is paid down. An owner's policy is optional, is paid once at closing, and protects the owner (and heirs) for as long as they hold title.

questions.q: A standard owner's title policy issued without a survey reading would most likely exclude coverage for:
options: An encroachment that an accurate survey would have revealed
A forged deed from an earlier owner in the chain of title
A recorded judgment lien that the title searcher missed
A deed signed years ago by a prior owner who was a minor
questions.explanation: Title insurance covers specified title risks such as forgery, missed recorded liens, and incapacity of prior grantors. Survey matters like encroachments are standard exceptions unless a survey is provided and the exception is removed.

questions.q: A condensed history summarizing every recorded deed, mortgage, lien, and other instrument affecting a parcel is called:
options: The chain of title
A certificate of occupancy
An abstract of title
A title insurance policy
questions.explanation: An abstract of title is a summary of all recorded documents affecting the property. The chain of title is narrower: the sequence of ownership transfers from owner to owner. Distinguish the two.

questions.q: A title search shows a recorded deed from Adams to Baker and a recorded deed from Cole to Diaz, but no recorded deed from Baker to Cole. This is best described as:
options: An encroachment revealed by the public record of the deeds
A gap in the chain of title that must be cured before closing
A lis pendens that has been filed against the property
A normal record that requires no further action by the buyer
questions.explanation: A missing link between owners is a gap (break) in the chain of title. It is typically cured by obtaining and recording the missing deed, a quitclaim, or a court action to quiet title.
questions.citation: NY RPAPL Article 15 (action to determine claims to real property)

questions.q: A legal description begins at a fixed point, runs along stated directions and distances, and must return to that same starting point. Which method is this?
options: Rectangular (government) survey
Lot and block
Street address
Metes and bounds
questions.explanation: Metes and bounds describes boundaries by courses and distances from a point of beginning and must close back at that point. It is widely used in New York, often along with tax map or lot-and-block references.
questions.citation: NYS DOS Real Estate Salesperson 77-hr syllabus (legal descriptions)

questions.q: Which method of legal description is NOT used for land in New York?
options: The rectangular (government) survey system
Metes and bounds
Lot and block on a filed subdivision map
Tax map section, block, and lot
questions.explanation: The rectangular survey system of townships and sections is used in federal public-land states, not in New York. NY relies on metes and bounds and on references to filed maps and tax maps.
questions.citation: NYS DOS Real Estate Salesperson 77-hr syllabus (legal descriptions)

questions.q: For how long must a claimant's possession continue before title may be acquired by adverse possession in New York?
options: 5 years
15 years
10 years
20 years
questions.explanation: NY requires actual, open and notorious, exclusive, continuous, and hostile possession under a claim of right for 10 years. Long use alone is not enough; every element must be proven.

questions.q: For 12 years, a neighbor's hedge and a small fence have stood 18 inches over the boundary line. Can the neighbor claim that strip by adverse possession in New York?
options: Yes, because the 10-year statutory period has already run
No; fences and hedges are de minimis encroachments deemed permissive
Yes, but only after the neighbor records a notice of the adverse claim
No, because adverse possession in New York requires 20 years
questions.explanation: Since 2008, NY law treats de minimis non-structural encroachments such as fences, hedges, and shrubbery as permissive and not adverse. Simply passing the 10-year mark does not create title.

questions.q: Which of the following is an example of voluntary alienation of real property?
options: The state takes the land for a highway through eminent domain
A lender forecloses after the owner defaults
Land passes to the state by escheat
An owner deeds her house to her daughter as a gift
questions.explanation: Voluntary alienation is a transfer the owner chooses, such as by deed or will. Eminent domain, foreclosure, escheat, and adverse possession are involuntary transfers.
questions.citation: NYS DOS Real Estate Salesperson 77-hr syllabus (voluntary and involuntary alienation)

questions.q: In a will, a gift of real property is called a:
options: Devise
Bequest
Legacy
Codicil
questions.explanation: A devise is a gift of real property by will, made to a devisee. A bequest or legacy is a gift of personal property, and a codicil is an amendment to a will.
questions.citation: NY Estates, Powers and Trusts Law (EPTL) — wills

questions.q: A New York resident dies intestate, survived by a spouse and two children. How is the estate distributed?
options: The spouse receives the entire estate; the children receive nothing
The children share the entire estate equally; the spouse takes nothing
Spouse receives $50,000 plus half the balance; the children share the rest
The spouse and each of the two children receive one-third of the estate
questions.explanation: Under NY intestacy rules, a surviving spouse with issue takes $50,000 plus one-half of the residue, and the issue take the remainder. The spouse takes everything only when there are no surviving issue.

questions.q: Which of the following is a freehold estate?
options: Life estate
Estate for years
Periodic tenancy
Tenancy at sufferance
questions.explanation: Freehold estates (fee simple and life estates) are ownership interests of indefinite duration. Estates for years, periodic tenancies, tenancies at will, and tenancies at sufferance are leasehold (less-than-freehold) estates.

questions.q: A deed conveys land "to the Town of Clifton so long as the land is used as a public park." If the town stops using it as a park, what happens?
options: The grantor must first sue to exercise a right of re-entry
The town keeps title, because use conditions in deeds are void
Title automatically returns to the grantor (possibility of reverter)
The town's interest converts into a leasehold held from the grantor
questions.explanation: Words of duration such as "so long as" or "while" create a fee simple determinable, which ends automatically when the condition is broken. A fee on condition subsequent ("but if") requires the grantor to act.

questions.q: A deed conveys a lot to a buyer "but if alcohol is ever sold on the premises, the grantor may re-enter and reclaim the property." Alcohol is later sold. What is the result?
options: Title reverts to the grantor automatically on the sale
The buyer keeps title until the grantor acts to reclaim it
The deed is void from the date it was delivered
The buyer's estate becomes a leasehold estate
questions.explanation: "But if" or "provided that" language creates a fee simple on condition subsequent. Breach gives the grantor a right of re-entry (reacquisition), but the estate does not end until the grantor exercises it.

questions.q: An owner deeds a house "to Beth for life, then to Carlos." What interest does Carlos hold while Beth is alive?
options: A reversion
A life estate pur autre vie
A leasehold estate
A remainder
questions.explanation: A future interest held by a third party who takes when the life estate ends is a remainder (Carlos is the remainderman). If the property were to return to the original grantor instead, the grantor's interest would be a reversion.

questions.q: An owner deeds land "to Dana for the life of Eli." Dana dies while Eli is still living. What happens to the estate?
options: It passes to Dana's heirs or devisees until Eli dies
It ends immediately at Dana's death, since Dana was the holder
It reverts to the grantor at the moment of Dana's death
It becomes a fee simple absolute owned by Dana's heirs
questions.explanation: A life estate pur autre vie is measured by the life of someone other than the holder (here Eli). It continues for Eli's lifetime, so it passes to Dana's estate if Dana dies first.

questions.q: A residential tenant's one-year lease expired, and the tenant remains in possession without the landlord's consent. This tenant has a:
options: Tenancy at will
Periodic (month-to-month) tenancy
Tenancy at sufferance
Estate for years
questions.explanation: A tenancy at sufferance is a holdover after a lawful tenancy ends, without the landlord's consent; it is not a new agreed lease. A tenancy at will exists with the landlord's permission. Self-help eviction is still prohibited.

questions.q: Which of the following is a general lien?
options: A mortgage
A docketed money judgment
A mechanic's lien
A real property tax lien
questions.explanation: A general lien attaches to all of the debtor's property within its reach, such as a judgment lien on all real property in the county. Mortgages, mechanic's liens, and property tax liens are specific liens on one parcel.

questions.q: A creditor wins a money judgment and dockets it with the clerk of the county where the debtor owns two houses. What is the effect?
options: It is a lien only on the specific property named in the lawsuit
It is a lien on the debtor's personal property, but not on real estate
It attaches to a house only when the debtor later tries to sell it
It is a lien on his real property in that county, generally for 10 years
questions.explanation: A docketed judgment is a general lien on the debtor's real property in that county, generally for 10 years. It is involuntary and is not limited to a single parcel.

questions.q: A property has a mortgage recorded in 2019, a judgment lien docketed in 2021, and unpaid 2026 real property taxes. Which lien generally has first priority?
options: The real property tax lien
The mortgage, because it was recorded first
The judgment lien, because it is a general lien
They share equally, in proportion to their amounts
questions.explanation: Real property tax and special assessment liens generally take priority over other liens regardless of when those were recorded. "First recorded wins" does not override tax-lien priority.
questions.citation: NY Real Property Tax Law (tax lien priority)

questions.q: A contractor finishes a kitchen renovation on an owner-occupied single-family house on March 1. Under the NY Lien Law, the notice of mechanic's lien must be filed within:
options: 8 months after completion of the work
30 days after completion of the work
4 months after completion of the work
1 year after completion of the work
questions.explanation: For a single-family dwelling, a mechanic's lien must be filed within 4 months after the work is completed or the materials are last furnished. The 8-month period applies to other property.

questions.q: A supplier last delivered materials to an office building renovation on January 10. Under the NY Lien Law, the deadline to file a mechanic's lien is generally:
options: 4 months after the final furnishing of materials
8 months after the final furnishing of materials
90 days after the final furnishing of materials
2 years after the final furnishing of materials
questions.explanation: For property other than a single-family dwelling, a mechanic's lien must be filed within 8 months after the final performance of work or final furnishing of materials. The 4-month period is only for single-family dwellings.

questions.q: A buyer's title search reveals a notice of pendency (lis pendens) filed against the property. What does it mean?
options: A final judgment of foreclosure has already been entered against it
The property has unpaid real estate taxes that are now a lien
A neighbor holds a recorded easement over part of the lot
A lawsuit affecting title to or possession of the property is pending
questions.explanation: A notice of pendency warns that litigation affecting the property is pending. Anyone who later acquires an interest takes subject to the outcome. It is a cloud on title, not a judgment or a tax lien.

questions.q: The owner of a rear lot has a recorded right-of-way over the driveway on the front lot. The front lot is sold. What happens to the right-of-way?
options: It continues, and the new owner of the front lot takes subject to it
It ends, because easements are personal to the original parties
It continues only if the new owner signs a new easement agreement
It converts into a revocable license held by the rear owner
questions.explanation: This is an easement appurtenant: the rear lot is the dominant tenement and the front lot is the servient tenement. Appurtenant easements run with the land when either parcel is sold.
questions.citation: NY common law of easements; NY RPL § 291 (recording)

questions.q: An electric utility holds the right to run power lines across a farm. The utility owns no adjoining land. This right is best described as:
options: An easement appurtenant
An easement by necessity
An easement in gross
A license
questions.explanation: An easement in gross benefits a person or entity rather than a neighboring parcel, so there is no dominant tenement. Commercial easements in gross, like utility easements, are interests in land, unlike a revocable license.
questions.citation: NYS DOS Real Estate Salesperson 77-hr syllabus (easements)

questions.q: An owner sells the back half of his land, leaving the buyer's parcel with no access to any public road except across the seller's remaining land. What right does the law give the buyer?
options: An easement in gross
An easement by necessity
A license coupled with an interest
An encroachment
questions.explanation: When a parcel is landlocked as a result of dividing commonly owned land, the law implies an easement by necessity across the grantor's remaining land. It lasts as long as the necessity exists.

questions.q: For 11 years, a neighbor has openly and continuously used a path across your land, without permission and without any claim from you. What has the neighbor most likely acquired?
options: Title to the path by adverse possession
A license that you may revoke at any time
An easement in gross
An easement by prescription
questions.explanation: Open, notorious, continuous, and hostile use for 10 years in NY creates a prescriptive easement, which is a right of use, not ownership. Adverse possession requires exclusive possession and transfers title.
questions.citation: NY common law of prescriptive easements (10-year period, CPLR § 212(a))

questions.q: A homeowner verbally tells her neighbor he may fish in her pond whenever he likes. Which statement is true?
options: It is a revocable personal permission, not an interest in land
It is an oral easement appurtenant that runs with the land
It becomes a permanent easement after one year of regular use
It is an easement in gross that the neighbor may sell to others
questions.explanation: A license is personal permission to do something on another's land; it is not an interest in real property. It can generally be revoked and ends on the death of either party or the sale of the land.
questions.citation: NYS DOS Real Estate Salesperson 77-hr syllabus (licenses)

questions.q: A survey shows that a neighbor's garage extends two feet onto the buyer's lot. This is an example of:
options: An easement appurtenant
A license
An encroachment
A lis pendens
questions.explanation: An encroachment is an unauthorized intrusion of an improvement onto another's land. It is typically revealed by a survey, not a title search, and it is a common standard exception in title policies.
questions.citation: NYS DOS Real Estate Salesperson 77-hr syllabus (encroachments)

questions.q: Local zoning allows two-family houses, but a recorded deed restriction limits a lot to one single-family house. What may the owner build?
options: A two-family house, because zoning overrides private restrictions
Only a single-family house, because the stricter restriction applies
A two-family house, if the owner obtains a building permit
Anything allowed by zoning once the deed is 10 years old
questions.explanation: Private deed restrictions and public zoning both apply, so the owner must satisfy whichever is more restrictive. A building permit does not override a valid private restriction.
questions.citation: NYS DOS Real Estate Salesperson 77-hr syllabus (deed restrictions and zoning)

questions.q: In the MARIA test for whether an item is a fixture, the letters stand for:
options: Market value, Age, Removability, Insurability, Appraisal method
Method of payment, Assessment, Rights, Inspection, Agreement
Material used, Attachment, Reasonableness, Improvement, Agreement
Method of annexation, Adaptability, Relationship, Intention, Agreement
questions.explanation: Fixture analysis considers how the item is attached, whether it is adapted to the property, the relationship of the parties, their intention, and any agreement. A specific written agreement or exclusion carries great weight.
questions.citation: NYS DOS Real Estate Salesperson 77-hr syllabus (fixtures)

questions.q: A seller installed custom-fitted built-in bookcases and a dining room chandelier. The contract of sale is silent about them. At closing they:
options: Pass to the buyer as fixtures, since the contract does not exclude them
Remain the seller's personal property, which the seller may remove
Pass to the buyer only if they were listed in the property advertisement
May be removed by the seller if they were paid for separately
questions.explanation: Items permanently attached or adapted to the property are presumed fixtures that pass with the real property. A seller who wants to keep one should exclude it in the written contract before signing.
questions.citation: NYS DOS Real Estate Salesperson 77-hr syllabus (fixtures)

questions.q: A restaurant tenant bolted commercial ovens to the floor for its business. What are the tenant's rights at the end of the lease?
options: They became the landlord's property when they were bolted down
It may remove them at any time, even years after the lease ends
It may remove them before the lease ends, repairing damage from removal
They must stay unless the landlord pays the tenant for them
questions.explanation: Trade fixtures installed by a commercial tenant for its business remain the tenant's personal property and may be removed by the end of the lease, with any damage repaired. Items left behind may become the landlord's property by accession.
questions.citation: NYS DOS Real Estate Salesperson 77-hr syllabus (trade fixtures)

questions.q: Under New York's statute of frauds, which agreement must be in writing and signed by the party to be charged to be enforceable?
options: A lease of an apartment for six months
An agreement for a salesperson to show a home on Saturday
A contract for the sale of a single-family house
A month-to-month rental of a garage space
questions.explanation: GOL § 5-703 requires contracts for the sale of real property (and leases longer than one year) to be in a writing subscribed by the party to be charged. Leases of one year or less, like a six-month or month-to-month rental, may be oral.

questions.q: Before the tenant moves in, a landlord and tenant orally agree to a two-year lease of a store. The landlord then refuses to honor it. The oral lease is best described as:
options: Unenforceable, because a lease for more than one year must be in writing
Void, because a lease can never be created orally
Fully enforceable, because both parties clearly agreed to it
Voidable only at the tenant's option because the tenant relied on it
questions.explanation: A lease for more than one year falls within the statute of frauds, so this oral two-year lease cannot be enforced in court. Trap: it is unenforceable, not void — oral leases of one year or less are perfectly valid.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT an essential element of a valid real estate contract?
options: Competent parties who have legal capacity to contract
Consideration exchanged between the buyer and seller
A lawful object or purpose for the agreement
Recording in the county clerk's office
questions.explanation: A valid contract needs competent parties, mutual assent (offer and acceptance), consideration, and a lawful object, and a real estate sale contract must also be in writing. Recording gives constructive notice to the public; it is not required for the contract to be valid between the parties.
questions.citation: General contract law; NY GOL § 5-703; NY RPL § 291 (recording)

questions.q: A 17-year-old signs a contract to buy a vacant lot from an adult seller. The contract is:
options: Void from the start because minors cannot sign contracts
Voidable at the minor's option
Voidable at the seller's option only
Valid and binding on both parties because both signed
questions.explanation: In New York a person under 18 is a minor (infant). A minor's contract is generally voidable by the minor, who may disaffirm it, while the adult remains bound if the minor chooses to go through with it. Trap: voidable, not void.

questions.q: Two parties sign a contract whose stated purpose is to sell a building to be used for an illegal gambling operation. The contract is:
options: Void, because it lacks a lawful object
Voidable at the buyer's option
Valid but unenforceable until the buyer obtains a license
Valid, because transferring real property is itself legal
questions.explanation: A contract for an illegal purpose lacks the essential element of a lawful object, so it is void — it has no legal effect, and neither party can enforce it. Voidable contracts (such as those induced by fraud or a minor's contract) are valid until one party disaffirms.

questions.q: A buyer and a seller sign a written purchase contract in which the buyer promises to pay $410,000 and the seller promises to convey title. This contract is best described as:
options: Implied and unilateral
Express and unilateral
Express and bilateral
Implied and bilateral
questions.explanation: It is express because the terms are stated in words (written or oral), and bilateral because each side exchanges a promise for a promise. An implied contract arises from conduct, and a unilateral contract is a promise given in exchange for an act.

questions.q: A seller tells area brokers she will pay a $5,000 bonus to whichever cooperating agent first brings a buyer who closes. No agent promises to do anything. This arrangement is best described as:
options: A bilateral contract binding on every broker who hears it
An executed contract as soon as it is announced
A void contract for lack of any consideration
A unilateral contract, accepted only by performance
questions.explanation: A unilateral contract is a promise in exchange for an act: only the seller is bound, and an agent accepts by actually producing the buyer who closes. No agent is obligated to try, which is why it is not bilateral.

questions.q: A purchase contract has been signed by both buyer and seller, and the closing is scheduled for next month. Right now the contract is:
options: Executed, because both parties have signed it
Executory, because performance is still to come
Unilateral, because only the seller still has to act
Implied, because the closing terms are still pending
questions.explanation: An executory contract has obligations still to be performed; it becomes executed only when both sides have fully performed (here, at closing). Trap: 'executed' does not mean 'signed.'

questions.q: A buyer offers $500,000. The seller replies, 'I'll take $520,000.' The buyer declines. The next day the seller says, 'Fine, I accept your $500,000 offer.' What is the legal status?
options: No contract yet; the seller's statement is only a new offer the buyer may accept or reject
A binding contract at $500,000, because the seller accepted the buyer's exact original terms
A binding contract at $520,000, because that was the last price either party stated
A binding contract at $500,000, but the buyer may cancel within three days of the acceptance
questions.explanation: A counteroffer is a rejection of the original offer and terminates it. The buyer's $500,000 offer no longer exists to be accepted, so the seller's later 'acceptance' is only a new offer that the buyer is free to accept or reject.

questions.q: A buyer hands a salesperson a $20,000 earnest money check payable to the brokerage. What should the salesperson do?
options: Deposit it in the salesperson's own personal account and hold it there until closing
Keep it safely in a locked desk drawer at the office until the closing date is near
Promptly turn it over to the supervising broker for deposit in a separate escrow account
Give it directly to the seller, since the earnest money belongs to the seller once signed
questions.explanation: A salesperson must promptly turn over funds belonging to others to the supervising broker, who must keep them in a separate special (escrow) account. Mixing client money with personal or business money is commingling, and using it is conversion — both are prohibited.

questions.q: A buyer signs a binding purchase contract with no remaining contingencies, then changes her mind and refuses to close. She demands her earnest money back. Generally:
options: She is automatically entitled to a full refund because the deal never actually closed
The broker must refund it to her within 30 days, as required by the license law
The broker may keep the full deposit as its earned commission on the failed sale
No automatic refund; the contract's default terms decide who gets the deposit
questions.explanation: An earnest-money refund is not automatic just because the buyer changes her mind. Once contingencies are satisfied or have expired, the contract's default and liquidated damages terms decide who gets the deposit. The broker holds it in trust and cannot simply keep it as a commission.

questions.q: A contract's mortgage contingency gives the buyer until June 1 to get a loan commitment. The buyer applies promptly and in good faith but is denied, and gives the seller written notice on May 25 as the contract requires. The buyer most likely may:
options: Be forced to close with cash because loan denial is the buyer's risk
Cancel the contract and recover the deposit under the contingency
Cancel only if the seller agrees to waive the deadline
Keep the contract alive indefinitely until some loan is approved
questions.explanation: A mortgage contingency lets a buyer who makes a good-faith application and is denied cancel and get the deposit back, as long as the buyer follows the clause's notice and deadline terms. Missing the deadline or not applying in good faith can lose that protection.

questions.q: An upstate contract filled out by a salesperson has an attorney approval clause with a three-business-day review period. Neither party's attorney sends written disapproval within the period. What is the result?
options: The contingency is deemed waived and the contract is binding
The contract automatically terminates for lack of approval
The salesperson's broker must approve the contract instead
The parties automatically get 30 more days to obtain approval
questions.explanation: A standard attorney approval clause says the contingency is deemed waived unless an attorney sends written disapproval by the deadline. The clause lets licensees fill in a form contract without engaging in the unauthorized practice of law, while still giving each side's attorney a chance to review it.
questions.citation: NY Judiciary Law § 478 (unauthorized practice of law); standard attorney-approval clause

questions.q: A contract says that if the buyer defaults, the seller may keep the buyer's 10% down payment as the seller's sole remedy. This provision is a(n):
options: Specific performance clause
Rescission clause
Liquidated damages clause
Acceleration clause
questions.explanation: Liquidated damages are an amount the parties agree to in advance as compensation for a breach — often the earnest money. Specific performance forces completion of the sale, rescission cancels the contract and restores both parties, and acceleration is a mortgage clause.

questions.q: A seller signs a valid sale contract, then refuses to close because she got a higher offer. The buyer wants the property itself, not money. The buyer should sue for:
options: Liquidated damages
Rescission
A deficiency judgment
Specific performance
questions.explanation: Specific performance is an equitable remedy in which a court orders the breaching party to perform. Courts grant it in real estate cases because every parcel is unique. Rescission would cancel the deal, which is the opposite of what this buyer wants.

questions.q: After signing, a buyer discovers the seller knowingly lied about the house being connected to public sewer. The buyer wants to cancel and put both parties back where they were before the contract, including return of the deposit. This remedy is:
options: Specific performance
Rescission
Novation
Liquidated damages
questions.explanation: Fraud or misrepresentation makes a contract voidable by the injured party, who may seek rescission: the contract is canceled and each party is restored to its pre-contract position. Novation substitutes a new contract or party; it does not unwind the deal.

questions.q: Under an exclusive right to sell listing, the owner finds a buyer on her own (a coworker) and sells during the listing term without the broker's help. The broker is:
options: Entitled to the commission, because the broker is paid no matter who sells
Not entitled to anything, because the owner found the buyer herself
Entitled to half the commission by law
Entitled only to reimbursement of advertising costs
questions.explanation: Under an exclusive right to sell, the listing broker earns the agreed commission if the property sells during the term, no matter who finds the buyer — including the owner. That is the key difference from an exclusive agency listing.

questions.q: Which statement correctly distinguishes an exclusive agency listing from an exclusive right to sell listing?
options: Under exclusive agency, the broker is paid even if the owner sells on her own
Exclusive agency lets the owner list with several brokers at the same time
Exclusive agency must be oral, while exclusive right to sell must be written
Under exclusive agency, the owner owes no commission if she finds the buyer herself
questions.explanation: Exclusive agency names one broker but reserves the owner's right to sell on her own without owing a commission; under exclusive right to sell, the broker is paid regardless. Listing with several brokers at once is an open listing. NY regulations require exclusive listing agreements to include an explanation of this difference.

questions.q: An owner gives open listings to three brokers. Broker B is the procuring cause of the sale. Who earns a commission?
options: All three brokers, split equally
The first broker who signed a listing
Only Broker B
No broker, because open listings cannot be enforced
questions.explanation: In an open listing, only the broker who is the procuring cause of the sale earns the commission. If the owner sells the property herself, she owes no one.

questions.q: A tenant's lease gives the tenant a right of first refusal to buy the building. Which statement is correct?
options: The tenant can force the landlord to sell at a set price at any time during the lease
The tenant can match a bona fide offer the landlord is willing to accept, but cannot force a sale
The tenant is obligated to buy the building if the landlord decides to sell
A right of first refusal and an option to purchase are the same thing
questions.explanation: A right of first refusal only lets the holder match terms if the owner decides to sell; it cannot force a sale. An option, by contrast, lets the optionee (who pays consideration) compel the sale at a set price within the option period — the optionor is bound, the optionee is not.
questions.citation: General contract law (options and rights of first refusal)

questions.q: A buyer assigns her purchase contract to her brother with the seller's consent, but no agreement releasing the buyer is signed. If the brother fails to close:
options: The original buyer is automatically released because the seller consented
The seller can sue only the brokerage
The contract is void because real estate contracts cannot be assigned
The original buyer generally remains liable, because only a novation releases her
questions.explanation: In an assignment, the assignor generally stays secondarily liable if the assignee does not perform. A novation replaces the old contract or party with a new one and releases the original party. Consenting to an assignment is not the same as agreeing to a release.

questions.q: In parts of downstate New York, a licensee may prepare a binder. Which statement about a binder is most accurate?
options: A written outline of key terms that can be enforceable if it contains all essential terms
It is the title insurance policy that the title company delivers to the buyer at closing
It can never be enforced, because only a contract prepared by an attorney is binding
It replaces the deed and transfers title to the buyer once all parties have signed it
questions.explanation: A binder is a written outline of the main terms, often signed by the parties, after which attorneys draft the formal contract of sale. A binder may lack essential terms such as contingencies, but one that has all the required elements can be an enforceable contract.

questions.q: A buyer signs a promissory note and a mortgage to finance her home purchase. Which statement is accurate?
options: The buyer is the mortgagee, and the note pledges the property as security
The buyer is the mortgagor, and the mortgage is the security instrument that creates a lien
The lender is the mortgagor, and the mortgage is the buyer's personal promise to repay
The lender is the mortgagee, and recording the note is what creates the lien
questions.explanation: The note is the borrower's personal promise to repay the debt; the mortgage is the security instrument that pledges the property. The borrower gives the mortgage and is the mortgagor; the lender receives it and is the mortgagee. Trap: the '-or' is the borrower.

questions.q: What is the main role of Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac in the secondary mortgage market?
options: Making loans directly to homebuyers through their own retail bank branches
Insuring FHA loans against borrower default in exchange for a premium
Guaranteeing a portion of each VA loan made to an eligible veteran or service member
Buying conforming loans from lenders, replenishing lenders' funds for new loans
questions.explanation: In the primary market, lenders originate loans directly with borrowers. In the secondary market, Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac buy conforming loans from those lenders and pool them into securities, which replenishes the lenders' funds. FHA insures loans and VA guarantees them.
questions.citation: Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac charters (12 U.S.C. § 1716 et seq.; 12 U.S.C. § 1451 et seq.)

questions.q: Which statement best describes Ginnie Mae (GNMA)?
options: A government-owned corporation within HUD that guarantees securities backed by FHA and VA loans
A private lender that originates jumbo conventional loans for high-income borrowers
A government-sponsored enterprise that buys conventional loans carrying private mortgage insurance
The federal agency that writes and enforces the Truth in Lending Act disclosure rules
questions.explanation: Ginnie Mae is a wholly government-owned corporation within HUD. It guarantees timely payment on mortgage-backed securities backed by government-insured or government-guaranteed loans such as FHA and VA loans. Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac are the GSEs that buy conventional loans.

questions.q: Which statement correctly distinguishes FHA and VA loans?
options: FHA makes most of its loans directly to borrowers; VA only buys loans on the secondary market
Both are conventional loans that are protected by private mortgage insurance from the lender
FHA insures loans from approved lenders; VA guarantees part of loans to eligible veterans
VA loans always require 20% down, while FHA loans never require any down payment at all
questions.explanation: FHA insures loans made by approved lenders and charges the borrower a mortgage insurance premium (MIP); its minimum down payment is generally 3.5%. VA guarantees a portion of loans made to eligible veterans, often with no down payment required. Neither is a conventional loan, and neither uses private mortgage insurance.
questions.citation: National Housing Act (FHA); 38 U.S.C. Chapter 37 (VA home loans)

questions.q: A borrower has a conventional loan with private mortgage insurance on her principal residence and is current on her payments. Under the federal Homeowners Protection Act, PMI generally ends automatically when the balance is scheduled to reach what percentage of the home's original value?
questions.explanation: PMI ends automatically when the balance is scheduled to reach 78% of the original value. The borrower can request cancellation earlier, at 80%, if she meets the conditions. Trap: 80% is the borrower-request point. FHA's MIP follows different rules.
questions.citation: Homeowners Protection Act of 1998, 12 U.S.C. § 4901 et seq.

questions.q: A borrower misses several mortgage payments, and the lender declares the entire unpaid balance due immediately. Which clause allows this?
options: Defeasance clause
Alienation clause
Prepayment clause
Acceleration clause
questions.explanation: The acceleration clause lets the lender declare the entire balance due when the borrower defaults. The alienation clause can also make the loan due, but it is triggered by a transfer of the property, not by missed payments.

questions.q: A homeowner sells and lets the buyer take over her existing mortgage without the lender's approval. The lender demands full payment because of the transfer. The lender is relying on the:
options: Alienation (due-on-sale) clause
Defeasance (release of lien) clause
Subordination (lien priority) clause
Escalation (rate increase) clause
questions.explanation: An alienation (due-on-sale) clause lets the lender call the loan due when the property is sold or transferred without its consent, which prevents an unapproved assumption. Federal law exempts certain transfers, such as a transfer to a spouse or a transfer on the borrower's death.
questions.citation: Garn-St Germain Depository Institutions Act, 12 U.S.C. § 1701j-3

questions.q: When a borrower pays off a mortgage loan in full, which clause requires the lender to release its lien, for example by delivering a satisfaction of mortgage?
options: Acceleration clause
Prepayment penalty clause
Defeasance clause
Alienation clause
questions.explanation: The defeasance clause defeats the lender's lien once the debt is paid in full, so the lender must provide a satisfaction of mortgage for recording. A prepayment penalty clause charges a fee for paying off the loan early; it does not release the lien.
questions.citation: General mortgage law; NY RPAPL § 1921 (satisfaction of mortgage)

questions.q: A 30-year fixed-rate loan of $200,000 at 6% annual interest has a monthly principal-and-interest payment of $1,199.10. How much of the FIRST payment reduces the principal?
questions.explanation: First month's interest = $200,000 × 0.06 ÷ 12 = $1,000.00. Principal = $1,199.10 − $1,000.00 = $199.10. On an amortizing loan, early payments are mostly interest, and the principal portion grows with each payment.
questions.citation: Amortization math (NYS salesperson syllabus: real estate finance)

questions.q: An adjustable-rate mortgage started at 4.50%. At the first adjustment the index is 4.10% and the margin is 2.75%. The caps are 2% per adjustment and 5% over the initial rate for the life of the loan. What is the new rate?
questions.explanation: Fully indexed rate = index 4.10% + margin 2.75% = 6.85%, but the periodic cap limits the change to 4.50% + 2% = 6.50%. The lifetime cap of 9.50% is not reached, so the new rate is 6.50%. Trap: the margin is added to the index, not to the old rate.
questions.citation: ARM terms (index, margin, caps); Regulation Z, 12 CFR Part 1026

questions.q: A buyer purchases a home for $450,000 with a 90% loan-to-value loan and pays 1.5 discount points. How much do the points cost?
questions.explanation: Points are calculated on the loan amount, not the price. Loan = $450,000 × 0.90 = $405,000, and $405,000 × 1.5% = $6,075. Using the price would give $6,750, and using 1 point would give $4,050.
questions.citation: Points math (1 point = 1% of the loan amount)

questions.q: Under Regulation Z, which phrase in a home-loan ad is a triggering term that requires additional disclosures?
options: Annual percentage rate 6.25%
Easy monthly payments
Only $5,000 down
Low-cost financing available
questions.explanation: Triggering terms are the down payment amount or percentage, the number of payments or repayment period, the amount of any payment, and the amount of any finance charge. Using one requires the ad to also state the down payment, the terms of repayment, and the APR. Stating the APR alone, or a general phrase like 'easy payments,' is not a trigger.
questions.citation: Truth in Lending Act / Regulation Z, 12 CFR § 1026.24

questions.q: A title agency offers a salesperson $250 for every buyer she refers, calling it a 'marketing fee,' even though she performs no marketing services. Under RESPA, this payment is:
options: Legal if it is disclosed to the buyer on the Closing Disclosure
Legal because it is labeled as a marketing fee in a written agreement
Legal if the salesperson's supervising broker approves it in writing
A prohibited kickback for referring settlement service business
questions.explanation: RESPA Section 8 prohibits giving or accepting any fee or thing of value for referring settlement service business. A payment for services that are not actually performed is a kickback, no matter what it is called, and disclosing it or getting broker approval does not make it legal.

questions.q: For a covered residential mortgage under the TRID rule, when must the borrower receive the Closing Disclosure?
options: Within 3 business days after the loan application
At least 3 business days before consummation
At least 24 hours before the closing
At least 10 calendar days before consummation
questions.explanation: The borrower must receive the Closing Disclosure at least 3 business days before consummation. Trap: 'within 3 business days after application' is the deadline for the Loan Estimate.

questions.q: Which basis is protected under the federal Equal Credit Opportunity Act but is NOT one of the seven protected classes in the federal Fair Housing Act?
options: Marital status
Familial status
Disability
National origin
questions.explanation: ECOA prohibits credit discrimination based on race, color, religion, national origin, sex, marital status, age (if the applicant can contract), receipt of public assistance income, or good-faith exercise of consumer credit rights. Familial status and disability are Fair Housing Act classes, not ECOA classes, and national origin appears in both laws. NY Executive Law § 296 separately covers marital status in housing.
questions.citation: Equal Credit Opportunity Act, 15 U.S.C. § 1691; Regulation B, 12 CFR Part 1002

questions.q: How is a residential mortgage typically foreclosed in New York?
options: By a nonjudicial power-of-sale auction with no court involvement
By the lender simply taking possession after one missed payment
By a judicial foreclosure action in court that ends in a court-ordered sale
By strict foreclosure, in which the lender automatically keeps any equity
questions.explanation: New York is a judicial foreclosure state. The lender sues, files a lis pendens, gets a judgment of foreclosure and sale, and the property is sold at a court-ordered auction. Until that sale, the borrower keeps the equity of redemption — the right to pay the debt, interest, and costs and keep the property.

questions.q: In a New York foreclosure, the borrower owes $300,000 including costs. The property sells at auction for $220,000, and the court determines its fair market value is $260,000. What is the maximum deficiency judgment?
questions.explanation: In New York, the deficiency is the debt minus the HIGHER of the sale price or the court-determined fair market value: $300,000 − $260,000 = $40,000. This keeps a lender from profiting on a low auction bid. Trap: $300,000 − $220,000 = $80,000 ignores the fair market value credit.

questions.q: A seller agrees to finance part of the price by taking back a mortgage from the buyer at closing. This is a:
options: Wraparound mortgage
Reverse annuity mortgage
Blanket mortgage
Purchase-money mortgage
questions.explanation: A purchase-money mortgage secures part of the purchase price, and seller financing in which the seller 'takes back' a mortgage is the classic example. A wraparound loan wraps around an existing mortgage that stays in place; a blanket mortgage covers more than one parcel.

questions.q: A developer finances 40 lots with one mortgage and wants to sell the lots individually as homes are completed. The developer should use a:
options: Blanket mortgage with a partial release clause
Package mortgage with an acceleration clause
Reverse mortgage with a defeasance clause
Wraparound mortgage with a prepayment clause
questions.explanation: A blanket mortgage covers more than one parcel. A partial release clause lets each lot be released from the lien when a specified amount is paid, so the developer can deliver clear title lot by lot.
questions.citation: General mortgage law (blanket mortgage; partial release)

questions.q: A seller has an existing $150,000 mortgage. The buyer gives the seller a new $300,000 mortgage that includes the existing loan; the buyer pays the seller, and the seller keeps paying the original lender. This is a:
options: Package mortgage
Blanket mortgage
Wraparound mortgage
Reverse annuity mortgage
questions.explanation: A wraparound mortgage is a junior loan that wraps around an existing loan, which stays in place; the seller collects on the larger loan and keeps paying the underlying lender. An alienation clause in the existing mortgage can block this arrangement.

questions.q: A 70-year-old homeowner with significant equity wants to receive payments from a lender while continuing to live in her home, with no monthly loan payments. Which loan fits?
options: Package mortgage
Blanket mortgage
Wraparound mortgage
Reverse mortgage
questions.explanation: A reverse mortgage pays the owner from her equity. FHA's HECM program requires the borrower to be at least 62, and the loan is generally repaid when she sells, dies, or no longer lives there as a principal residence; she must still pay taxes and insurance. A package mortgage instead covers real property plus personal property such as appliances or furniture.
questions.citation: FHA Home Equity Conversion Mortgage program, 12 U.S.C. § 1715z-20

questions.q: A lender keeps persuading an elderly homeowner to refinance every few months, charging new points and fees each time while giving her little or no real benefit. This predatory practice is called:
options: Redlining
Loan flipping
Blockbusting
Steering
questions.explanation: Loan flipping is repeated refinancing that strips equity through fees without giving the borrower a real benefit. New York Banking Law § 6-l restricts flipping for high-cost home loans. Redlining is refusing credit or services in certain areas, and blockbusting and steering are fair-housing violations.

questions.q: Which governmental power is the legal basis for a municipality's zoning ordinance?
options: Police power
Eminent domain
Escheat
Taxation
questions.explanation: Zoning is an exercise of the police power: regulating private property use to protect public health, safety, morals and general welfare. Eminent domain takes property (with compensation); escheat transfers property of an owner who dies without heirs or a will.
questions.citation: NY Town Law § 261; NY Village Law § 7-700

questions.q: A town downzones an area, reducing permitted density, and an owner's lot loses some market value. What is the general rule on compensation?
options: Just compensation is always owed for any loss in market value caused by a zoning change
