The town must buy the lot at its pre-rezoning appraised value whenever the owner demands
No compensation is owed for a valid regulation unless it goes so far as to be a taking
The owner may ignore the new zoning until compensation is paid in full
questions.explanation: A valid police-power regulation does not require payment merely because it reduces value. Compensation is required for a taking under eminent domain, or where regulation is so severe that courts treat it as a regulatory taking.
questions.citation: U.S. Const. 5th Amendment; NY Const. Art. I § 7

questions.q: The State acquires part of a farm by condemnation to widen a highway. Which pair of requirements must the taking satisfy?
options: Owner consent and a fair hearing
Public use and just compensation
Public use and a majority vote of neighbors
A recorded deed and owner consent
questions.explanation: Eminent domain lets government take private property without the owner's consent, but only for a public use and upon payment of just compensation. Consent is exactly what condemnation does not require.
questions.citation: U.S. Const. 5th Amendment; NY Const. Art. I § 7; NY Eminent Domain Procedure Law

questions.q: In an eminent domain taking, just compensation is generally measured by:
options: The owner's original purchase price plus the cost of any improvements made since
The assessed value currently shown for the property on the municipal tax roll
The cost the government expects to incur to build the planned public project
The fair market value of the property taken, considering its highest and best use
questions.explanation: Just compensation is generally the property's fair market value at the time of the taking, considering its highest and best use. Purchase price and assessed value are not the measure.
questions.citation: NY Eminent Domain Procedure Law; NY Const. Art. I § 7

questions.q: An owner in a residential-only district wants to open a retail store. Because retail is not a permitted use there, what must the owner show the zoning board of appeals to obtain relief?
options: Practical difficulty balanced against detriment to the neighborhood
That the store would earn more than the house currently does
That a majority of adjoining owners signed letters of support
Unnecessary hardship, including no reasonable return from any permitted use
questions.explanation: A use variance requires unnecessary hardship: no reasonable return under any permitted use (shown by competent financial evidence), a unique hardship, no change to neighborhood character, and a hardship that is not self-created. Merely wanting a more profitable use is insufficient.

questions.q: A homeowner wants to build a deck that would extend 6 feet into a required rear-yard setback. What type of relief is needed?
options: A use variance
An area variance
A rezoning of the district
A nonconforming use certificate
questions.explanation: A setback is a dimensional requirement, so relief is an area variance. The ZBA balances the benefit to the applicant against any detriment to the health, safety and welfare of the neighborhood.

questions.q: When deciding an area variance, how does New York law treat a difficulty that the applicant created?
options: It is relevant but does not by itself preclude granting the variance
It automatically requires the board to deny the area variance request
It is irrelevant, and the board may not consider it in deciding the variance
It converts the request into a use variance with a stricter hardship test
questions.explanation: For an area variance, self-created difficulty is one factor in the balancing test and does not necessarily bar relief. Trap: for a use variance, the hardship must not be self-created.

questions.q: A town's zoning ordinance lists day-care centers as allowed in residential districts if specified conditions on parking and lot size are met. A provider seeking approval needs:
options: A use variance
An area variance
A special use permit
A spot zoning amendment
questions.explanation: A special use permit authorizes a use the ordinance already contemplates for the district, once its conditions are met. It is not a variance, because the use is not prohibited.

questions.q: A gas station has operated legally on a corner since before the area was zoned residential. Under the new zoning, the station:
options: May generally continue as a lawful nonconforming use
Must close immediately because it is now an illegal use
Automatically receives a use variance from the zoning board
May expand freely because it existed before the zoning
questions.explanation: A use that was lawful before a zoning change may generally continue as a nonconforming use. That status does not authorize unlimited expansion, and it is not the same as an illegal use.
questions.citation: NY zoning law: nonconforming use doctrine (local zoning ordinance)

questions.q: Which statement about a lawful nonconforming use is generally accurate?
options: It may be enlarged or extended at any time without any approval from the town
It may be changed to any other nonconforming use without zoning board review
It may be lost if abandoned or discontinued for the period set by the ordinance
It automatically becomes a permitted use after ten years of continuous operation
questions.explanation: Ordinances typically restrict expansion or change of a nonconforming use and terminate it if the use is discontinued or abandoned for a stated period. The goal is to phase nonconforming uses out over time.
questions.citation: NY zoning law: nonconforming use doctrine (local zoning ordinance)

questions.q: A city council rezones one owner's small lot to commercial, solely for that owner's benefit, while all surrounding land stays residential and the change conflicts with the comprehensive plan. This is:
options: Cluster zoning, which is generally valid
Spot zoning, which is generally invalid
Incentive zoning, which is generally valid
A lawful area variance by the council
questions.explanation: Spot zoning singles out a small parcel for a classification different from the surrounding area, for private benefit and inconsistent with the comprehensive plan. Courts generally strike it down.
questions.citation: NY Town Law § 263 (zoning in accordance with comprehensive plan)

questions.q: A developer groups homes on smaller lots and leaves the rest of the tract as permanent open space, without exceeding the density a conventional subdivision would allow. This is:
options: Spot zoning
Downzoning
A use variance
Cluster zoning
questions.explanation: Cluster development concentrates buildings to preserve open space while keeping overall density no greater than a conventional layout. The planning board may approve it when authorized by the town board.

questions.q: A developer plans to divide a 40-acre parcel into 25 building lots. Before lots are sold, the developer generally must obtain:
options: A use variance from the zoning board of appeals
A certificate of occupancy for each lot
A deed restriction approved by the assessor
Subdivision plat approval from the planning board
questions.explanation: Subdivision regulations require planning board approval of the plat (lots, streets, utilities, drainage) before it is filed and lots are sold. Variances and COs address different issues.

questions.q: Outside New York City, which code sets statewide minimum construction and fire-safety standards that local building departments enforce?
options: The Real Property Actions and Proceedings Law
The Uniform Fire Prevention and Building Code
The State Environmental Quality Review Act
The Multiple Residence Law of New York
questions.explanation: The Uniform Fire Prevention and Building Code sets minimum construction and fire-safety standards. Municipalities enforce it through permits and inspections; New York City has its own construction codes.

questions.q: What does a certificate of occupancy (CO) indicate?
options: The building was inspected and may be legally occupied for its stated use
The property has clear, marketable title insured against all defects
The owner has permission to begin construction on the lot
The building is free of every physical defect and needs no repairs
questions.explanation: A CO is issued after completed work is found to comply with approved plans and applicable codes, allowing legal occupancy for the stated use. It does not guarantee title or the absence of every defect.
questions.citation: NY Executive Law Article 18; local building code

questions.q: A contractor has just received a building permit for a new house. A buyer under contract asks whether they can move in once the walls are up. The best answer is:
options: Yes; a building permit also authorizes occupancy once the framing inspection is passed
Yes; occupancy is legally allowed as soon as the buyer closes and takes title to the house
No; a permit only authorizes construction; occupancy generally needs a certificate of occupancy
No; occupancy additionally requires a new variance from the zoning board of appeals
questions.explanation: A building permit is issued before work starts and authorizes construction. A certificate of occupancy (or equivalent) is issued after completion and inspection, and that is what allows legal occupancy.
questions.citation: NY Executive Law Article 18; local building code

questions.q: Under New York's town zoning enabling law, zoning regulations must be adopted:
options: In accordance with a comprehensive plan
Only after a vote of all property owners
Only with approval from the Department of State
In accordance with each owner's deed restrictions
questions.explanation: Town Law requires zoning to be made in accordance with a comprehensive (master) plan, which guides long-term land use, transportation and community facilities.

questions.q: Under SEQR, the lead agency determines a proposed project may have a significant adverse environmental impact. What happens next?
options: It issues a negative declaration and the project proceeds without further review
The project is automatically denied and may not be resubmitted
It issues a positive declaration and an environmental impact statement is required
The application is transferred to the Department of State for a decision
questions.explanation: A positive declaration means an EIS must be prepared. A negative declaration means no significant adverse impact, so no EIS. Not every project requires an EIS.

questions.q: Under SEQR, an action classified as Type II:
options: Is presumed likely to require an environmental impact statement
Has been determined not to require further environmental review
Must be reviewed by the Adirondack Park Agency
May proceed only after a positive declaration is issued
questions.explanation: Type II actions (e.g., many routine actions and minor residential construction) are listed as not requiring SEQR review. Type I actions are more likely to require an EIS; unlisted actions get case-by-case review.

questions.q: A buyer plans to build a home on private land inside the Adirondack Park. In addition to local approvals, the buyer should check whether a permit is needed from:
options: The New York State Board of Real Estate
The Federal Housing Administration
The county tax assessor's office
The Adirondack Park Agency
questions.explanation: The Adirondack Park Agency regulates land use and development on private land within the Park through its own land-use plan and permit system, in addition to local rules.
questions.citation: NY Executive Law Article 27 (Adirondack Park Agency Act)

questions.q: A buyer wants to fill and build on land near a freshwater wetland. Which statement is most accurate?
options: Only local zoning applies, because wetlands are governed solely by the town or village
No wetland permit is needed once the buyer closes and holds a recorded deed to the land
Only federal law applies, because New York State does not regulate freshwater wetlands
State, federal and local rules may each apply; get a current jurisdictional determination
questions.explanation: NYS DEC regulates freshwater wetlands under ECL Article 24 (including adjacent areas), the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers regulates fill under the Clean Water Act, and localities may add rules. Get a current determination rather than assuming.
questions.citation: NY ECL Article 24; Clean Water Act § 404

questions.q: Zoning allows two-family homes in a district, but a recorded deed restriction on a lot limits it to one single-family home. Which rule controls?
options: The zoning, because public law always overrides private covenants
The deed restriction, because the more restrictive rule governs
Neither, because the two conflict and cancel each other out
Whichever was recorded or enacted more recently
questions.explanation: When zoning and a private deed restriction differ, the more restrictive one controls. An owner must satisfy both, so the single-family limit applies.
questions.citation: NY zoning law; restrictive covenants (deed restrictions)

questions.q: In which framing method do wall studs run continuously from the sill plate up to the roof line, creating hollow vertical channels that can spread fire unless firestops are installed?
options: Platform framing
Post-and-beam framing
Balloon framing
Modular framing
questions.explanation: Balloon framing uses long, continuous studs from the foundation sill to the rafters; without firestops the open wall cavities act like chimneys. Platform framing, the most common method today, builds each floor as a separate platform so studs stop at every level; post-and-beam uses heavy, widely spaced timbers.
questions.citation: NYS DOS 77-hr Salesperson Syllabus, Subject 7: Construction (platform, post and beam construction)

questions.q: A buyer tours a house that has no basement and no crawl space; the concrete floor was poured directly on the ground at grade level. What type of foundation is this?
options: Slab-on-grade
Full basement
Crawl space
Pier and girder
questions.explanation: A slab-on-grade foundation is a concrete slab poured directly on prepared ground, often with plumbing or ducts embedded in or beneath it. A crawl space leaves a shallow open area under the floor, and a full basement provides a below-grade story.
questions.citation: NYS DOS 77-hr Salesperson Syllabus, Subject 7: Construction (slab-on-grade construction)

questions.q: What is the primary purpose of a footing in residential construction?
options: To anchor the wood sill plate and floor framing to the top of the foundation wall
To act as a vapor barrier that keeps ground moisture from rising through the basement slab
To carry roof loads down to the ceiling joists
To spread the building's weight over a wider soil area below the frost line
questions.explanation: The footing is the wide concrete base beneath foundation walls and columns; it distributes the structure's load over more soil and is set below the frost line to prevent heaving. Anchoring the wood framing to the foundation is the job of the sill plate and its anchor bolts.
questions.citation: NYS DOS 77-hr Salesperson Syllabus, Subject 7: Construction (footing, foundation walls)

questions.q: A home inspector reports rot in the lowest horizontal wood member, which rests directly on top of the foundation wall and is secured with anchor bolts. Which component is damaged?
options: Ridge board
Sill plate
Header
Rafter
questions.explanation: The sill plate is the first wood member of the frame, bolted to the foundation; floor joists rest on it. A header spans a door or window opening, and the ridge board and rafters are roof components.
questions.citation: NYS DOS 77-hr Salesperson Syllabus, Subject 7: Construction (sill plates)

questions.q: Which structural members slope from the ridge down to the exterior walls and support the roof sheathing?
options: Rafters
Floor joists
Studs
Girders
questions.explanation: Rafters are the sloped roof framing members. The common trap is joists: joists are horizontal members that support floors and ceilings, studs are vertical wall members, and girders are main beams that support joists.
questions.citation: NYS DOS 77-hr Salesperson Syllabus, Subject 7: Construction (rafter, joists, studs, girder)

questions.q: A buyer compares two attics, one insulated to R-19 and the other to R-38. Which statement is correct?
options: The R-19 attic insulates better because a lower R-value means less heat escapes through the ceiling
R-value rates the BTU output of the furnace, not the insulation
Both insulate equally because R-value measures only the material's thickness
The R-38 attic insulates better because higher R-values mean more resistance to heat flow
questions.explanation: R-value measures a material's resistance to heat flow; the higher the R-value, the better the insulation. BTU is a separate measure of heat quantity used to rate heating and cooling equipment.
questions.citation: NYS DOS 77-hr Salesperson Syllabus, Subject 7: Construction (R-value, insulation)

questions.q: A British thermal unit (BTU) is the amount of heat required to:
options: raise the temperature of one gallon of water by 1°F
raise the temperature of one pound of water by 1°F
raise the temperature of one cubic foot of air by 10°F
keep a 100-square-foot room at 68°F for one hour
questions.explanation: One BTU is the heat needed to raise one pound of water by one degree Fahrenheit. Furnaces, boilers, and air conditioners are rated in BTUs (per hour); the gallon option is the common trap.
questions.citation: NYS DOS 77-hr Salesperson Syllabus, Subject 7: Construction (BTU/British Thermal Unit)

questions.q: During a showing, a circuit breaker trips every time the seller runs the microwave and space heater at the same time. What does this most likely indicate?
options: The insulation's R-value is too low for the heating system
The breaker is defective, because properly working breakers never trip
The circuit is drawing more current (amps) than it is rated to carry
The home has too much amperage at the main service panel
questions.explanation: Circuit breakers (and older fuses) cut power when the current on a circuit exceeds its amperage rating, preventing overheated wiring; tripping under heavy load is the breaker doing its job. A licensee should note the condition and refer electrical evaluation to a licensed electrician rather than diagnose it.
questions.citation: NYS DOS 77-hr Salesperson Syllabus, Subject 7: Construction (amperage, circuit breaker, fuse)

questions.q: What is the main function of the U-shaped trap installed beneath a sink drain?
options: It holds a water seal that keeps sewer gases from entering the home
It increases water pressure in the supply lines
It carries sewer gases up and out through the vent stack on the roof
It filters sediment and debris out of the drinking water supply
questions.explanation: The trap retains water that blocks sewer gas from backing up through the fixture. Venting gases through the roof and admitting air to the drain lines is the vent stack's job, and supply lines (under pressure) are a separate system from gravity drain-waste-vent lines.
questions.citation: NYS DOS 77-hr Salesperson Syllabus, Subject 7: Construction (plumbing systems)

questions.q: A one-and-a-half-story house with a steep gable roof, dormer windows, and a symmetrical front with a center door best describes which architectural style?
options: Ranch
Split-level
Cape Cod
Colonial
questions.explanation: A Cape Cod is a compact 1½-story home with a steep roof and dormers that make the upper half-story usable. A Colonial has two full stories with a symmetrical facade, a Ranch is a single-story home, and a split-level has three or more levels offset by half-flights of stairs.
questions.citation: NYS DOS 77-hr Salesperson Syllabus, Subject 7: Construction (architectural styles)

questions.q: A developer wants to fill a freshwater wetland on a parcel in upstate New York. Which statement is most accurate?
options: Only the local zoning board regulates wetlands, so no state or federal review applies
A federal Clean Water Act permit and a NYS DEC freshwater wetlands permit may both be required
Wetlands may be filled freely once the parcel is zoned residential
Wetland rules apply only to tidal areas on the coast, not inland parcels
questions.explanation: Filling wetlands can require a U.S. Army Corps of Engineers permit under Clean Water Act § 404 and a NYS DEC permit under the Freshwater Wetlands Act, plus any local review. Zoning does not override these rules, so get a current jurisdictional determination rather than assume no rules apply.
questions.citation: Clean Water Act § 404 (33 U.S.C. § 1344); NY ECL Article 24 (Freshwater Wetlands)

questions.q: A buyer is under contract to buy a single-family home built in 1962. Under the federal lead-based paint disclosure rule, the buyer must be given:
options: a lead-free certificate that the seller must obtain by having a certified inspector test all painted surfaces
a 3-day right to cancel the contract after receiving the seller's Property Condition Disclosure Statement
nothing, because the federal lead rule applies only to rental housing
a 10-day opportunity for a lead inspection or risk assessment, unless changed or waived in writing
questions.explanation: For pre-1978 target housing, the seller must disclose known lead information and reports, give the EPA pamphlet, and include the lead warning; the buyer gets a 10-day inspection/risk-assessment opportunity that can be changed by mutual written agreement or waived. The rule does not require the seller to test or remove lead.

questions.q: For the sale of pre-1978 housing, how long must the seller and the listing agent keep a copy of the signed lead-based paint disclosure and acknowledgment?
options: 1 year after closing
At least 3 years from the completion of the sale
6 years from the date of the listing agreement
Until the buyer resells the property
questions.explanation: The seller and any agent must keep the completed lead disclosure attachment for at least 3 years from the completion date of the sale. Lessors and agents likewise keep lease disclosures for 3 years from the start of the lease term.

questions.q: A radon test in the lowest lived-in level of a home reads 6.2 pCi/L. Which statement is accurate under EPA guidance?
options: Radon matters only in commercial buildings, so no action is needed for a home
The result is acceptable because EPA's action level for homes is 10 pCi/L
It exceeds EPA's 4 pCi/L action level, so professional mitigation is recommended
A retest is unnecessary because radon at that level can be detected by its smell
questions.explanation: EPA recommends fixing homes at 4 pCi/L or higher (and considering mitigation between 2 and 4). Radon is an odorless, invisible radioactive gas, so only testing reveals levels, and a reading below 4 is not a guarantee of no risk.
questions.citation: EPA, A Citizen's Guide to Radon (4 pCi/L action level)

questions.q: During a showing, a buyer notices crumbling insulation wrapped around old basement heating pipes and asks whether it is asbestos. What should the salesperson do?
options: Advise against disturbing it and recommend evaluation by a qualified asbestos professional
Break off a small sample herself and mail it to a testing lab to save the buyer the inspection fee
Assure the buyer it is safe because asbestos was banned from all residential products in 1978
Tell the seller to sweep it up and repaint the pipes before closing
questions.explanation: Crumbling (friable) asbestos can release dangerous fibers, and appearance alone cannot identify it, so the licensee should not sample or disturb it and should refer testing to qualified professionals. There is no blanket ban date that clears older materials.
questions.citation: EPA asbestos guidance; Clean Air Act asbestos NESHAP (40 CFR Part 61, Subpart M)

questions.q: Urea-formaldehyde foam insulation (UFFI) is an environmental concern primarily because it:
options: contains radioactive particles that enter through foundation cracks
leaks petroleum into the groundwater from buried tanks
contains PCBs like those used in older electrical transformers
can release formaldehyde gas into the indoor air
questions.explanation: UFFI, a foam insulation used mostly in the 1970s, can emit formaldehyde gas that irritates the eyes and lungs. Radon is the radioactive soil gas, PCBs are associated with older electrical equipment, and petroleum leaks come from storage tanks.
questions.citation: NYS DOS 77-hr Salesperson Syllabus, Subject 7: Environmental Issues (UFFI)

questions.q: Before listing, a seller wants to paint over a damp, moldy basement wall. What is the best advice?
options: Painting is enough because federal law sets a maximum indoor mold level that a sealed wall will satisfy
Fix the moisture source and remediate properly; known material defects must not be concealed
Mold is never a disclosure issue because it is a naturally occurring substance found in every home
Have the buyer sign a waiver promising never to test for mold
questions.explanation: Mold grows from moisture, so lasting remediation starts with fixing the water source; painting over it hides the problem without solving it. There is no federal indoor mold limit that serves as a pass/fail standard, and concealing a known material defect can expose the seller and agent to liability.
questions.citation: EPA mold guidance; NY Labor Law Article 32 (mold assessment and remediation)

questions.q: A property inspection finds an abandoned underground heating-oil tank. What is the main environmental risk?
options: A corroded tank can leak petroleum into the soil and groundwater
The tank will emit radon gas into the living space
The tank lowers the R-value of the foundation walls
The tank violates the federal lead-based paint disclosure rule
questions.explanation: Aging steel tanks can corrode and leak oil, contaminating soil and groundwater and creating costly cleanup liability. NY law imposes strict liability for petroleum discharges, so buyers should have tanks evaluated, tested, or properly removed and closed.
questions.citation: NY Navigation Law Article 12 (petroleum discharges); NYS DEC tank regulations

questions.q: Under New York's Amanda's Law, carbon monoxide alarms are required in one- and two-family dwellings that:
options: are located within 1,000 feet of a highway, truck route, or other major source of vehicle exhaust
were built before the NYS Uniform Fire Prevention and Building Code took effect in 1984
have a fuel-burning appliance or system that can emit carbon monoxide, or an attached garage
have more than three bedrooms or more than one sleeping floor
questions.explanation: Amanda's Law requires CO alarms in homes with a CO source, such as a fossil-fuel-burning furnace, boiler, water heater, or fireplace, or an attached garage. This is separate from the smoke-alarm requirement; CO is odorless, and an alarm means leave the building and call for help.

questions.q: A company buys an industrial site and later discovers contamination dumped by a prior owner decades ago. Under CERCLA (Superfund), the current owner:
options: is never liable because it did not cause the pollution
is liable only for the share of waste it personally dumped
is automatically protected as an innocent purchaser, with no prior investigation needed
can be held liable because liability is strict, joint and several, and retroactive
questions.explanation: CERCLA can impose cleanup liability on current owners regardless of fault (strict), for the entire cleanup (joint and several), and for contamination that occurred before the law (retroactive). Innocent-landowner type defenses require 'all appropriate inquiry,' such as a Phase I assessment, before buying; they are not automatic.

questions.q: What distinguishes a Phase II Environmental Site Assessment from a Phase I?
options: Phase II is limited to reviewing historical records and interviewing owners
Phase II involves sampling and lab testing of soil, groundwater, or building materials
Phase II is the cleanup stage in which contamination is physically removed
Phase II is required for every residential sale in New York
questions.explanation: A Phase I is an investigative review (records, site reconnaissance, interviews) with no sampling; if it flags concerns, a Phase II samples and tests to confirm contamination. Remediation is a later, separate phase. These assessments are used mainly in commercial transactions.
questions.citation: ASTM E1527 / EPA All Appropriate Inquiries Rule (40 CFR Part 312)

questions.q: The seller of a covered single-family home in New York offers the buyer a $500 credit at closing instead of delivering a Property Condition Disclosure Statement. Under current law:
options: the credit is still an acceptable alternative to the statement as long as the buyer agrees to it in writing
the credit must now be given in addition to the statement, and both are due at or before the closing
the statement must be delivered before the buyer signs a binding contract, because the $500 credit was repealed in 2024
the seller may skip both because the statement became optional for all residential sellers in 2024
questions.explanation: Amendments effective March 20, 2024 repealed the old $500 credit, so covered sellers of 1-4 family homes must deliver the PCDS before the buyer signs a binding contract unless an exemption applies (condo and co-op units are not covered). The statement reflects the seller's actual knowledge and is not a warranty.

questions.q: The four characteristics that must be present for real property to have value are commonly remembered as DUST. They are:
options: Demand, utility, scarcity, and transferability
Demand, usefulness, supply, and taxation
Durability, utility, stability, and transferability
Desirability, uniqueness, scarcity, and title
questions.explanation: Value requires effective demand (desire plus purchasing power), utility, scarcity, and transferability of ownership rights. Uniqueness and durability are characteristics of land itself, not the elements of value.
questions.citation: Appraisal principles; NYS DOS Salesperson Syllabus (Valuation)

questions.q: A buyer eager to win a bidding war pays $410,000 for a house that an appraiser values at $400,000. The builder's cost to construct it new today would be $380,000. The $410,000 figure is the property's:
options: Market value
Reproduction cost
Price
Assessed value
questions.explanation: Price is what was actually paid in a particular transaction; it can be above or below market value. Market value is the appraiser's estimate of the most probable price ($400,000), and cost is what it takes to build ($380,000).
questions.citation: Appraisal principles; NYS DOS Salesperson Syllabus (Valuation)

questions.q: Which description best matches the appraisal definition of market value?
options: The amount the seller needs to net after paying off the mortgage and closing costs
The most probable price in an open, competitive market with informed, typically motivated parties
The total cost of the land plus the cost to build the improvements new at today's prices
The highest price any single buyer has offered for the property during its listing period
questions.explanation: Market value assumes an arm's-length sale, reasonable market exposure, informed and typically motivated parties, and no unusual financing or pressure. A seller's needs, construction cost, or one buyer's offer do not define market value.
questions.citation: Appraisal principles; NYS DOS Salesperson Syllabus (Valuation)

questions.q: A buyer will not pay $520,000 for a house when nearly identical homes on the same street are readily available for $490,000. Which valuation principle does this illustrate?
options: Anticipation
Contribution
Conformity
Substitution
questions.explanation: Substitution holds that a prudent buyer will not pay more than the cost of acquiring an equally desirable substitute. It is the foundation of the sales comparison approach.
questions.citation: Appraisal principles; NYS DOS Salesperson Syllabus (Valuation)

questions.q: An analyst finds that a gas station would be the most profitable use of a vacant lot and is physically possible and financially feasible, but current zoning prohibits it. As a highest-and-best-use candidate, the gas station fails because it is not:
options: Legally permissible
Physically possible
Financially feasible
Maximally productive
questions.explanation: Highest and best use must be legally permissible, physically possible, financially feasible, and maximally productive. A use barred by zoning fails the legal test no matter how profitable it would be.
questions.citation: Appraisal principles; NYS DOS Salesperson Syllabus (Valuation)

questions.q: An owner builds a $1.2 million house in a neighborhood where most homes sell for about $400,000. The principle that the neighborhood will tend to pull the house's value down is:
options: Progression
Contribution
Regression
Anticipation
questions.explanation: Regression: the value of a superior property is reduced by lesser surrounding properties. Progression is the opposite effect on an inferior property among better ones.
questions.citation: Appraisal principles; NYS DOS Salesperson Syllabus (Valuation)

questions.q: A modest two-bedroom cottage sits on a street lined with large, expensive homes. Its value benefits from the more valuable homes around it. This is an example of:
options: Regression
Conformity
Contribution
Progression
questions.explanation: Progression: an inferior property gains value from superior neighboring properties. Regression is the reverse, where a superior property loses value from inferior surroundings.
questions.citation: Appraisal principles; NYS DOS Salesperson Syllabus (Valuation)

questions.q: A homeowner spends $40,000 installing an in-ground pool, but buyers in the area will pay only about $15,000 more for a home with a pool. Which principle explains why the pool adds only $15,000 in value?
options: Substitution
Contribution
Highest and best use
Supply and demand
questions.explanation: Contribution: a component's value is what it adds to the whole property's market value, not what it cost. Here the $40,000 pool contributes only $15,000.
questions.citation: Appraisal principles; NYS DOS Salesperson Syllabus (Valuation)

questions.q: The principle holding that value is maximized when a property is reasonably similar in style, use, and quality to the properties around it is:
options: Conformity
Anticipation
Progression
Contribution
questions.explanation: Conformity: reasonable homogeneity of land uses and improvements tends to maximize value, which is one reason zoning and subdivision restrictions can protect value.
questions.citation: Appraisal principles; NYS DOS Salesperson Syllabus (Valuation)

questions.q: An investor values an apartment building based on the net income it is expected to produce over the coming years. Which principle is the investor relying on most directly?
options: Conformity
Regression
Anticipation
Substitution
questions.explanation: Anticipation: value is the present worth of expected future benefits. It underlies the income approach, which converts expected income into value.
questions.citation: Appraisal principles; NYS DOS Salesperson Syllabus (Valuation)

questions.q: Two developers finish 300 new condominium units in a small town at the same time, while the number of buyers stays the same. Prices for existing condos in town begin to fall. This best illustrates:
options: Regression
Highest and best use
Conformity
Supply and demand
questions.explanation: When supply rises faster than demand, prices tend to fall; when demand outpaces supply, prices tend to rise. Regression concerns one superior property among lesser ones, not a market-wide supply shift.
questions.citation: Appraisal principles; NYS DOS Salesperson Syllabus (Valuation)

questions.q: A comparable sold for $350,000. It has a two-car garage valued at $15,000; the subject property has no garage. Otherwise they are similar. What is the comparable's adjusted sale price?
questions.explanation: Adjust the comparable, never the subject. The comp is superior (it has the garage), so subtract: $350,000 − $15,000 = $335,000. Adding the $15,000 is the classic trap.
questions.citation: Appraisal principles — sales comparison approach; NYS DOS Salesperson Syllabus (Valuation)

questions.q: The subject property has a fireplace that the market values at $5,000. A comparable without a fireplace sold for $300,000. What is the comparable's adjusted sale price?
questions.explanation: The comparable is inferior to the subject (it lacks the fireplace), so add to the comparable: $300,000 + $5,000 = $305,000. Comps are adjusted to look like the subject; the subject is never adjusted.
questions.citation: Appraisal principles — sales comparison approach; NYS DOS Salesperson Syllabus (Valuation)

questions.q: Using the cost approach: land value is $90,000, replacement cost of the improvements new is $300,000, and accrued depreciation is $45,000. What is the indicated value?
questions.explanation: Cost approach = land + cost new of improvements − accrued depreciation: $90,000 + $300,000 − $45,000 = $345,000. Depreciation is taken from the improvements only; land is not depreciated.
questions.citation: Appraisal principles — cost approach; NYS DOS Salesperson Syllabus (Valuation)

questions.q: An appraiser valuing a 1890s Victorian estimates the cost to build a structure of equal utility using modern materials and current methods, rather than an exact duplicate with hand-carved trim. This estimate is:
options: Reproduction cost
Historical cost
Effective age cost
Replacement cost
questions.explanation: Replacement cost produces equivalent utility with modern materials and design; reproduction cost builds an exact replica with the same materials. Replacement cost is usually used for older, ornate buildings.
questions.citation: Appraisal principles — cost approach; NYS DOS Salesperson Syllabus (Valuation)

questions.q: A well-maintained four-bedroom house has only one bathroom, and one bedroom can be reached only by walking through another bedroom. This loss in value is best classified as:
options: Physical deterioration
Functional obsolescence
External obsolescence
Economic life
questions.explanation: Functional obsolescence is a loss from poor design, layout, or outdated features within the property. Physical deterioration is wear and tear; external obsolescence comes from outside the property.
questions.citation: Appraisal principles — depreciation; NYS DOS Salesperson Syllabus (Valuation)

questions.q: After a new landfill opens next to a subdivision, home values there decline. Why is this type of depreciation generally considered incurable?
options: The cause is outside the property, so the owner cannot correct it
The roof and siding would cost more to replace than they add
The floor plan cannot be changed without demolition
Land itself loses value as it physically wears out
questions.explanation: External (economic) obsolescence is caused by factors outside the property lines, such as a nearby landfill or highway, which the owner cannot fix; it is treated as incurable. Wear on the roof is physical deterioration, and a poor floor plan is functional obsolescence.
questions.citation: Appraisal principles — depreciation; NYS DOS Salesperson Syllabus (Valuation)

questions.q: An apartment building has potential gross income of $150,000, vacancy and collection loss of 5%, operating expenses of $46,500, and annual mortgage payments of $40,000. At an 8% capitalization rate, what is the indicated value?
questions.explanation: EGI = $150,000 − $7,500 = $142,500; NOI = $142,500 − $46,500 = $96,000; value = $96,000 ÷ 0.08 = $1,200,000. Mortgage payments are not an operating expense, so deducting them ($700,000) is wrong; a higher cap rate would lower the value.
questions.citation: Appraisal principles — income approach; NYS DOS Salesperson Syllabus (Valuation)

questions.q: A comparable single-family home sold for $270,000 and rents for $1,800 per month. Using that comparable's monthly gross rent multiplier, what is the indicated value of a similar home that rents for $2,000 per month?
questions.explanation: GRM = price ÷ monthly rent = $270,000 ÷ $1,800 = 150. Value = $2,000 × 150 = $300,000. Use the same time period (monthly vs. annual) for the multiplier and the rent.
questions.citation: Appraisal principles — gross rent multiplier; NYS DOS Salesperson Syllabus (Valuation)

questions.q: After completing the sales comparison, cost, and income approaches, an appraiser arrives at a single opinion of value. In reconciliation, the appraiser:
options: Averages the three indications equally so that no single approach dominates the result
Weighs each indication by its reliability and relevance to the property type
Always selects the highest of the three indications to protect the seller's equity
Uses only the cost approach for the final value because it is the most objective
questions.explanation: Reconciliation is a weighing process, not a simple average. For a single-family home the sales comparison approach typically gets the most weight; for an income property, the income approach.
questions.citation: Appraisal principles — reconciliation; NYS DOS Salesperson Syllabus (Valuation)

questions.q: A seller asks a salesperson for an 'appraisal' to use in her divorce settlement. The salesperson holds no appraiser credential. What is the best response?
options: Prepare a written appraisal, since a real estate salesperson license already authorizes formal valuations
Prepare the appraisal but have the supervising broker sign it, since the broker's license covers appraisals
Refuse to discuss value at all, because licensees may never give any estimate of a property's value
Offer a CMA clearly labeled as not an appraisal and refer her to a state-licensed or certified appraiser
questions.explanation: A salesperson may prepare a comparative market analysis for pricing, but it must not be represented as an appraisal; appraisals are performed by appraisers licensed or certified by New York State. The broker's name does not cure the lack of an appraiser credential.
questions.citation: NY Executive Law Article 6-E (real estate appraisers)

questions.q: A lender handling a foreclosed property asks a broker for an estimate of its likely selling price based on recent sales and an exterior inspection. This estimate is generally called a:
options: Broker price opinion
Certified appraisal
Tax assessment
Uniform residential appraisal report
questions.explanation: A broker price opinion (BPO) is a broker's estimate of probable selling price, often ordered by lenders for REO or short-sale decisions. It is not an appraisal and does not substitute for one where an appraisal is legally required.
questions.citation: NYS DOS Salesperson Syllabus (Valuation); NY Executive Law Article 6-E

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT a protected class under the federal Fair Housing Act?
options: Familial status
Disability
Marital status
National origin
questions.explanation: The federal FHA protects seven classes: race, color, religion, national origin, sex, familial status, and disability. Marital status is protected under NY Executive Law § 296, not the federal FHA — a classic federal-vs-state trap.
questions.citation: Federal Fair Housing Act, 42 U.S.C. § 3604; NY Executive Law § 296

questions.q: The 1988 amendments to the federal Fair Housing Act added which protected classes?
options: Disability and familial status
Sex and sexual orientation
Age (55 and older) and marital status
Religion and national origin
questions.explanation: The Fair Housing Amendments Act of 1988 added disability (handicap) and familial status. Religion and national origin were in the original 1968 Act and sex was added in 1974; age, marital status, and sexual orientation are not listed classes in the federal statute.
questions.citation: Fair Housing Amendments Act of 1988; 42 U.S.C. § 3604

questions.q: A homeowner selling her own single-family house without a broker and without advertising refuses to sell to a buyer because of the buyer's race, claiming the FHA single-family exemption. Which statement is correct?
options: The refusal is lawful because the owner used no broker and placed no advertising
The refusal is lawful only if the owner owns no more than three single-family homes
The refusal is lawful if the owner lived in the house at some point in the past 24 months
The refusal is unlawful because the Civil Rights Act of 1866 bars racial discrimination
questions.explanation: The Civil Rights Act of 1866 prohibits racial discrimination in property transactions with no exemptions, as confirmed by Jones v. Alfred H. Mayer Co. (1968). An FHA exemption never authorizes race discrimination.

questions.q: An Albany landlord rejects an applicant who meets all of the landlord's lawful income and credit criteria solely because part of the rent would be paid by a Housing Choice (Section 8) voucher. Under New York law, this is:
options: Lawful, because a voucher is not wage income
Unlawful lawful-source-of-income discrimination
Lawful if the building has fewer than six units
Unlawful only within New York City limits
questions.explanation: NY Executive Law § 296 protects lawful source of income statewide, including housing assistance vouchers. A landlord may apply neutral qualification criteria but may not reject an otherwise qualified applicant because assistance pays part of the rent; the trap is thinking this is NYC-only.

questions.q: A property manager learns that a rental applicant has an order of protection against a former partner and denies the application 'to avoid trouble in the building.' Under New York law, the denial is:
options: Lawful if the manager applies the policy to every such applicant
Lawful because domestic violence creates a safety risk
Unlawful discrimination based on status as a domestic violence victim
Unlawful only if the applicant also has minor children
questions.explanation: NY Executive Law § 296 protects status as a victim of domestic violence in housing. Applying the exclusion consistently does not cure it — a uniform policy of rejecting victims is still discrimination based on that status.

questions.q: Which protected category appears in the New York City Human Rights Law but not in the federal Fair Housing Act or NY Executive Law § 296?
options: Lawful occupation
Religion
Familial status
Disability
questions.explanation: The NYC Human Rights Law adds local categories such as lawful occupation and partnership status. Religion, familial status, and disability are already federal FHA classes, so local law layers on top of state and federal protections.
questions.citation: NYC Human Rights Law, NYC Admin. Code § 8-107

questions.q: Without being asked, a salesperson shows an Asian American buyer only listings in neighborhoods with large Asian populations, explaining that the buyer 'will feel more comfortable there.' This is:
options: Blockbusting
Redlining
Acceptable service because it is well intended
Steering
questions.explanation: Steering is guiding buyers or renters toward or away from areas based on a protected characteristic. Good intentions do not excuse it; the licensee must offer the same available options and let the buyer choose.
questions.citation: Federal Fair Housing Act, 42 U.S.C. § 3604; NY Executive Law § 296; DOS-2156 Fair Housing Disclosure

questions.q: To generate listings, a licensee mails flyers warning homeowners that 'families of a different religion are moving in — sell now before values fall.' This conduct is:
options: Steering (channeling buyers by area)
Blockbusting (panic peddling)
Redlining (area-based loan denial)
Lawful market advice to owners
questions.explanation: Blockbusting is inducing sales or listings by representing that protected-class members are entering a neighborhood and that harm (lower values, crime, worse schools) will follow. It is not market advice; it exploits fear tied to a protected status.
questions.citation: Federal Fair Housing Act, 42 U.S.C. § 3604(e); NY Executive Law § 296; DOS-2156 Fair Housing Disclosure

questions.q: A lender refuses to make mortgage loans anywhere in certain neighborhoods because of the racial composition of those areas, regardless of individual applicants' qualifications. This practice is:
options: Redlining
Steering
Blockbusting
Puffing
questions.explanation: Redlining is denying or restricting loans, insurance, or services in an area based on discriminatory geographic classification rather than the individual applicant's or property's legitimate risk. Steering and blockbusting are licensee conduct aimed at buyers and sellers.
questions.citation: Federal Fair Housing Act, 42 U.S.C. § 3605; NY Executive Law § 296

questions.q: Which advertisement wording is permissible for a New York rental listing?
options: Ideal for a single professional, no kids
Section 8 vouchers not accepted
Christian household strongly preferred
Two bedrooms, fenced yard, near train station
questions.explanation: Ads should describe the property, not the preferred occupant. The other choices express a preference based on familial status, lawful source of income, or religion, and adding an Equal Housing Opportunity logo would not cure them.
questions.citation: Federal Fair Housing Act, 42 U.S.C. § 3604(c); NY Executive Law § 296(5)

questions.q: A tenant who uses a wheelchair asks to install grab bars and widen the bathroom doorway in her rental apartment. Under the federal Fair Housing Act, this request is best classified as a:
options: Reasonable accommodation, always paid by the landlord
Rent concession the landlord may decline
Reasonable modification, generally at the tenant's expense
Request the landlord may refuse in a pre-1991 building
questions.explanation: A physical change to the premises is a reasonable modification; in ordinary private housing it is generally at the tenant's expense, and the landlord may reasonably condition interior work on restoration. A reasonable accommodation is a change to a rule, policy, or service; federally assisted housing and NY law can shift costs in some cases.
questions.citation: Federal Fair Housing Act, 42 U.S.C. § 3604(f)(3)(A); NY Executive Law § 296(18)

questions.q: A building has a strict no-pets policy. A tenant with a disability provides reliable documentation of a disability-related need for an emotional support animal. Under the New York State Human Rights Law, the landlord should generally:
options: Deny it, because the no-pets rule applies equally to everyone
Grant it as a reasonable accommodation without a pet deposit or fee
Grant it only if the tenant pays the standard pet deposit
Grant it only if the animal is a specially trained dog
questions.explanation: An assistance animal is not a pet; allowing it is a reasonable accommodation to the no-pets rule, and pet fees or deposits may not be charged (the tenant remains liable for actual damage). The 'trained dog' limit is the ADA service-animal definition, which does not narrow New York housing duties. Note: HUD withdrew its 2020 federal assistance-animal guidance (FHEO-2020-01) in September 2025, but the FHA statute and NY Executive Law § 296(18) still require reasonable accommodations.
questions.citation: NY Executive Law § 296(18)(2); Federal Fair Housing Act, 42 U.S.C. § 3604(f)(3)(B)

questions.q: Under the New York State Human Rights Law, the owner-occupied rental exemption applies only to a building with housing for no more than how many families, with the owner living in one unit?
options: Two
Three
Four
Six
questions.explanation: New York's owner-occupied exemption covers a building for no more than two families with the owner in residence. The federal 'Mrs. Murphy' exemption is broader (up to four units), so don't import the federal number into NY law.

questions.q: An owner lives in one unit of a four-family building in Buffalo and personally refuses to rent to a qualified applicant because of the applicant's religion. Which statement is most accurate?
options: It is lawful because owner-occupied buildings of four or fewer units are always exempt
It is lawful under New York law but still violates the federal Fair Housing Act
A federal exemption may apply, but NY's two-family limit makes it unlawful
It violates only the Civil Rights Act of 1866, not the NY Human Rights Law
questions.explanation: The federal owner-occupied exemption covers up to four units, but New York's covers only two-family buildings, so the owner still violates NY Executive Law § 296. The 1866 Act covers race, not religion, and a federal exemption never removes state liability.

questions.q: An owner who lives in one unit of a two-family house hires a salesperson to rent the other unit and says, 'Advertise it as adults only — no children.' The salesperson should:
options: Comply, because the owner-occupied exemption covers the listing
Comply, but add the Equal Housing Opportunity logo to the ad
Advertise 'adults only' but still show the unit to families who ask
Decline; the owner's exemption doesn't cover the licensee or the ad
questions.explanation: Owner-occupancy exemptions belong to the owner, not the licensee, and the ban on discriminatory advertising survives them. A client's instruction never authorizes a licensee to discriminate, and a logo does not cure a 'no children' ad.
questions.citation: Federal Fair Housing Act, 42 U.S.C. § 3604(c); NY Executive Law § 296(5)

questions.q: To qualify for the federal 55-and-older 'housing for older persons' exemption, at least what percentage of occupied units must have at least one occupant age 55 or older (along with published policies and age verification)?
questions.explanation: The 55+ category requires at least 80% of occupied units to have at least one person 55 or older, plus policies showing intent and age verification. The separate 62+ category requires all occupants to be 62 or older; either exemption excuses only familial-status exclusion, not race or disability discrimination.
questions.citation: Housing for Older Persons Act of 1995; 42 U.S.C. § 3607(b)

questions.q: When must a New York licensee provide the Housing and Anti-Discrimination Disclosure Form (DOS-2156) to a prospective buyer, seller, tenant, or landlord?
options: At the first substantive contact
When the purchase contract or lease is signed
Before the first showing, but only if the client asks
At closing, together with the deed
questions.explanation: 19 NYCRR § 175.28 requires the DOS-2156 at first substantive contact, delivered in writing or electronically; an oral explanation alone does not satisfy it. The broker keeps the signed acknowledgment (or documented refusal) for three years.

questions.q: Under DOS fair housing regulations, where must the Fair Housing and Anti-Discrimination Notice be displayed?
options: Only inside the main office, posted next to the broker's license certificate
In each office/branch window, on licensee websites, and at open houses
Only on the brokerage's website home page and its social media profiles
Only on listing agreements and leases for one-to-four family residential homes
questions.explanation: 19 NYCRR § 175.29 requires the notice in the window of every office and branch office, prominently on licensee-operated websites, and at each open house. Posting does not replace delivering the individual DOS-2156 disclosure.

questions.q: Under New York's standardized operating procedures law, a brokerage's written procedures for prospective homebuyers must state whether the brokerage requires buyers to:
options: Disclose their household size and religious affiliation
Show a credit score above a brokerage-set minimum
Pay a nonrefundable retainer before any showing
Show ID, sign an exclusive agreement, or get pre-approval
questions.explanation: RPL § 442-h requires brokers to adopt procedures stating whether ID, an exclusive buyer agreement, and pre-approval are required before services, apply them uniformly to every buyer, and post them on their websites/apps and make them available at the office. The law does not require the broker to demand these items — only to decide and apply the policy consistently.

questions.q: A renter believes a landlord violated the federal Fair Housing Act. Generally, how long does the renter have to file an administrative complaint with HUD?
options: 180 days
One year
Two years
Three years
questions.explanation: A HUD complaint is generally due within one year of the discriminatory act. A private federal FHA lawsuit generally has two years, and a complaint with the NYS Division of Human Rights currently has three years — the periods are not interchangeable.
questions.citation: 42 U.S.C. § 3610 (HUD complaint); 42 U.S.C. § 3613 (civil action); NY Executive Law § 297(5)

questions.q: A fair housing organization sends paired testers with similar qualifications but different races to inquire about the same apartment through a brokerage. Which statement is correct?
options: Testing is lawful, and unequal treatment of testers is evidence
Testing is illegal entrapment, so tester evidence is inadmissible
Licensees may refuse to deal with anyone they suspect is a tester
Testers lack standing to sue because they never intended to rent
questions.explanation: Paired testing is a recognized, lawful way to detect discrimination, and the Supreme Court held in Havens Realty Corp. v. Coleman (1982) that a tester falsely told a unit was unavailable has standing to sue. The safe practice is to treat every inquiry the same way.
questions.citation: Federal Fair Housing Act, 42 U.S.C. § 3604(d); Havens Realty Corp. v. Coleman (1982)

questions.q: Which law most directly requires a real estate brokerage's public office to be accessible to customers with disabilities?
options: The Equal Credit Opportunity Act (Regulation B)
The Real Estate Settlement Procedures Act (RESPA)
Title III of the Americans with Disabilities Act
Section 1982 of the Civil Rights Act of 1866
questions.explanation: ADA Title III covers places of public accommodation, which include a brokerage office open to the public. Disability issues in residential dwelling units are generally analyzed under the Fair Housing Act instead, so 'ADA' is not the answer to every housing-disability question.
questions.citation: Americans with Disabilities Act, Title III, 42 U.S.C. § 12181 et seq.

questions.q: A home sells for $640,000 with a 5.5% commission. The listing and cooperating brokers split the commission 50/50, and the listing salesperson receives 60% of the listing broker's share. How much does the listing salesperson earn?
questions.explanation: Total commission = $640,000 × 5.5% = $35,200; listing broker's half = $35,200 × 50% = $17,600; salesperson = $17,600 × 60% = $10,560. Trap: $21,120 takes 60% of the whole commission and skips the co-broke split, and $17,600 stops at the broker's share.
questions.citation: NY RPL § 442-a (salesperson paid only through own broker); DOS Salesperson Syllabus Subject 10 (commissions)

questions.q: A listing agreement calls for a commission of 6% on the first $500,000 of the sale price and 4% on any amount above $500,000. The property sells for $725,000. What is the total commission?
questions.explanation: 6% × $500,000 = $30,000; the excess is $725,000 − $500,000 = $225,000, and 4% × $225,000 = $9,000; total = $30,000 + $9,000 = $39,000. Trap: applying one rate to the whole price ($43,500 at 6% or $29,000 at 4%) ignores the tiered terms.
questions.citation: Listing agreement terms (commission rates are negotiable); DOS Salesperson Syllabus Subject 10 (commissions)

questions.q: A buyer's-side salesperson receives a $6,300 commission check. The total commission was 5% of the sale price, split equally between the listing and selling brokers, and she receives 70% of her broker's share. What was the sale price?
questions.explanation: Her share = price × 5% × 50% × 70% = price × 0.0175, so price = $6,300 ÷ 0.0175 = $360,000 (check: $360,000 × 5% = $18,000; ÷ 2 = $9,000; × 70% = $6,300). Trap: skipping the 50% co-broke split gives $180,000, and skipping her 70% split gives $252,000.
questions.citation: NY RPL § 442-a; DOS Salesperson Syllabus Subject 10 (commissions)

questions.q: A seller accepts a $480,000 offer. The commission is 5%, the seller's mortgage payoff is $212,000, and the seller's other closing costs (transfer tax, attorney fee, etc.) total $6,800. What are the seller's net proceeds?
questions.explanation: Commission = $480,000 × 5% = $24,000; net = $480,000 − $24,000 − $212,000 − $6,800 = $237,200. Trap: the commission is figured on the full sale price, not on the seller's $268,000 equity (which would give $247,800).
questions.citation: DOS Salesperson Syllabus Subject 3 (closing costs and adjustments) and Subject 10 (percentages)

questions.q: A seller wants to net $280,000 after paying a 6% commission, a $182,500 mortgage payoff, and $7,500 of other closing costs. What is the minimum sale price that achieves this?
questions.explanation: Price = (net + payoff + costs) ÷ (1 − commission rate) = ($280,000 + $182,500 + $7,500) ÷ 0.94 = $470,000 ÷ 0.94 = $500,000 (check: $500,000 − $30,000 − $182,500 − $7,500 = $280,000). Trap: adding 6% to $470,000 gives $498,200, which nets only $278,308 because the commission is charged on the price. This is only a pricing estimate — a net listing is prohibited in New York.
questions.citation: 19 NYCRR § 175.19 (net listings prohibited); DOS Salesperson Syllabus Subject 10 (percentages)

questions.q: A house outside New York City sells for $412,300, with no exemptions or continuing liens. What is the New York State real estate transfer tax?
questions.explanation: The tax is $2 for each $500 or fractional part: $412,300 ÷ $500 = 824.6, which rounds UP to 825 units; 825 × $2 = $1,650. Trap: the 0.4% shortcut ($1,649.20) or rounding down to 824 units ($1,648) ignores the fractional-part rule.

questions.q: An Albany County seller sells a house for $540,000 and pays off a $200,000 mortgage at closing. Assuming no exemptions, what is the NYS real estate transfer tax, and who ordinarily pays it?
options: $1,360, ordinarily paid by the seller
$2,160, ordinarily paid by the seller
$2,160, ordinarily paid by the buyer
$800, ordinarily paid by the seller
questions.explanation: $540,000 ÷ $500 = 1,080 units × $2 = $2,160 (the same as $4 per $1,000), owed by the grantor (seller) unless the contract shifts it. Trap: a mortgage the seller pays off at closing does not reduce the taxable consideration, so $1,360 (tax on $340,000) is wrong.

questions.q: A Bronx condominium unit sells for exactly $500,000. Using the residential rates, what is the New York City Real Property Transfer Tax (RPTT)?
questions.explanation: NYC residential RPTT is 1% when the consideration is $500,000 or less and 1.425% when it exceeds $500,000: $500,000 × 1% = $5,000. Trap: exactly $500,000 is not over $500,000, so 1.425% ($7,125) does not apply, and $2,000 is the separate NYS transfer tax.

questions.q: A one-family house in Queens sells for $640,000. What is the NYC Real Property Transfer Tax (RPTT)?
questions.explanation: Because $640,000 exceeds $500,000, the 1.425% residential rate applies to the entire consideration: $640,000 × 1.425% = $9,120. Trap: RPTT is not a marginal bracket, so $5,000 + 1.425% × $140,000 = $6,995 is wrong, and $6,400 uses the 1% rate.

questions.q: A buyer purchases a one-family home in Westchester County for exactly $1,000,000. What is the NYS additional ("mansion") tax, and who ordinarily pays it?
options: $10,000, paid by the seller
$0 (threshold not exceeded)
$10,000, paid by the buyer
$4,000, paid by the buyer
questions.explanation: The mansion tax is 1% of the entire consideration for residential property at $1,000,000 or more, paid by the grantee: $1,000,000 × 1% = $10,000, paid by the buyer. Trap: the threshold is $1 million OR MORE, so exactly $1,000,000 is taxed; $4,000 ($1,000,000 ÷ $500 × $2) is the seller's separate basic transfer tax.

questions.q: A Nassau County one-family home sells for $1,350,000 with no exemptions. How are the NYS basic transfer tax and the mansion tax ordinarily allocated?
options: Seller pays $13,500; buyer pays $5,400
Seller pays $5,400; buyer pays $13,500
Seller pays $5,400; buyer pays $3,500
Seller pays $18,900; buyer pays $0
questions.explanation: Basic transfer tax = $1,350,000 ÷ $500 = 2,700 units × $2 = $5,400, paid by the seller (grantor); mansion tax = $1,350,000 × 1% = $13,500, paid by the buyer (grantee). Trap: the mansion tax applies to the full price, not just the $350,000 above $1 million ($3,500).

questions.q: A buyer contracts to purchase a home for $450,000, but it appraises at $430,000. The lender will lend 80% of the lower of the price or the appraised value. Before closing costs, how much cash must the buyer bring toward the purchase price?
questions.explanation: Loan = 80% × $430,000 (the lower value) = $344,000; cash needed = $450,000 price − $344,000 loan = $106,000. Trap: 20% of the price ($90,000) or of the appraisal ($86,000) misses that the buyer also covers the $20,000 appraisal shortfall ($86,000 + $20,000 = $106,000).
questions.citation: DOS Salesperson Syllabus Subject 5 (Real Estate Finance) and Subject 10 (basic mortgage qualifying)

questions.q: A buyer purchases a $400,000 home with a 90% loan and agrees to pay 2 discount points. How much do the points cost?
questions.explanation: One point = 1% of the LOAN amount: loan = $400,000 × 90% = $360,000, and 2 points = $360,000 × 2% = $7,200. Trap: $8,000 applies the points to the purchase price, and $720 treats 2 points as 0.2%.

questions.q: A borrower originally borrowed $200,000; the current balance is $186,000 at 7.25% annual interest. Using the annual rate ÷ 12, how much interest will be charged for the next month?
questions.explanation: Monthly interest = current balance × annual rate ÷ 12 = $186,000 × 0.0725 ÷ 12 = $13,485 ÷ 12 = $1,123.75. Trap: interest accrues on the current balance, not the original $200,000 ($1,208.33), and $13,485 is a full year's interest.

questions.q: A $320,000, 30-year fixed-rate loan at 6% has a monthly principal-and-interest payment of $1,918.56. Using the annual rate ÷ 12, how much of the first payment goes to principal, and what is the new balance?
options: Principal $1,600.00; new balance $318,400.00
Principal $318.56; new balance $319,681.44
Principal $318.56; new balance $318,081.44
Principal $1,918.56; new balance $318,081.44
questions.explanation: First month's interest = $320,000 × 0.06 ÷ 12 = $1,600; principal = $1,918.56 − $1,600 = $318.56; new balance = $320,000 − $318.56 = $319,681.44. Trap: only the principal portion reduces the balance, so subtracting the whole payment ($318,081.44) or the interest ($318,400) is wrong.

questions.q: A developer buys a 5-acre tract and must reserve 20% of the land for roads. How many building lots of 10,890 square feet each can be created from the remaining land?
options: 20 lots
24 lots
4 lots
16 lots
questions.explanation: 5 acres × 43,560 = 217,800 sq ft; usable land = 217,800 × 80% = 174,240 sq ft; 174,240 ÷ 10,890 = 16 lots. Trap: 20 lots ignores the road reservation, and 4 lots uses the 20% set aside for roads instead of the 80% remaining.
questions.citation: DOS Salesperson Syllabus Subject 10 (acre = 43,560 sq ft)

questions.q: An irregular lot consists of a rectangle 242 feet wide by 300 feet deep plus an adjoining triangular section with a 242-foot base (along the rectangle's rear line) and a 120-foot height. At $45,000 per acre, what is the lot worth?
questions.explanation: Rectangle = 242 × 300 = 72,600 sq ft; triangle = 242 × 120 ÷ 2 = 14,520 sq ft; total = 87,120 sq ft ÷ 43,560 = 2 acres × $45,000 = $90,000. Trap: forgetting to halve the triangle gives 101,640 sq ft ($105,000), and leaving the triangle out gives $75,000.
questions.citation: DOS Salesperson Syllabus Subject 10 (irregular lot size, acre)

questions.q: A commercial lot has 80 feet of street frontage and a depth of 150 feet. It sells for $2,250 per front foot. What is the sale price?
questions.explanation: Front-foot pricing uses only the street frontage: 80 front feet × $2,250 = $180,000. Trap: using the 150-ft depth ($337,500) or adding frontage and depth ($517,500) misapplies the unit.

questions.q: An L-shaped one-story house measures 50 ft across the front and 55 ft from front to back at its deepest point. It consists of a front section 50 ft wide × 30 ft deep and a rear wing 20 ft wide × 25 ft deep. Similar homes sell for $280 per square foot. What is the indicated value?
questions.explanation: Split the L into rectangles: 50 × 30 = 1,500 sq ft plus 20 × 25 = 500 sq ft = 2,000 sq ft; 2,000 × $280 = $560,000. Trap: multiplying the outer dimensions (50 × 55 = 2,750 sq ft, $770,000) counts space that is not part of the house.
questions.citation: DOS Salesperson Syllabus Subject 10 (square feet, price per square foot)

questions.q: A house has a market value of $240,000 and a taxable assessed value of $180,000. The tax rate is 32.5 mills. What is the annual property tax?
questions.explanation: One mill is $1 per $1,000 (0.001), so tax = taxable assessed value × mills ÷ 1,000 = $180,000 × 32.5 ÷ 1,000 = $5,850. Trap: the rate applies to the assessed value, not the market value ($240,000 × 0.0325 = $7,800).
questions.citation: NY Real Property Tax Law; DOS Salesperson Syllabus Subject 10 (real property tax rate)

questions.q: A town must raise a $6,300,000 property tax levy, and the total taxable assessed value in the town is $180,000,000. What is the tax rate, and what is the tax on a home assessed at $90,000?
questions.explanation: Tax rate = levy ÷ total assessed value = $6,300,000 ÷ $180,000,000 = 0.035 = 35 mills ($3.50 per $100); tax = $90,000 × 0.035 = $3,150. Trap: dividing assessed value by the levy inverts the formula (28.57), and misplacing the decimal gives 3.5 or 350 mills.
questions.citation: NY Real Property Tax Law (tax levy); DOS Salesperson Syllabus Subject 14 (Taxes and Assessments)

questions.q: A town's equalization rate is 40%, meaning properties are assessed at 40% of full market value. A home's assessed value is $120,000. What is its estimated full market value?
questions.explanation: Full market value = assessed value ÷ equalization rate = $120,000 ÷ 0.40 = $300,000. Trap: multiplying by the rate ($120,000 × 0.40 = $48,000) goes the wrong direction, because the assessment is the smaller figure.
questions.citation: NY Real Property Tax Law (state equalization rates, NYS ORPTS); DOS Salesperson Syllabus Subject 14 (equalization)

questions.q: Closing is June 15 of a non-leap year. The calendar-year property taxes of $9,125 are unpaid and will be paid in full by the buyer later in the year. Using a 365-day year with actual days, and with the buyer owning the day of closing, what is the tax proration?
options: Debit seller and credit buyer $4,150
Credit seller and debit buyer $5,000
Credit seller and debit buyer $4,125
Debit seller and credit buyer $4,125
questions.explanation: Daily rate = $9,125 ÷ 365 = $25; seller's days Jan 1–June 14 = 31 + 28 + 31 + 30 + 31 + 14 = 165; 165 × $25 = $4,125, debited to the seller and credited to the buyer because the buyer will pay the seller's share later. Trap: giving the seller the closing day (166 days) yields $4,150.
questions.citation: Contract of sale apportionment clause; DOS Salesperson Syllabus Subject 3 (arithmetic of prorations)

questions.q: On September 1, the seller of a two-family house collected the tenant's $3,000 rent for September. Closing is September 21, and the seller is entitled to the rent for the day of closing. Prorating on the actual 30 days in September, what is the rent adjustment?
options: Credit seller and debit buyer $900
Debit seller and credit buyer $900
Debit seller and credit buyer $1,000
Debit seller and credit buyer $2,100
questions.explanation: Daily rent = $3,000 ÷ 30 = $100; the seller keeps Sept 1–21 (21 days), so the buyer is owed Sept 22–30 = 9 days × $100 = $900, debited to the seller and credited to the buyer. Trap: giving the buyer the closing day (10 days) yields $1,000, and $2,100 is the seller's own share.
questions.citation: Contract of sale apportionment clause; DOS Salesperson Syllabus Subject 3 (arithmetic of prorations)

questions.q: The seller has already paid the $5,400 school tax for the fiscal year July 1 through June 30. Closing is October 11, and the buyer owns the day of closing. Using a 360-day year (30-day months), what is the proration?
options: Credit seller and debit buyer $3,900
Debit seller and credit buyer $3,900
Credit seller and debit buyer $1,200
Credit seller and debit buyer $1,500
questions.explanation: Daily rate = $5,400 ÷ 360 = $15; seller's days July 1–Oct 10 = 30 + 30 + 30 + 10 = 100, so the buyer's share is 360 − 100 = 260 days × $15 = $3,900, credited to the seller (who prepaid) and debited to the buyer. Trap: counting from January 1 instead of the July 1 fiscal year gives $1,200, and $1,500 is the seller's own share.
questions.citation: Contract of sale apportionment clause; DOS Salesperson Syllabus Subject 3 (arithmetic of prorations)

questions.q: A buyer assumes the seller's $180,000 mortgage at 6% interest, which is paid in arrears; the seller's March 1 payment covered February's interest. Closing is March 16, and the seller owns the day of closing. Using a 360-day year, what is the interest proration?
options: Credit seller and debit buyer $480
Debit seller and credit buyer $450
Debit seller and credit buyer $480
Debit seller and credit buyer $420
questions.explanation: Daily interest = $180,000 × 0.06 ÷ 360 = $30, and the seller owes March 1–16 = 16 days × $30 = $480. Because the buyer will pay all of March's interest with the April 1 payment, debit the seller and credit the buyer $480; giving the buyer the closing day (15 days) would yield $450.
questions.citation: Contract of sale apportionment clause; DOS Salesperson Syllabus Subject 3 (arithmetic of prorations)

questions.q: An apartment building has potential gross income of $240,000, 5% vacancy and collection loss, $6,000 of other income, $96,000 of operating expenses, and $60,000 of annual mortgage debt service. Using an 8% capitalization rate, what is the indicated value?
questions.explanation: EGI = $240,000 − $12,000 vacancy + $6,000 other income = $234,000; NOI = $234,000 − $96,000 = $138,000; value = $138,000 ÷ 0.08 = $1,725,000. Trap: debt service is not an operating expense, so subtracting it ($78,000 ÷ 0.08 = $975,000) confuses NOI with cash flow.
questions.citation: Income approach (value = NOI ÷ cap rate); DOS Salesperson Syllabus Subject 16 (valuation via capitalization)

questions.q: An office building sells for $1,500,000. Its annual gross income is $165,000 and its annual operating expenses are $67,500. What capitalization rate does the sale indicate?
questions.explanation: NOI = $165,000 − $67,500 = $97,500; cap rate = NOI ÷ value = $97,500 ÷ $1,500,000 = 0.065 = 6.5%. Trap: dividing gross income by the price (11.0%) skips operating expenses.
questions.citation: Income approach (rate = NOI ÷ value); DOS Salesperson Syllabus Subject 16 (determining the cap rate)

questions.q: A two-family house sold for $432,000 when its total monthly rent was $3,600. A similar two-family house rents for $3,250 per month. Using the monthly gross rent multiplier from the sale, what is the subject's indicated value?
questions.explanation: Monthly GRM = $432,000 ÷ $3,600 = 120; value = 120 × $3,250 = $390,000. Trap: the multiplier and the rent must use the same period, so an annual GRM of 10 ($432,000 ÷ $43,200) times monthly rent gives a meaningless $32,500.
questions.citation: Gross rent multiplier (price ÷ gross rent); DOS Salesperson Syllabus Subject 8 (income approach)

questions.q: A retail lease requires base rent of $4,000 per month plus 5% of the tenant's annual gross sales above $600,000. This year's gross sales are $850,000. What is the total annual rent?
questions.explanation: Annual base rent = $4,000 × 12 = $48,000; percentage rent = 5% × ($850,000 − $600,000) = $12,500; total = $48,000 + $12,500 = $60,500. Trap: taking 5% of all sales ($42,500) on top of base gives $90,500, and forgetting to annualize the base gives $16,500.
questions.citation: Percentage lease terms; DOS Salesperson Syllabus Subject 16 (retail percentage lease)

questions.q: Using the cost approach, a building's replacement cost new is $400,000, its effective age is 12 years, and its total economic life is 50 years (straight-line depreciation). The land is valued at $120,000. What is the indicated property value?
questions.explanation: Depreciation = 12 ÷ 50 = 24% × $400,000 = $96,000; depreciated building = $400,000 − $96,000 = $304,000; plus land: $304,000 + $120,000 = $424,000. Trap: land is not depreciated, so depreciating the $520,000 total (giving $395,200) is wrong, and $304,000 omits the land.
questions.citation: Cost approach; DOS Salesperson Syllabus Subject 8 (depreciation) and Subject 10 (appreciation and depreciation)

questions.q: An investor buys a residential rental property for $440,000, of which $110,000 is allocated to land. Using straight-line depreciation over 27.5 years (ignoring the first-year mid-month convention), what is the annual depreciation deduction?
questions.explanation: Depreciable basis excludes land: $440,000 − $110,000 = $330,000; $330,000 ÷ 27.5 years = $12,000 per year. Trap: including land gives $16,000, and 39 years is the nonresidential period ($330,000 ÷ 39 = $8,461.54).
questions.citation: IRC § 168 (27.5-year residential rental property); DOS Salesperson Syllabus Subject 17 (straight-line depreciation)

questions.q: A homeowner bought a house for $320,000, and it is now worth $384,000. By what percentage has it appreciated?
questions.explanation: Percent change = (new − original) ÷ original = ($384,000 − $320,000) ÷ $320,000 = $64,000 ÷ $320,000 = 20%. Trap: dividing by the new value ($64,000 ÷ $384,000 = 16.67%) uses the wrong base.
questions.citation: DOS Salesperson Syllabus Subject 10 (appreciation and depreciation)

questions.q: An investor bought a lot for $80,000, spent $20,000 on improvements, and sold the property for $125,000. What was the percentage of profit on the investor's total cost?
questions.explanation: Total cost = $80,000 + $20,000 = $100,000; profit = $125,000 − $100,000 = $25,000; $25,000 ÷ $100,000 = 25%. Trap: dividing by the sale price ($25,000 ÷ $125,000 = 20%) or ignoring the improvements ($45,000 ÷ $80,000 = 56.25%) uses the wrong figures.

questions.q: An owner wants an entire neighborhood's zoning district changed from residential to commercial. In a New York town, which body has the power to amend the zoning ordinance and map?
options: The town board
The zoning board of appeals
The planning board
The building inspector
questions.explanation: Adopting and amending zoning is a legislative act of the town board (city council or village board of trustees). The ZBA grants variances and interprets the ordinance; it cannot rezone.

questions.q: In a New York village, which elected body adopts the zoning law and the village budget?
options: The zoning board of appeals
The planning board
The board of trustees
The board of assessment review
questions.explanation: A village's legislative body is its board of trustees, which adopts local laws including zoning, plus the budget and tax rate. Appointed boards such as the planning board and ZBA do not.

questions.q: Which statement about a town planning board is accurate?
