options: Its members are elected by town voters, and it grants use and area variances
Its members are appointed by the town board, and it reviews subdivision plats
Its members are appointed by the governor, and it collects town property taxes
Its members are elected by town voters, and it adopts the annual town budget
questions.explanation: Planning board members are appointed by the legislative body. The board performs authorized land-use review such as subdivision plats and site plans, and advises on the comprehensive plan.

questions.q: A company wants to build an office building on a lot where offices are a permitted use. The town requires review of the parking layout, lighting, drainage and landscaping. This is:
options: A use variance hearing before the zoning board of appeals
A rezoning before the town board
A certificate of occupancy inspection
Site plan review, typically by the planning board
questions.explanation: Site plan review examines how a permitted use is laid out on the parcel: parking, access, lighting, drainage and landscaping. No variance is needed because the use is allowed.

questions.q: A building inspector denies a permit because he interprets a proposed garage apartment as a prohibited second dwelling. The owner believes the ordinance allows it. Where does the owner first appeal the interpretation?
options: The town board of assessment review
The County Clerk
The Department of State
The zoning board of appeals
questions.explanation: The ZBA hears appeals from orders, interpretations and determinations of the administrative official charged with enforcing the zoning ordinance. It acts as the ordinance's interpreter.

questions.q: Which description of a zoning board of appeals is most accurate?
options: A legislative body that rewrites the zoning map when owners request it
A quasi-judicial body that applies legal standards to appeals and variances
An elected body that sets the tax rate and adopts the budget
An advisory body whose decisions are never binding on applicants
questions.explanation: The ZBA is administrative and quasi-judicial: it decides appeals, interpretations and variance requests under statutory standards. Rezoning is legislative and belongs to the governing board.

questions.q: A property owner in a designated design district wants to replace a storefront facade and add a large sign. Which local body typically reviews exterior appearance, signs and fences where established?
options: The architectural review board
The board of assessment review
The conservation advisory council
The county health department
questions.explanation: An architectural review board reviews the effect of new construction or alterations on the surrounding area, especially exteriors, signs and fences. Its approval is separate from zoning and building-code compliance.
questions.citation: NY Town Law; NY Village Law (local architectural review law)

questions.q: What is the primary role of a municipal conservation advisory council?
options: To issue building permits for new homes proposed near wetlands
To grant area and use variances for building in environmental zones
To study and advise on the community's natural resources and open space
To set assessed values for undeveloped open land on the tax roll
questions.explanation: A conservation advisory council is an appointed body that inventories and advises on natural resources and open space. It does not issue building permits, grant variances, or replace a DEC wetland permit.

questions.q: A buyer's agent wants to confirm that a finished basement was built with permits and passed inspection. Which local office should be contacted?
options: The building department or code enforcement office
The receiver of taxes or the town assessor's office
The zoning board of appeals or the planning board
The town board clerk's election office
questions.explanation: The building department issues building permits, conducts inspections, issues certificates of occupancy/completion and handles violations. It is the gatekeeper for construction activity.
questions.citation: NY Executive Law Article 18; local building code

questions.q: A homeowner complains that her property tax bill is too high and asks who set the tax rate. Which statement is correct?
options: The assessor sets both the assessed value and the tax rate
The receiver of taxes sets both the assessed value and the tax rate
The assessor values property; the legislative body sets the levy and tax rate
The planning board sets the tax rate as part of the master plan
questions.explanation: The assessor estimates value for the assessment roll. The governing body adopts the budget and tax levy, from which the rate is derived, and the receiver of taxes collects. These roles are separate.

questions.q: A buyer is purchasing a rural lot with no public sewer. Which agency typically must approve the design of a new septic system?
options: The zoning board of appeals
The county health department
The architectural review board
The town assessor
questions.explanation: Septic system design approval is typically handled by the county (or state) health department under sanitary code standards, not by zoning or design boards.
questions.citation: NY Public Health Law; county sanitary code

questions.q: A town proposes rezoning a parcel within 500 feet of a state highway. Before final action, New York law generally requires the town to:
options: Obtain approval from the State Department of Transportation
Hold a referendum of all town voters
Obtain a positive declaration under SEQR
Refer the proposal to the county planning agency for review
questions.explanation: Certain zoning actions affecting property within 500 feet of a municipal boundary, state or county road, park or other listed facilities must be referred to the county planning agency. If the county recommends disapproval or modification, the local board can act contrary to it only by a vote of a majority plus one of all its members.

questions.q: An owner of a designated landmark building in New York City wants to replace its original windows. Which agency must approve the work?
options: The Board of Standards and Appeals
The City Planning Commission
The local community board
The Landmarks Preservation Commission
questions.explanation: NYC's Landmarks Preservation Commission designates landmarks and historic districts and regulates alterations to designated properties. Historic age alone is not landmark status.
questions.citation: NYC Administrative Code § 25-301 et seq. (Landmarks Law)

questions.q: In New York City, which agency issues building permits and certificates of occupancy and enforces the construction codes?
options: The City Planning Commission
The Department of Buildings
The Board of Standards and Appeals
The Department of Finance
questions.explanation: The NYC Department of Buildings issues permits and COs, inspects work and enforces the construction codes and Zoning Resolution. CPC handles planning/zoning changes; BSA grants variances.
questions.citation: NYC Charter Chapter 26; NYC Construction Codes

questions.q: An owner in New York City needs a zoning variance for a building that cannot meet a setback requirement because of the lot's irregular shape. Which body decides the variance?
options: The Board of Standards and Appeals
The City Planning Commission
The NYC Department of Buildings
The local community board
questions.explanation: In NYC, the Board of Standards and Appeals grants zoning variances and certain special permits and hears appeals from Department of Buildings determinations. It plays the role a ZBA plays elsewhere.

questions.q: In New York City, which body votes on zoning map amendments during ULURP, after the community board and borough president have made recommendations?
options: The Board of Standards and Appeals
The Department of Buildings
The City Planning Commission
The Landmarks Preservation Commission
questions.explanation: Under ULURP, the City Planning Commission holds a hearing and votes after the community board and borough president review. Its approvals then go to the City Council for review.

questions.q: Which is the correct order of review under NYC's Uniform Land Use Review Procedure (ULURP) after an application is certified complete?
options: Community board, borough president, City Planning Commission, City Council
Borough president, community board, City Council, City Planning Commission
City Planning Commission, City Council, community board, borough president
Community board, City Council, borough president, City Planning Commission
questions.explanation: ULURP runs: Department of City Planning certifies the application, then community board review, borough president review, City Planning Commission vote, and City Council review, with a possible mayoral veto.

questions.q: Under ULURP, a community board votes to disapprove a proposed rezoning. What is the effect?
options: The application is automatically denied and may not proceed
The application must be refiled with the Board of Standards and Appeals
The recommendation is advisory; the application continues to later review stages
The rezoning may proceed only if the mayor overrides the board
questions.explanation: Community board and borough president recommendations are advisory. Binding decisions are made by the City Planning Commission and the City Council.

questions.q: Under ULURP, how long does the community board have to hold a public hearing and submit its recommendation after receiving a certified application?
options: 30 days
60 days
50 days
90 days
questions.explanation: The community board has 60 days, the borough president 30 days, the City Planning Commission 60 days, and the City Council 50 days. Don't mix up the 30-day borough president period.

questions.q: Before a town zoning board of appeals decides a variance application, Town Law requires the board to:
options: Obtain the town board's written consent
Get approval from the county clerk
Get a certificate of occupancy for the parcel
Hold a public hearing after giving public notice
questions.explanation: The ZBA must fix a time for a public hearing, give public notice (including newspaper publication), and let interested parties be heard before deciding.

questions.q: A neighbor believes the town ZBA wrongly granted a use variance next door. How is the decision generally challenged in court?
options: An Article 78 proceeding, which may be brought at any time within six years after the decision
An appeal to the town board, which may reverse any decision of the zoning board of appeals
A complaint to the Department of State, which may revoke the variance
An Article 78 proceeding, generally within 30 days after the decision is filed with the town clerk
questions.explanation: ZBA decisions are reviewed by an Article 78 proceeding in State Supreme Court. Town Law sets a short deadline: 30 days after the decision is filed in the town clerk's office. The town board does not sit as an appeals body over the ZBA.

questions.q: In an Article 78 proceeding challenging a planning board decision, what does the court generally decide?
options: Whether the court itself would have voted the same way after holding a new hearing
Whether the decision was illegal, arbitrary and capricious, or lacked a rational basis
Whether the applicant's project would be the most profitable use of the property
Whether a majority of residents support the planning board's decision
questions.explanation: Article 78 review is deferential. The court asks whether the agency acted lawfully and rationally (not arbitrarily or capriciously) and does not substitute its own judgment or rehear the application from scratch.

questions.q: Which homeowner's policy form is the most widely used for owner-occupied homes and covers the dwelling against all losses except those specifically excluded?
options: HO-2 (broad form)
HO-3 (special form)
HO-4 (tenants form)
HO-8 (market value form)
questions.explanation: HO-3, the special form, covers the dwelling on an open-peril basis: everything is covered unless it is excluded. Personal property under an HO-3 is usually covered only for named perils, while HO-2 is a named-peril form for both.
questions.citation: NYS DOS 77-hr Salesperson Syllabus, Subject 12: Property Insurance (HO-3 Special Form)

questions.q: A tenant renting an apartment wants insurance for her furniture, clothing, and personal liability. Which policy form fits her needs?
options: HO-3
HO-6
HO-8
HO-4
questions.explanation: HO-4 is the tenant's (renter's) form covering contents and personal liability; the building itself is insured by the landlord. HO-6 is for condominium unit owners, and HO-3 and HO-8 insure owner-occupied dwellings.
questions.citation: NYS DOS 77-hr Salesperson Syllabus, Subject 12: Property Insurance (HO-4 Tenants Policy)

questions.q: A condominium association carries a master policy on the building. Which policy should an individual unit owner buy to cover personal property, interior improvements, and personal liability?
options: HO-6
HO-2
HO-4
HO-1
questions.explanation: HO-6 is the condominium unit-owner form; the master policy does not automatically cover everything inside each unit. The DOS syllabus lists HO-6 for condominium owners and HO-4 for tenants and cooperative owners.
questions.citation: NYS DOS 77-hr Salesperson Syllabus, Subject 12: Property Insurance (HO-6 Condominium Owners)

questions.q: An 1890s Victorian has a market value of $350,000 but would cost $700,000 to rebuild with its original ornate materials. Which policy form is designed for this situation?
options: HO-5
HO-3
HO-8
HO-6
questions.explanation: HO-8 is the modified (market value) form for older homes whose rebuilding cost exceeds market value; it is a modified version of HO-1 that pays actual cash value or repair with common modern materials rather than full replacement cost. Don't assume it pays the home's sale price.
questions.citation: NYS DOS 77-hr Salesperson Syllabus, Subject 12: Property Insurance (HO-8 Market Value Policy)

questions.q: Which homeowner's form includes all of the HO-3 coverage and also extends open-peril coverage to personal property, making it the broadest of the standard forms?
options: HO-1
HO-2
HO-4
HO-5
questions.explanation: HO-5, the comprehensive form, covers both the dwelling and personal property against all perils not excluded. HO-3 covers personal property for named perils only; HO-1 and HO-2 are named-peril forms.
questions.citation: NYS DOS 77-hr Salesperson Syllabus, Subject 12: Property Insurance (HO-5 Comprehensive Form)

questions.q: Under a named-peril homeowner's policy such as an HO-2, a loss is covered only if:
options: it was caused by a peril specifically listed in the policy
it was not specifically excluded by the policy
the homeowner reports it within 24 hours
the home is insured for at least 80% of its market value
questions.explanation: A named-peril policy covers only the perils it lists, such as fire, windstorm, or theft. 'Covered unless excluded' describes open-peril (special) coverage, like the dwelling coverage in an HO-3; that difference is the key trap.
questions.citation: NYS DOS 77-hr Salesperson Syllabus, Subject 12: Property Insurance (HO-1, HO-2 named perils)

questions.q: A single policy that combines property coverage for the dwelling and contents with personal liability coverage is called a:
options: monoline policy
umbrella policy
package policy
title policy
questions.explanation: A package policy bundles several coverages, such as property and liability, in one contract; the standard homeowner's policy is a package. A monoline policy covers a single line, such as fire only.
questions.citation: NYS DOS 77-hr Salesperson Syllabus, Subject 12: Property Insurance (monoline vs. package policy)

questions.q: A guest slips on a homeowner's icy front steps and sues for her injuries. Which part of a standard homeowner's policy is designed to respond?
options: Dwelling coverage (Coverage A)
Personal liability coverage (Coverage E)
Loss-of-use coverage (Coverage D)
Other structures coverage (Coverage B)
questions.explanation: Personal liability coverage pays for covered claims when the insured's negligence injures others or damages their property, including legal defense. Dwelling, other-structures, and loss-of-use coverages pay for the insured's own property losses and extra living costs.
questions.citation: ISO homeowners policy (Section II liability); NYS DOS 77-hr Syllabus, Subject 12 (liability coverage)

questions.q: What is the key difference between replacement cost coverage and actual cash value (ACV) coverage?
options: ACV subtracts depreciation from the cost to replace; replacement cost pays to replace without that deduction
ACV pays the original purchase price of the item; replacement cost pays the current value of the land
Replacement cost always pays less than ACV for the same loss because it excludes upgrades
ACV applies only to flood losses, and replacement cost applies only to fire and windstorm losses
questions.explanation: Actual cash value equals replacement cost minus depreciation, while replacement cost coverage pays to repair or replace with like kind and quality without deducting depreciation. Land value is irrelevant because insurance covers rebuilding the structure.
questions.citation: NYS DOS 77-hr Salesperson Syllabus, Subject 12: Property Insurance (actual cash value or replacement cost)

questions.q: A covered fire destroys a homeowner's living room furniture. New replacement furniture costs $3,000, applicable depreciation is $1,800, and the policy pays actual cash value with a $500 deductible. Assuming no other limits, how much will the insurer pay?
questions.explanation: ACV = $3,000 − $1,800 = $1,200; payment = $1,200 − $500 deductible = $700. $2,500 wrongly applies the deductible to replacement cost and ignores depreciation.
questions.citation: NYS DOS 77-hr Salesperson Syllabus, Subject 12: Property Insurance (actual cash value, deductibles)

questions.q: A home has a replacement cost of $450,000, and its policy has an 80% coinsurance clause. What is the minimum coverage needed to avoid a coinsurance penalty on partial losses?
questions.explanation: $450,000 × 0.80 = $360,000. Meeting 80% avoids the partial-loss penalty, but it does not mean a total loss will be paid in full; payment is still capped at the policy limit.
questions.citation: Coinsurance (80% rule); NYS DOS 77-hr Syllabus, Subject 12 (amount of insurance needed)

questions.q: A home's replacement cost is $400,000, and the owner carries $320,000 of coverage under a policy with an 80% coinsurance clause. A kitchen fire causes $50,000 of covered damage. Ignoring the deductible, how much will the insurer pay?
questions.explanation: Required coverage = $400,000 × 0.80 = $320,000. The owner carries $320,000, which meets the requirement, so the full $50,000 partial loss is paid. $40,000 is the trap of paying only 80% of the loss.
questions.citation: Coinsurance (80% rule); NYS DOS 77-hr Syllabus, Subject 12 (amount of insurance needed)

questions.q: A home's replacement cost is $300,000, and the owner carries only $180,000 of coverage under a policy with an 80% coinsurance clause. A storm causes $40,000 of covered damage. Ignoring the deductible, how much will the insurer pay?
questions.explanation: Required = $300,000 × 0.80 = $240,000. Payment = ($180,000 ÷ $240,000) × $40,000 = 0.75 × $40,000 = $30,000. $24,000 wrongly divides by the full $300,000 replacement cost instead of the 80% requirement.
questions.citation: Coinsurance (80% rule); NYS DOS 77-hr Syllabus, Subject 12 (amount of insurance needed)

questions.q: A homeowner raises the policy deductible from $500 to $2,500. What is the most likely effect?
options: The premium goes down, and the homeowner pays more out of pocket on each claim
The premium goes up because the insurer now pays a larger share of each covered claim
The policy limits automatically double to match the higher deductible
Flood losses become covered under the policy
questions.explanation: The deductible is the portion of a covered loss the insured pays before the insurer pays. A higher deductible shifts more risk to the insured, so the premium is usually lower; it does not change limits or add excluded perils.
questions.citation: NYS DOS 77-hr Salesperson Syllabus, Subject 12: Property Insurance (insurance policy deductibles)

questions.q: A buyer assumes her new HO-3 policy will cover damage if a nearby river overflows into the house. Which statement is accurate?
options: Standard homeowner's policies cover all water damage, including river and storm-surge flooding
Flood is generally excluded, so she needs a separate flood policy, such as one through the NFIP
Flood is covered automatically under an HO-3 only if the home is outside a mapped flood zone
Her owner's title insurance policy will cover any flood losses that happen after closing
questions.explanation: Standard homeowner's and renter's policies generally exclude flood; flood coverage is bought separately through FEMA's National Flood Insurance Program or a private flood insurer. Homes outside high-risk zones can still flood and are not automatically covered.
questions.citation: National Flood Insurance Program (FEMA); NYS DOS 77-hr Syllabus, Subject 12

questions.q: A buyer is financing a home with an FHA-insured mortgage, and the property lies in a FEMA-designated Special Flood Hazard Area. Which statement is correct?
options: Flood insurance is optional because FHA loans are exempt
Flood insurance is required only if the home has flooded in the last 10 years
Flood insurance is required as a condition of the federally backed loan
The seller must buy flood insurance covering the buyer's first year
questions.explanation: Under the Flood Disaster Protection Act of 1973, loans made, insured, or guaranteed by federal agencies or federally regulated lenders on buildings in Special Flood Hazard Areas require flood insurance. The requirement depends on the flood zone and federal connection, not on past flooding.
questions.citation: Flood Disaster Protection Act of 1973, 42 U.S.C. § 4012a

questions.q: A homeowner with no pending mortgage transaction buys an NFIP flood policy on June 1. Flooding damages the home on June 15. What is the likely result?
options: The loss is fully covered because the premium was paid before the flood occurred
The loss is covered at half the policy limit because it occurred within the first 30 days
It is generally not covered, because NFIP policies typically have a 30-day waiting period
The loss is covered only if the homeowner also carries an HO-3 policy on the dwelling
questions.explanation: NFIP coverage generally becomes effective 30 days after purchase. Exceptions include a policy bought in connection with making, increasing, extending, or renewing a loan, which can take effect at closing, so buying when a storm is forecast is usually too late.
questions.citation: National Flood Insurance Act, 42 U.S.C. § 4013(c); FEMA NFIP rules

questions.q: Which statement correctly distinguishes title insurance from hazard insurance?
options: Both are paid as monthly premiums and protect the owner against future fire and storm damage
Hazard insurance protects against forgeries and defects in the chain of title, while title insurance covers fire losses
Title insurance covers physical damage occurring after closing; hazard insurance covers prior liens
Title insurance covers title defects existing before the policy date; hazard insurance covers future physical losses
questions.explanation: Title insurance looks backward: a one-time premium paid at closing protects against covered defects in title, such as forgeries or undisclosed liens, that existed on the policy date. Hazard (homeowner's) insurance looks forward, with ongoing premiums for physical losses such as fire.
questions.citation: NY Insurance Law Article 64 (title insurance); NYS DOS 77-hr Syllabus (title insurance; homeowner's insurance)

questions.q: A homeowner wants extra liability protection above the limits of his homeowner's and auto policies. Which coverage fits?
options: Umbrella (excess liability) policy
HO-8 modified coverage form
NFIP flood policy
Owner's title insurance policy
questions.explanation: An umbrella policy provides additional liability coverage that kicks in after the underlying policies' liability limits are exhausted. It does not add property coverage such as flood protection for the house.
questions.citation: NYS DOS 77-hr Salesperson Syllabus, Subject 12: Property Insurance (umbrella policies)

questions.q: A landlord insures a rental two-family house under a landlord's (dwelling) policy. A tenant's laptop is stolen from her unit. Which statement is correct?
options: The landlord's policy covers the laptop because the theft occurred inside the landlord's insured building
The landlord's policy generally does not cover tenants' belongings; she needs her own renter's (HO-4) policy
NY law requires the landlord to reimburse tenants for any theft that occurs inside a rental unit
The landlord's owner's title insurance policy covers theft losses suffered by tenants
questions.explanation: A landlord's policy insures the building, the landlord's own property, and typically liability and loss of rents, not the tenants' personal property. Tenants protect their contents and liability with an HO-4.
questions.citation: NYS DOS 77-hr Salesperson Syllabus, Subject 12: Property Insurance (HO-4; commercial/landlord policies)

questions.q: A buyer's insurance agent warns that the home's CLUE report shows two prior water-damage claims. What is a CLUE report?
options: A municipal record of open building permits and code violations filed against the property
A credit bureau report on the buyer's mortgage payment history and outstanding debts
A FEMA map showing the flood zone boundaries and base flood elevations for the property
An insurance-industry report of a property's claims history, typically for up to seven years
questions.explanation: The Comprehensive Loss Underwriting Exchange (CLUE) report lists past insurance claims on a property, typically for up to seven years. Prior claims can raise premiums or affect insurability, so sellers can order a report on their own property before listing.
questions.citation: Comprehensive Loss Underwriting Exchange (LexisNexis); Fair Credit Reporting Act

questions.q: Which comparison of the HO-1 and HO-2 forms is correct?
options: Both are named-peril forms, but HO-2 (broad) covers more listed perils than HO-1 (basic)
HO-1 is an open-peril form covering all losses not excluded, while HO-2 is named-peril
HO-2 is designed only for renters, and HO-1 is designed only for condominium unit owners
HO-1 covers flood damage from rising water, while HO-2 excludes flood entirely
questions.explanation: HO-1 (basic) covers a limited list of named perils, and HO-2 (broad) covers those plus additional named perils. Neither is open-peril, and neither covers flood.
questions.citation: NYS DOS 77-hr Salesperson Syllabus, Subject 12: Property Insurance (HO-1 Basic, HO-2 Broad)

questions.q: A real property tax described as "ad valorem" is one that is:
options: Based on the value of the property
Charged at a flat amount per parcel
Based on the owner's annual income
Imposed only when the property is sold
questions.explanation: Ad valorem means "according to value": the tax is the taxable assessed value times the tax rate. A flat per-parcel fee or a tax triggered by a sale (transfer tax) is a different kind of charge.

questions.q: A home has a taxable assessed value of $180,000 and the tax rate is 32 mills. What is the annual property tax?
questions.explanation: One mill is $1 per $1,000 (0.001). $180,000 × 32 ÷ 1,000 = $5,760. The trap is misplacing the decimal ($576 or $57,600).

questions.q: A school district needs a tax levy of $4,500,000. The total taxable assessed value in the district is $150,000,000. What is the tax rate?
options: $3 per $1,000 of assessed value (3 mills)
$30 per $1,000 of assessed value (30 mills)
$300 per $1,000 of assessed value
$0.30 per $1,000 of assessed value
questions.explanation: Tax rate = levy ÷ taxable assessed value: $4,500,000 ÷ $150,000,000 = 0.03, which is $30 per $1,000, or 30 mills.

questions.q: In the municipal budget process, the property tax levy is best described as:
options: The total approved budget, before state aid and fees are counted
The total assessed value of all taxable parcels in the municipality
The tax rate multiplied by a single parcel's full market value
The approved budget minus revenue from non-property-tax sources
questions.explanation: The levy is what must be raised by real property taxes: total appropriations minus non-property-tax revenue (state aid, fees, etc.). The levy is then divided by the total taxable assessed value to set the rate.

questions.q: A town's equalization rate is 45%. A house in that town is assessed at $90,000. What is its estimated full market value?
questions.explanation: Full market value = assessed value ÷ equalization rate: $90,000 ÷ 0.45 = $200,000. Multiplying ($90,000 × 0.45 = $40,500) is the common trap.

questions.q: Why does New York State calculate equalization rates for municipalities?
options: To set each homeowner's individual tax bill directly from the state level
To fairly apportion taxes among towns that assess at different percentages of value
To determine the minimum opening bid for property sold at a county tax auction
To convert a property's market value into its replacement cost for insurance
questions.explanation: New York municipalities may assess at a uniform percentage of value that differs from place to place. When a county or school district spans several municipalities, equalization rates put their assessments on a common full-value basis so the levy is apportioned fairly.

questions.q: A property has an assessed value of $200,000 and qualifies for a $30,000 exemption. The tax rate is 25 mills. What is the tax?
questions.explanation: Exemptions reduce the taxable assessed value: $200,000 − $30,000 = $170,000. Then $170,000 × 25 ÷ 1,000 = $4,250. Taxing the full $200,000 ($5,000) ignores the exemption.
questions.citation: NY RPTL (exemptions and taxable assessed value)

questions.q: A village installs new sidewalks and charges only the owners whose lots front the new sidewalk. This charge is a:
options: Special assessment
General ad valorem tax
Real estate transfer tax
Mortgage recording tax
questions.explanation: A special assessment is levied only against the specific properties that benefit from a local improvement, and it becomes a specific lien on those parcels. A general ad valorem tax is spread over all taxable property.
questions.citation: NY RPTL (special ad valorem levies and special assessments)

questions.q: A homeowner has a first mortgage recorded in 2019 and stops paying property taxes in 2026. Regarding lien priority, the unpaid real property tax lien generally:
options: Takes priority over the mortgage even though the mortgage was recorded first
Is junior to the mortgage because the mortgage was recorded seven years earlier
Has equal priority with the mortgage, and the two share any sale proceeds pro rata
Does not become a lien on the property until the owner sells or refinances
questions.explanation: Real property tax liens are given priority over private liens such as mortgages regardless of recording date. That is why lenders often escrow taxes. "First in time, first in right" does not apply to property tax liens.

questions.q: Which statement about the STAR program is correct?
options: Basic STAR is available only to owner-occupants age 65 or older
STAR reduces county and town property taxes but never school taxes
Enhanced STAR is for seniors 65+ with income under a lower limit than Basic STAR
STAR is available for any rental or investment property the owner holds
questions.explanation: STAR (School Tax Relief) reduces school taxes on an owner-occupied primary residence. Basic STAR has no age requirement. Enhanced STAR gives a larger benefit to income-qualified seniors age 65 and over.

questions.q: A couple buys their first home in New York in 2026 and wants STAR school tax relief. How do new STAR applicants generally receive the benefit?
options: As a seller credit against the purchase price applied at closing
As a STAR credit check from NYS after registering with Tax and Finance
As an itemized deduction claimed on their federal income tax return only
As an automatic exemption the assessor applies with no registration needed
questions.explanation: Since 2016, new STAR applicants register with NYS Tax and Finance and receive a STAR credit check rather than a new exemption on the assessment roll. Existing exemption holders could keep the exemption.
questions.citation: NY RPTL § 425; NY Tax Law § 606(eee) (STAR credit)

questions.q: An owner who is 70, lives in the home, and has limited income may qualify for a partial real property tax exemption of up to 50% under which program?
options: The alternative veterans exemption
The agricultural assessment
The Basic STAR credit
The senior citizens exemption
questions.explanation: The senior citizens exemption lets localities give owners 65 and over with limited income a partial exemption, up to 50% of assessed value. The veterans and agricultural programs have different eligibility rules.

questions.q: A farmer's land in an agricultural district is valued for tax purposes on its farming value instead of its development value. This is called:
options: A special assessment
An equalization adjustment
A tax certiorari
An agricultural assessment
questions.explanation: The agricultural assessment program taxes qualifying farmland on its agricultural value. Land converted to non-farm use can owe payments for the taxes it was spared.

questions.q: A homeowner thinks her assessment is too high. What is generally her FIRST formal step to challenge it?
options: File a Small Claims Assessment Review petition before the tentative roll is filed
File a grievance (complaint) with the Board of Assessment Review by Grievance Day
Start a tax certiorari proceeding in State Supreme Court
Stop paying taxes until the assessor reduces the value
questions.explanation: Administrative review comes first: a written complaint to the Board of Assessment Review (BAR) by Grievance Day. SCAR or tax certiorari follow only after the BAR decides. Withholding taxes creates a tax lien and penalties.

questions.q: In most New York towns, Grievance Day, when the Board of Assessment Review hears complaints, falls on:
options: The first Monday in January
March 1, the taxable status date
The fourth Tuesday in May
The last business day of December
questions.explanation: In towns, the BAR generally meets on the fourth Tuesday in May. March 1 is the usual taxable status date, not Grievance Day. Dates can differ in cities, villages, and some counties, so owners should check locally.

questions.q: Which owner may use Small Claims Assessment Review (SCAR)?
options: An owner-occupant of a one- to three-family home who first filed a BAR grievance
The owner of a 40-unit apartment building who skipped the BAR grievance
Any commercial owner whose assessment exceeds $1 million after BAR review
A rent-stabilized tenant who disputes the annual increase set by the RGB
questions.explanation: SCAR is an informal, low-cost review mainly for owner-occupied 1–3 family residential property, and it requires a prior BAR complaint. Commercial and larger properties challenge assessments through tax certiorari in Supreme Court.

questions.q: A county takes title to a home through tax foreclosure for $12,000 in unpaid taxes and later sells it for $250,000. Under the U.S. Supreme Court's 2023 ruling, the former owner:
options: Is entitled to the surplus value above the tax debt and allowed costs
Loses all equity because the taxes were unpaid
Receives only the original $12,000 back
Must pay the county the difference between the tax and the sale price
questions.explanation: In Tyler v. Hennepin County (2023), the Court held that a government keeping surplus equity beyond the tax debt is an unconstitutional taking. New York amended its tax foreclosure law afterward to provide for surplus claims.
questions.citation: Tyler v. Hennepin County, 598 U.S. 631 (2023); NY RPTL Article 11

questions.q: A homeowner who itemizes on her federal return may generally deduct which pair of items for her main home?
options: Mortgage principal payments and homeowners insurance premiums on the home
Depreciation on the home and the cost of routine repairs and painting
Qualified mortgage interest and real property taxes, subject to the SALT cap
Real property taxes with no dollar cap, plus monthly HOA or condo dues
questions.explanation: Itemizers can deduct qualified home mortgage interest and state and local taxes (including property taxes), but state and local taxes together are subject to an annual cap. Principal, insurance, repairs, and depreciation on a personal residence are not deductible.

questions.q: A married couple filing jointly bought their home for $400,000, added $50,000 of capital improvements, lived there 6 years, and sold it for $1,050,000 with $50,000 of selling costs. How much gain is taxable after the home-sale exclusion?
questions.explanation: Amount realized = $1,050,000 − $50,000 = $1,000,000. Adjusted basis = $400,000 + $50,000 = $450,000. Gain = $550,000. Minus the $500,000 joint exclusion = $50,000 taxable.

questions.q: A single seller wants to exclude up to $250,000 of gain on the sale of her home. Which test must she generally meet?
options: She owned the home for at least 5 consecutive years before the sale
She reinvests the proceeds in a more expensive home within 2 years
She is at least 55 years old and has never claimed the exclusion
She owned and lived in it as her main home 2 of the 5 years before sale
questions.explanation: The § 121 exclusion ($250,000 single / $500,000 joint) requires ownership and use as a main home for 2 of the 5 years before sale. The old age-55 rule and "roll-over into a pricier home" rule were repealed in 1997.

questions.q: An investor sells a rental building and wants to defer gain with a Section 1031 exchange. Which statement is correct?
options: She may exchange into a new personal residence she plans to live in
She may receive the cash proceeds directly and still defer all gain
The exchange permanently eliminates federal tax on the deferred gain
She must identify a replacement within 45 days and close within 180 days
questions.explanation: A 1031 exchange applies to real property held for investment or business use and defers (does not eliminate) gain. Replacement property must be identified within 45 days and acquired within 180 days, and a qualified intermediary should hold the funds. Cash received (boot) is taxable.

questions.q: An investor buys a residential rental for $350,000, of which $75,000 is land. Using simple straight-line depreciation over 27.5 years, the annual depreciation is:
questions.explanation: Land is not depreciable, so the basis is $350,000 − $75,000 = $275,000. $275,000 ÷ 27.5 = $10,000 per year. Using the full $350,000 gives $12,727, which is the trap. A personal residence cannot be depreciated at all.

questions.q: A buyer closes on the purchase of an apartment in a New York cooperative. What does the buyer actually acquire?
options: A deed to the apartment plus an undivided interest in the common elements
Shares in the cooperative corporation plus a proprietary lease for the apartment
A recorded leasehold estate in the apartment plus a deed to a share of the land
Fee title to the apartment, with the corporation owning only the lobby and grounds
questions.explanation: A co-op corporation owns the building (or its ground lease); the purchaser receives stock in the corporation and a proprietary lease giving occupancy rights. No deed to the unit is delivered; a deed plus an undivided common interest describes a condominium.
questions.citation: NY cooperative ownership (corporate shares and proprietary lease); contrast NY RPL Article 9-B

questions.q: Which best describes what a condominium unit owner owns in New York?
options: Stock in a corporation that owns the building, plus a lease for the unit
Fee title to the unit only, while the association separately owns all land and common areas
Fee title to the unit plus an appurtenant undivided percentage interest in the common elements
A long-term leasehold in the unit from the sponsor, renewable by the board of managers
questions.explanation: A condo owner holds the unit as real property (commonly in fee simple) plus an undivided interest in the common elements, which can include the land. The common interest travels with the unit. An association owning all common areas describes a typical HOA, not a condo.

questions.q: For legal purposes, how are the shares a co-op shareholder holds in the cooperative corporation classified?
options: Real property, because they are tied to a specific apartment
A fixture, because the apartment is attached to the building
A real property interest conveyed by deed and recorded
Personal property
questions.explanation: Co-op shares are personal property, even though they carry the right to occupy a specific apartment under the proprietary lease. That is why co-op sales use stock transfers and share loans rather than deeds and real-property mortgages.
questions.citation: NY cooperative ownership; NY UCC Article 9 (shares as personal property collateral)

questions.q: How are real estate taxes handled for an individual condominium unit in New York?
options: Each unit is separately assessed and taxed, and the owner receives the unit's own tax bill
The whole building is taxed as a single parcel, and the board pays the bill out of common charges
Taxes are paid by the sponsor until every unit in the building is sold
The unit owner pays a share of taxes through monthly maintenance to the corporation
questions.explanation: Under the Condominium Act each unit, with its common interest, is a separate tax parcel billed to its owner. A single building tax paid through monthly maintenance describes a co-op, where the corporation owns the building.

questions.q: A co-op shareholder asks what the monthly maintenance payment covers. Which answer is most accurate?
options: Only the shareholder's personal share-loan payment to the bank
A proportionate share of building operating costs, real estate taxes, and the underlying mortgage debt service
Only cleaning, staff, and utilities for the common areas, since each shareholder receives a separate tax bill
Installments of the flip tax owed to the city on each apartment
questions.explanation: Maintenance funds the corporation's operations plus the shareholder's allocated share of the building's real estate taxes and any underlying (blanket) mortgage. A personal share loan is paid separately to the shareholder's own lender.
questions.citation: NY cooperative ownership (proprietary lease maintenance obligations)

questions.q: A condo seller accepts a buyer's offer. The condominium's declaration and bylaws give the board of managers a right of first refusal. What must happen before closing?
options: The board must interview the buyer and may then reject the purchase without stating any reason
The buyer must purchase shares in the condominium and sign a proprietary lease with the board of managers
The board must be offered the chance to buy on the same terms, or must waive that right in writing
Nothing, because New York condominiums cannot restrict a unit owner's resale
questions.explanation: Where the governing documents create a right of first refusal, the board may elect to acquire the unit on the same terms or waive the right; a waiver is commonly delivered before closing. A co-op-style admission interview and shares belong to cooperatives, not condos.
questions.citation: Condominium declaration and bylaws; NY RPL Article 9-B

questions.q: A co-op board reviewing a purchase application may NOT lawfully reject an applicant on which of these grounds?
options: Liquid assets below the board's written post-closing reserve standard
An incomplete board package after repeated requests for documents
A debt-to-income ratio above the board's financial policy
The applicant's household includes two young children
questions.explanation: Co-op boards have broad business-judgment discretion over financial qualifications and often need not state reasons, but they may not reject on a protected basis. Familial status (children under 18) is protected under both federal and New York fair housing law.
questions.citation: NY Executive Law § 296; Federal Fair Housing Act, 42 U.S.C. § 3604

questions.q: Which government office reviews and accepts for filing the offering plans for new condominiums and co-op conversions in New York?
options: The New York Attorney General's Real Estate Finance Bureau
The Department of State's Division of Licensing Services
New York State Homes and Community Renewal
The local building department that issues the certificate of occupancy
questions.explanation: Under the Martin Act, sponsors offering condo or co-op interests to the public must file an offering plan with the Attorney General, whose Real Estate Finance Bureau reviews it. DOS licenses brokers and salespersons; it does not accept offering plans.

questions.q: In a New York condo or co-op offering, what is the 'red herring'?
options: The final offering plan as printed and distributed after the Attorney General accepts it for filing
A preliminary version of the offering plan that has not yet been accepted for filing
A notice the sponsor sends to purchasers when it abandons the offering plan before closing
A tenant's formal objection to a conversion plan
questions.explanation: The red herring is the preliminary offering plan, named for the red legend stating it is not final and not yet accepted. Once accepted for filing, the plan is commonly called the black book.
questions.citation: NY GBL § 352-e (Martin Act); NY AG offering-plan regulations

questions.q: A sponsor's salesperson tells a prospect: 'The Attorney General accepted our offering plan, so the state has confirmed these prices are a good investment.' Why is this statement wrong?
options: The Attorney General accepts offering plans only for buildings outside New York City; NYC plans go to HPD
Offering plans are reviewed and accepted by the Department of State's Division of Licensing Services instead
Acceptance for filing reflects disclosure review only; it does not endorse the price or investment value
The Attorney General's acceptance certifies only that construction is free of defects, not that prices are fair
questions.explanation: Acceptance for filing is a disclosure review under the Martin Act, not a government guarantee of fair price, value, profit, or construction quality. Representing it as an endorsement is misleading.

questions.q: A sponsor has an accepted CPS-1 application to test the market for a new condo, but the offering plan has not yet been accepted. A prospect offers a $2,000 fully refundable payment to hold a unit. What may the sponsor do?
options: Accept it, because a fully refundable payment is permitted during an accepted CPS-1 market-testing period
Accept it, as long as the money is held in a segregated escrow account by the sponsor's attorney
Take a nonbinding reservation without collecting money, then collect the deposit once the plan is accepted
Accept no deposit or reservation; it may only note the prospect's nonbinding indication of interest
questions.explanation: Under CPS-1, no deposits and no reservations, binding or nonbinding, may be accepted until the offering plan is accepted for filing. Refundability or escrow does not cure the violation; only a nonbinding indication of interest is allowed.
questions.citation: NY AG Cooperative Policy Statement No. 1 (CPS-1)

questions.q: A co-op contract says the seller will pay the 'flip tax.' What is a flip tax?
options: A transfer fee imposed by the co-op corporation under its documents, usually paid by the seller
The New York State real estate transfer tax as it applies to transfers of co-op shares
A New York City surcharge imposed on investors who resell an apartment within one year of buying
A penalty the Attorney General imposes on sponsors who sell units too quickly
questions.explanation: Despite its name, a flip tax is not a government tax; it is a charge the co-op corporation levies on transfers under its proprietary lease or bylaws, commonly paid by the seller and often credited to the building's reserves. Government transfer taxes are a separate item.

questions.q: In co-op financing, what is a recognition agreement?
options: An agreement in which the buyer and seller formally recognize which broker was the procuring cause and earned the commission
An agreement among the share lender, the co-op corporation, and the shareholder acknowledging the lender's security interest
A letter from the Attorney General recognizing the offering plan as effective so the sponsor can begin closings
The board's written approval recognizing the purchaser as a shareholder after the admissions interview
questions.explanation: The recognition agreement is signed by the share lender, the cooperative corporation, and the borrowing shareholder. It acknowledges the lender's security interest and sets duties such as notifying the lender of a maintenance default.
questions.citation: Co-op share financing; NY UCC Article 9

questions.q: A co-op buyer financing the purchase asks whether the bank will record a mortgage against the apartment with the county clerk. What is the best answer?
options: Yes; a co-op loan is recorded with the county clerk against the unit exactly like a house mortgage
No; the bank instead takes and holds a deed to the apartment until the loan is fully paid off
No; the loan is secured by the shares and proprietary lease, perfected by a UCC financing statement
No; the co-op corporation itself becomes the borrower and adds the loan to its underlying mortgage
questions.explanation: Because co-op shares are personal property, the purchaser's financing is a share loan secured by the stock and proprietary lease, perfected through UCC filing. It is not a recorded real-property mortgage on an individual unit.

questions.q: Which document submits a property to New York's Condominium Act and describes the units, common elements, and each unit's common interest?
options: The proprietary lease
The preliminary offering plan
The house rules
The declaration
questions.explanation: The recorded declaration creates the condominium regime and defines units, common elements, and percentage interests. Bylaws govern administration; a proprietary lease is a co-op document.

questions.q: A condo unit owner stops paying common charges for six months. What remedy does the board of managers generally have?
options: A lien on the unit for the unpaid common charges, which can be foreclosed
Cancellation of the owner's proprietary lease and forfeiture of the owner's shares
No remedy, because common charges are voluntary contributions
A complaint asking the Attorney General to fine the owner under the offering plan
questions.explanation: Unpaid condo common charges become a lien on the unit that the board can enforce, including by foreclosure. Cancelling a proprietary lease is a co-op remedy because only co-ops use proprietary leases.

questions.q: A rental building is being converted to a co-op under a non-eviction plan. A tenant in occupancy decides not to buy. What is the tenant's status?
options: The tenant must vacate when the plan is declared effective
The tenant may remain as a tenant and cannot be evicted for failing to buy
The tenant must buy within 90 days or lose the apartment
The tenant may be evicted one year after the plan is declared effective
questions.explanation: A non-eviction plan does not permit eviction of non-purchasing tenants merely because they decline to buy; they remain tenants, subject to ordinary lawful grounds such as nonpayment. Eviction plans are a different, now heavily restricted category.

questions.q: What is a 'condop'?
options: A co-op whose bylaws permit unlimited subletting and no board interview, so it operates like a condo
A condo whose board interviews and approves every buyer the way a co-op does, although buyers still receive deeds
A condominium in which the residential portion is one unit owned by a co-op corporation, whose buyers receive shares
A townhouse community where owners hold their own lots and belong to a homeowners' association
questions.explanation: In a true condop, the building is a condominium in which one unit (the residential part) is owned by a cooperative corporation, often with separately owned commercial units. Residential buyers get shares and a proprietary lease, not condo deeds; flexible rules alone do not make a co-op a condop.
questions.citation: NY RPL Article 9-B; cooperative ownership structure

questions.q: In a typical homeowners' association (HOA) subdivision, what does each homeowner own?
options: Shares in the association plus a proprietary lease for the home, as in a co-op building
An undivided percentage interest in all land in the community, including the clubhouse and roads
Nothing; the association owns the homes and leases them to residents
Fee title to the home and lot; the association owns the common areas, funded by assessments
questions.explanation: HOA homeowners own their own lots and homes in fee; the association holds title to the common areas and charges assessments to maintain them. An undivided interest in common elements is the condo model.
questions.citation: Homeowners' association declaration; NY GBL § 352-e (HOA offerings)

questions.q: Which homeowners insurance form is designed for a condominium unit owner to cover the unit's interior improvements, personal property, and liability?
options: HO-6
HO-3
HO-4
HO-2
questions.explanation: HO-6 is the unit-owner form used for condos (and commonly co-ops), complementing the association's master policy on the building. HO-4 is a renter's policy; HO-2 and HO-3 are for owners of whole houses.

questions.q: An owner who bought a co-op apartment ten years ago is now reselling it. Must the owner file an offering plan with the Attorney General?
options: Yes; every resale requires the seller to file an amendment to the building's offering plan
No; offering-plan filing applies to sponsor public offerings, not an ordinary owner's resale
Yes, but only if the price exceeds $1 million and the mansion tax applies
Only if the buyer is financing the purchase with a share loan
questions.explanation: The Martin Act filing requirement covers public offerings by sponsors (and holders of unsold shares under the plan). An ordinary shareholder's resale of an apartment is not automatically a new public offering.

questions.q: For federal income tax purposes, what may a tenant-stockholder in a qualifying cooperative generally deduct?
options: Nothing, because co-op shares are personal property
The entire monthly maintenance payment, including the building's operating and staff costs
Their proportionate share of the corporation's real estate taxes and mortgage interest
Only the flip tax paid when they bought the apartment
questions.explanation: IRC § 216 lets tenant-stockholders of a qualifying cooperative deduct their proportionate share of the corporation's real estate taxes and mortgage interest. Operating costs in maintenance are not deductible, and the corporation must meet § 216's tests.

questions.q: Under a typical gross lease, which statement is correct?
options: The tenant pays base rent plus its share of property taxes, insurance, and maintenance costs
The tenant pays fixed rent; the landlord pays operating costs like taxes, insurance, and maintenance
The tenant's rent is calculated solely as a percentage of the tenant's gross sales revenue
The tenant leases only the land and constructs and maintains its own building improvements
questions.explanation: In a gross lease the landlord pays the operating expenses out of the rent; it is common for residential and many office leases. Shifting taxes, insurance, and maintenance to the tenant describes a net lease; always read the actual clause for exceptions such as utilities.
questions.citation: Commercial leasing principles; NYS DOS Salesperson Syllabus (Commercial and Investment Property)

questions.q: A drugstore chain signs a triple net (NNN) lease. Conventionally, this means the tenant pays:
options: Base rent plus property taxes, insurance, and maintenance/repairs
Base rent plus the property taxes only, with the landlord paying the rest
Base rent plus property taxes and insurance only
Only base rent, with the landlord paying all taxes, insurance, and maintenance
questions.explanation: Conventional shorthand: single net = taxes; double net = taxes + insurance; triple net = taxes + insurance + maintenance. The lease language still controls items like roof replacement or capital repairs.
questions.citation: Commercial leasing principles; NYS DOS Salesperson Syllabus (Commercial and Investment Property)

questions.q: A tenant's lease is described as a double net (net-net) lease. In addition to base rent, the tenant conventionally pays:
options: Property taxes only
Utilities only
Property taxes and insurance
Property taxes, insurance, and maintenance
questions.explanation: Double net conventionally adds taxes and insurance; taxes alone is single net, and adding maintenance makes it triple net. Labels are shorthand only; the clause controls.
questions.citation: Commercial leasing principles; NYS DOS Salesperson Syllabus (Commercial and Investment Property)

questions.q: A retail lease requires base rent of $3,000 per month plus 4% of annual gross sales over $600,000. The tenant's gross sales this year were $850,000. What is the total annual rent?
questions.citation: Commercial leasing principles — percentage lease; NYS DOS Salesperson Syllabus (Commercial and Investment Property)

questions.q: A percentage lease has annual base rent of $60,000 and percentage rent of 6% of gross sales. Assuming a natural breakpoint, at what level of annual gross sales does percentage rent begin?
questions.explanation: Natural breakpoint = annual base rent ÷ percentage rate = $60,000 ÷ 0.06 = $1,000,000. Above that, 6% of sales exceeds the base rent. A lease may instead set a negotiated (artificial) breakpoint.
questions.citation: Commercial leasing principles — percentage lease; NYS DOS Salesperson Syllabus (Commercial and Investment Property)

questions.q: A boutique's percentage lease requires 5% of gross sales over a breakpoint. Sales exceeded the breakpoint, but the owner tells the landlord no percentage rent is owed because the store lost money this year. Is the owner correct?
options: No, percentage rent is based on gross sales, not on profit
Yes, percentage rent is owed only when the tenant shows a net profit
Yes, a loss year automatically suspends percentage rent
No, percentage rent is based on the landlord's operating expenses
questions.explanation: Percentage rent is computed on defined gross sales above the breakpoint, regardless of whether the tenant's business is profitable. These leases are most common for retail tenants in shopping centers.
questions.citation: Commercial leasing principles — percentage lease; NYS DOS Salesperson Syllabus (Commercial and Investment Property)

questions.q: An index lease sets annual rent at $80,000 when the Consumer Price Index is 250. The rent adjusts by the full percentage change in the CPI, with no cap. If the CPI rises to 260, what is the new annual rent?
questions.explanation: CPI change = (260 − 250) ÷ 250 = 10 ÷ 250 = 4%. New rent = $80,000 × 1.04 = $83,200. Treating the 10-point rise as 10 percent or adding points to the rent are the traps.
questions.citation: Commercial leasing principles — index lease; NYS DOS Salesperson Syllabus (Commercial and Investment Property)

questions.q: An office lease sets rent at $30 per square foot in year 1, $32 in year 2, and $34 in year 3, as written in the lease from the start. This is a:
options: Index lease
Percentage lease
Net lease
Graduated lease
questions.explanation: A graduated (step-up) lease raises rent by fixed, pre-set amounts on a schedule. An index lease instead moves rent with an outside measure such as the CPI, so the future amounts are not known in advance.
questions.citation: Commercial leasing principles — graduated lease; NYS DOS Salesperson Syllabus (Commercial and Investment Property)

questions.q: A fast-food chain leases a vacant parcel for 49 years and constructs its own restaurant on it. This arrangement is best described as a:
options: Ground lease
Gross lease
Percentage lease
Graduated lease
questions.explanation: A ground lease is a long-term lease of land only, with the tenant building and usually paying expenses on the improvements. Unless the lease provides otherwise, the improvements commonly pass to the landowner when the lease ends.
questions.citation: Commercial leasing principles — ground lease; NYS DOS Salesperson Syllabus (Commercial and Investment Property)

questions.q: In an office building, how does rentable square footage differ from usable square footage?
options: Rentable area excludes the lobbies and corridors that are included in usable area
Rentable area adds the tenant's pro-rata share of common areas like lobbies and restrooms
Rentable and usable area are always identical; the terms are interchangeable in office leases
Rentable area counts only the finished space with carpeting and ceilings installed
questions.explanation: Usable area is the space the tenant actually occupies; rentable area adds its share of building common areas. Rent is usually quoted per rentable square foot, so rentable is the larger number.
questions.citation: Commercial leasing principles — area measurement; NYS DOS Salesperson Syllabus (Commercial and Investment Property)

questions.q: A suite has 10,000 rentable square feet and 8,500 usable square feet. What is the loss factor?
questions.explanation: Loss factor = (rentable − usable) ÷ rentable = 1,500 ÷ 10,000 = 15%. Dividing by usable (1,500 ÷ 8,500 ≈ 17.6%) gives the add-on/load percentage instead, and 85% is the efficiency (usable ÷ rentable).
questions.citation: Commercial leasing principles — loss factor; NYS DOS Salesperson Syllabus (Commercial and Investment Property)

questions.q: A tenant needs 4,000 usable square feet. The building has a 20% add-on (load) factor applied to usable area, and rent is $45 per rentable square foot per year. What is the monthly rent?
questions.explanation: Rentable = 4,000 × 1.20 = 4,800 sq ft. Annual rent = 4,800 × $45 = $216,000; monthly = $216,000 ÷ 12 = $18,000. Using usable area (4,000 × $45 ÷ 12 = $15,000) ignores the load.
questions.citation: Commercial leasing principles — load factor; NYS DOS Salesperson Syllabus (Commercial and Investment Property)

questions.q: A tenant occupies 3,000 square feet in a 60,000-square-foot shopping center. Annual common area maintenance (CAM) costs are $240,000, shared pro rata by square footage. What is the tenant's annual CAM charge?
questions.explanation: Pro-rata share = 3,000 ÷ 60,000 = 5%. CAM = $240,000 × 0.05 = $12,000 per year ($1,000 per month). CAM is a cost-sharing charge for common areas such as parking lots and landscaping, not a measurement of space.
questions.citation: Commercial leasing principles — CAM charges; NYS DOS Salesperson Syllabus (Commercial and Investment Property)

questions.q: A lease provides a tenant improvement (TI) allowance of $40 per rentable square foot on 5,000 rentable square feet. The tenant's build-out costs $260,000, and the lease says the tenant pays any excess. How much does the tenant pay toward the build-out?
questions.explanation: TI allowance = $40 × 5,000 = $200,000 paid by the landlord. Tenant pays the excess: $260,000 − $200,000 = $60,000. TI allowances are a negotiated landlord concession to customize space.
questions.citation: Commercial leasing principles — tenant improvements; NYS DOS Salesperson Syllabus (Commercial and Investment Property)

questions.q: An investor buys a building with $350,000 cash invested. NOI is $120,000 and annual debt service is $85,000. What is the investor's cash-on-cash return?
questions.explanation: Before-tax cash flow = NOI − debt service = $120,000 − $85,000 = $35,000. Cash-on-cash = $35,000 ÷ $350,000 = 10%. Dividing NOI by cash invested (34.3%) skips debt service.
questions.citation: Real estate investment analysis; NYS DOS Salesperson Syllabus (Commercial and Investment Property)

questions.q: An investor finances a purchase mostly with borrowed money. Positive leverage occurs when:
options: The loan's interest rate is higher than the property's rate of return
The investor pays all cash so no debt service is owed
The property's NOI is less than the annual debt service
The property's rate of return exceeds the cost of the borrowed funds
questions.explanation: Leverage uses borrowed money to increase the return on the investor's own cash. It is positive when the property earns more than the debt costs; if the debt costs more, leverage is negative and magnifies losses.
questions.citation: Real estate investment analysis; NYS DOS Salesperson Syllabus (Commercial and Investment Property)

questions.q: A building listed at $1,100,000 has gross scheduled income of $96,000, operating expenses of $30,000, and annual mortgage payments of $40,000. What is the capitalization rate at the list price?
questions.explanation: NOI = $96,000 − $30,000 = $66,000 (mortgage payments are not operating expenses). Cap rate = NOI ÷ price = $66,000 ÷ $1,100,000 = 6%. Using gross income (8.7%) or deducting debt service (2.4%) are traps.
questions.citation: Real estate investment analysis — capitalization rate; NYS DOS Salesperson Syllabus (Commercial and Investment Property)

questions.q: In an ordinary deferred Section 1031 exchange, after the relinquished property is transferred, the investor must identify replacement property and then receive it within what time limits?
options: Identify within 45 days; receive within 180 days or by the tax-return due date, if earlier
Identify within 30 days; receive within 90 days or by the tax-return due date, if earlier
Identify within 60 days; receive within 120 days of closing on the relinquished property
Identify within 45 days; receive within one year
questions.explanation: Replacement property must be identified in writing within 45 days and received by the earlier of 180 days after the transfer or the tax-return due date (with extensions). A qualified intermediary should hold the proceeds so the investor never receives them.

questions.q: An investor exchanges a rental building for a larger warehouse under Section 1031 and also receives $40,000 in cash. The $40,000 is:
options: Like-kind property, so it is fully tax-deferred
A qualified intermediary fee deductible as an expense
Boot, generally taxable up to the amount of realized gain
Excluded from tax because the exchange was between real properties
questions.explanation: Cash or other non-like-kind property received is boot and can trigger taxable gain up to the realized gain. A rental building for a warehouse is like-kind because both are investment/business real property; a personal home does not qualify.

questions.q: A salesperson represents a buyer of a 20,000-square-foot warehouse in New York. Which statement about required disclosure forms is correct?
options: Both the RPL § 443 agency disclosure form and the fair housing and discrimination notice are required
Neither form is required because commercial transactions are exempt from all DOS notices
Only the RPL § 443 agency disclosure form is required
The RPL § 443 agency disclosure form is not required, but the fair housing and discrimination notice is
questions.explanation: The RPL § 443 agency disclosure form covers residential (1-4 family, condo, co-op) transactions, so it does not apply to a warehouse. The DOS Fair Housing and Discrimination notice under 19 NYCRR § 175.28 applies to all real property, including commercial and vacant land.

questions.q: A restaurant tenant wants to lease space in a zoning district where restaurants are allowed only if the zoning board finds that specified conditions in the ordinance (parking, hours, traffic) are met. The tenant should apply for a:
options: Use variance
Special use permit
Nonconforming use designation
Spot zoning amendment
questions.explanation: A special use permit (special exception) allows a use the ordinance already permits subject to stated conditions. A use variance is needed for a use the ordinance prohibits and requires proof of unnecessary hardship.
questions.citation: NY Town Law § 274-b; NY Village Law § 7-725-b

questions.q: A retail tenant's lease says the tenant is solely responsible for ADA compliance. A customer who uses a wheelchair cannot enter the store because of steps at the entrance. Under ADA Title III, who may be responsible to the public?
options: Only the tenant, because the lease validly shifted all ADA compliance responsibility to it
Only the landlord, because it owns the building and controls the common entrance and steps
Both the landlord and the tenant; the lease allocates the burden but does not erase either's duty
Neither, because ADA Title III applies only to residential housing
questions.explanation: Title III covers public accommodations such as stores, and both the landlord and the tenant can be liable; a lease can allocate the burden between them but cannot waive duties owed to the public. Existing facilities must remove barriers where readily achievable.
questions.citation: Americans with Disabilities Act Title III, 42 U.S.C. § 12181 et seq.; 28 CFR § 36.201(b)

questions.q: A property manager handles leasing, rent collection, and repairs for an owner's apartment building under an ongoing management agreement. The manager is best described as a:
options: Universal agent
Special agent
General agent
Dual agent
questions.explanation: A manager with ongoing authority over a range of tasks for one business is a general agent. A universal agent can act on all of the principal's affairs (e.g., broad power of attorney), and a special agent is limited to one transaction, like a typical listing.
questions.citation: NY agency law; NY RPL Article 12-A

questions.q: An unlicensed company offers, for a fee, to negotiate leases and collect rents for several building owners. Under New York law, the company:
options: Needs no license because management is not a sale
Needs a real estate broker license, since this is brokerage activity
Needs only an assumed-name certificate from the county clerk
Needs a license only if it manages more than ten units
questions.explanation: RPL § 440 defines brokerage to include negotiating rentals and collecting rent for another for compensation, so the company needs a broker license and its salespersons work under that broker. An owner managing his own property or a maintenance-only contractor is a different case.

questions.q: Which document creates the property manager's authority and should spell out the manager's fees, spending limits, reporting duties, and termination terms?
options: Management proposal
Rent roll
Operating budget
Management agreement
questions.explanation: The written management agreement creates the agency relationship and defines authority, compensation, budgets, spending limits, reporting, and termination. A management proposal only recommends a plan; the rent roll and budget are reports/tools used under the agreement.
questions.citation: NY RPL Article 12-A; property management agency principles

questions.q: A management agreement lets the manager approve repairs up to $1,500 without owner consent, except in emergencies. A contractor quotes $14,000 to replace the building's aging but working boiler next spring. The manager should:
options: Get the owner's approval before authorizing the replacement
Authorize it, since a general agent decides all building matters
Split the job into ten $1,400 invoices to stay under the limit
Pay from tenant security deposits and bill the owner later
questions.explanation: A planned capital replacement above the agreed limit, with no emergency, needs the owner's approval; general-agent status does not override the agreement's spending terms. Splitting invoices evades the limit, and security deposits are tenant trust money, never operating cash.
questions.citation: Management agreement / agency law; NY GOL § 7-103

questions.q: A plumbing contractor offers a property manager a $200 personal 'thank-you' rebate on each job billed to the owner. Under DOS rules, the manager may:
options: Keep it, since it does not raise the owner's cost
Keep it if it is reported as personal income
Accept it only with the owner's full knowledge and consent
Accept it whenever the contractor is the lowest bidder
questions.explanation: A broker managing property may not accept a commission, rebate, or profit on expenditures made for the owner without the owner's full knowledge and consent. Secretly pocketing it breaches the fiduciary duties of loyalty and disclosure even if the price is fair.

questions.q: An owner wants to set money aside each year for a roof replacement expected in six years. That planned set-aside belongs in the:
options: Operating budget as a routine repair
Capital reserve budget
Rent roll as a tenant charge
Security deposit escrow account
questions.explanation: A capital reserve budget plans for large, infrequent replacements and improvements like a roof. The operating budget covers recurring income and expenses; patching a small leak is operating, replacing the roof is capital.
questions.citation: Property management budgeting (NYS 77-hr syllabus, Property Management)

questions.q: A report listing each unit, the tenant, lease start and end dates, the monthly rent, and any balance owed is called a:
options: Operating statement
Management proposal
Capital reserve schedule
Rent roll
questions.explanation: A rent roll lists units, tenants, lease terms, scheduled rents, and arrears. It shows what is scheduled and owed — it is not proof that every scheduled dollar was actually collected.
questions.citation: Property management reporting (NYS 77-hr syllabus, Property Management)

questions.q: A building has potential gross rent of $180,000, a 5% vacancy and collection loss, $2,000 of laundry income, $70,000 of operating expenses, and $40,000 of annual mortgage payments. What is the net operating income?
questions.explanation: EGI = $180,000 × 0.95 + $2,000 = $171,000 + $2,000 = $173,000; NOI = $173,000 − $70,000 = $103,000. Mortgage debt service is not an operating expense, so subtracting it ($63,000) is the trap.
questions.citation: Income property analysis: NOI = effective gross income − operating expenses

questions.q: Replacing furnace and air-conditioner filters on a fixed quarterly schedule, before any problem appears, is an example of:
options: Corrective maintenance
Construction
Preventive maintenance
Cosmetic maintenance
questions.explanation: Preventive maintenance is periodic servicing that prevents wear and failure, such as scheduled filter changes. Corrective maintenance fixes something already broken, like a leaky faucet a tenant reports.
questions.citation: Property management maintenance categories (NYS 77-hr syllabus, Property Management)

questions.q: Remodeling a vacant office suite to a new commercial tenant's specifications (tenant improvements) is classified as:
options: Preventive maintenance
Corrective maintenance
Routine maintenance
Construction
questions.explanation: Construction covers budgeted remodeling, tenant build-outs, and new capital improvements. Routine maintenance is day-to-day upkeep like cleaning common areas; corrective maintenance repairs a reported defect.
questions.citation: Property management maintenance categories (NYS 77-hr syllabus, Property Management)

questions.q: A property manager advises the owner to buy a general liability policy covering injuries in the building's common areas. Which risk management technique is this?
options: Avoiding the risk
Transferring the risk
Retaining the risk
Controlling the risk
questions.explanation: Buying insurance shifts the financial risk to the insurer, which is risk transfer. Insurance does not excuse leaving a known hazard unrepaired — control (inspections, repairs) still applies.
questions.citation: Property management risk management (NYS 77-hr syllabus, Property Management)

questions.q: Rather than face drowning liability, an owner decides to close and fill in the building's swimming pool. This risk management technique is:
options: Avoiding the risk
Transferring the risk
Retaining the risk
Controlling the risk
questions.explanation: Eliminating the activity that creates the risk is avoidance. Adding fencing or lifeguards would be control, buying insurance would be transfer, and self-insuring or carrying a large deductible would be retention.
questions.citation: Property management risk management (NYS 77-hr syllabus, Property Management)

questions.q: A non-rent-regulated apartment in Rochester rents for $1,950 per month. At lease signing, what is the most the landlord may collect for the first month's rent plus security?
options: $5,850 for first month, last month, and security
$1,950 for first month only, with no deposit
$3,900 for first month plus one month's security
$4,875 for first month plus 1.5 months' security
questions.explanation: GOL § 7-108 caps any security deposit or advance at one month's rent: $1,950 first month + $1,950 security = $3,900. Demanding last month's rent on top of security is an extra advance and exceeds the cap.

questions.q: A tenant in a non-regulated apartment moves out on June 1. To keep any part of the security deposit for damage, the landlord must give an itemized statement and return the balance within:
options: 30 days after the tenant vacates
7 days after the tenant vacates
45 days after the scheduled lease end
14 days after the tenant vacates
questions.explanation: GOL § 7-108 requires an itemized statement of deductions and return of the balance within 14 days after the tenant vacates; missing the deadline forfeits the right to keep any of the deposit. Deductions are limited to items like unpaid rent and damage beyond ordinary wear and tear.

questions.q: A landlord of a building with six or more apartments must keep tenants' security deposits in an interest-bearing New York bank account. How much of the interest may the landlord keep?
options: An administrative fee of 1% per year of the deposit
All interest, because the landlord holds the account
Half of the interest, split with the tenant
None; all interest must be paid to the city
questions.explanation: Under GOL § 7-103 the landlord may retain 1% per year of the deposit for administrative expenses; the rest of the interest belongs to the tenant (paid annually, applied to rent, or paid at lease end). The tenant must be told in writing the bank's name and address and the deposit amount.

questions.q: A property manager deposits tenants' security deposits into the management company's operating account to cover payroll until rent comes in. This is:
options: Permitted if repaid within 30 days
Unlawful commingling of trust funds
Permitted if the owner verbally approves
Permitted in buildings with fewer than six units
