questions.explanation: Security deposits remain the tenant's money held in trust and may not be commingled with the landlord's or manager's funds, regardless of building size or owner approval. Broker rules separately require client funds to be kept in a separate special account.

questions.q: An owner tells the property manager, 'Don't rent the third-floor walk-up to families with kids — the stairs are too dangerous for children.' The manager should:
options: Follow it, because the instruction protects children's safety on the stairs
Follow it only if the owner puts the instruction in writing and signs it
Refuse; a safety-based ban on children is familial status discrimination
Rent to families only if the parents sign a stair-injury liability waiver
questions.explanation: Limiting units for families with children based on paternalistic safety concerns is familial status discrimination. A principal's instruction never authorizes a manager to discriminate; screening must use the same lawful criteria for everyone.
questions.citation: Federal Fair Housing Act, 42 U.S.C. § 3604; NY Executive Law § 296(5)

questions.q: A property manager oversees an existing shopping center. Under Title III of the Americans with Disabilities Act, the manager must generally:
options: Rebuild the whole center to new-construction standards at once
Wait until a customer with a disability files a complaint
Comply only if the center receives federal funding
Remove barriers where readily achievable, such as adding ramps
questions.explanation: Existing places of public accommodation must remove architectural barriers where it is readily achievable (easily accomplished without much difficulty or expense). The duty is ongoing, applies without federal funding, and does not require an immediate full rebuild.
questions.citation: Americans with Disabilities Act, Title III, 42 U.S.C. § 12182

questions.q: A tenant is two months behind on rent. The property manager changes the locks while the tenant is at work and puts the tenant's belongings on the curb. Under New York law this is:
options: A lawful self-help remedy after 30 days of nonpayment
An unlawful eviction; a court summary proceeding is required
Lawful if the lease contains a lockout clause
Lawful if a 14-day rent demand was served first
questions.explanation: Residential self-help (lockouts, utility shutoffs, removing belongings) is prohibited; possession must be recovered through a summary proceeding and a warrant executed by a marshal or sheriff. The 2019 HSTPA made unlawful eviction a crime, and a lease clause cannot waive these protections.

questions.q: Before starting a nonpayment summary proceeding against a residential tenant, the landlord must generally serve a written rent demand giving the tenant at least:
options: 14 days to pay
3 days to pay
5 days to pay
30 days to pay
questions.explanation: The 2019 Housing Stability and Tenant Protection Act lengthened the rent demand from 3 days to 14 days. The 5-day figure is the separate late-rent notice/late-fee trigger, a common mix-up.

questions.q: A tenant in a non-regulated New York apartment pays $1,800 per month and pays rent more than five days late. What is the maximum late fee the landlord may charge?
questions.explanation: The late fee may not exceed the lesser of $50 or 5% of monthly rent: 5% × $1,800 = $90, so the cap is $50. A fee may be charged only when rent is more than five days late.

questions.q: In New York City, the maximum allowable rent increases for rent-stabilized lease renewals are set by the:
options: NYC Rent Guidelines Board
NYS Department of State
Landlord, up to the Good Cause 5% + CPI cap
U.S. Department of HUD
questions.explanation: The NYC Rent Guidelines Board votes annual renewal increases for stabilized apartments, and stabilized tenants have renewal rights. The Good Cause Eviction rent test applies to covered unregulated units, and the 2019 HSTPA ended high-rent/high-income deregulation.
questions.citation: NYC Rent Stabilization Law (NYC Admin. Code § 26-501 et seq.); HSTPA 2019

questions.q: A landlord in Albany charges rental applicants a $50 application fee. The actual cost of the credit and background check is $35. What is the most the landlord may lawfully charge?
questions.explanation: RPL § 238-a caps the combined background/credit check charge at the actual cost or $20, whichever is less. The lesser of $35 and $20 is $20; no separate application or processing fee is allowed.

questions.q: A rental applicant gives the landlord a credit and background check report obtained three weeks ago. What must the landlord do about the background-check fee?
options: Waive the fee, because the applicant supplied a report from within the past 30 days
Charge the $20 fee anyway, since the landlord may always require and bill for its own report
Charge half the usual fee for verifying the applicant's report
Charge actual cost up to $50 for a fresh report
questions.explanation: Under RPL § 238-a, the landlord must waive the fee when the applicant provides a background or credit check conducted within the past 30 days. Three weeks falls inside that window.

questions.q: A landlord of an ordinary (non-regulated) apartment renting for $2,600 per month asks the new tenant for first month's rent, last month's rent, and a two-month security deposit at lease signing. What is the most the landlord may collect at signing?
questions.explanation: GOL § 7-108 caps any deposit or advance at one month's rent, and a 'last month's rent' advance counts toward that cap. The landlord may collect first month's rent ($2,600) plus a deposit/advance of $2,600, for $5,200 total.

questions.q: After a tenant of an ordinary residential rental moves out, how long does the landlord have to return the security deposit with an itemized statement of any deductions?
options: 30 days
10 business days
14 days
60 days
questions.explanation: GOL § 7-108 requires the landlord to provide an itemized statement and return any remaining deposit within 14 days after the tenant vacates. Missing the deadline forfeits the landlord's right to retain any portion.

questions.q: Which statement correctly describes a New York tenant's pre-move-out inspection right for an ordinary residential rental?
options: The landlord inspects only after the tenant returns the keys, and no advance notice to the tenant is required
The landlord must inspect monthly during the final 90 days of the lease, on 24 hours' oral notice to the tenant each time
Inspection is required only at move-in; any later damage is settled from the deposit after the tenant leaves
On the tenant's request, inspect 1 to 2 weeks before move-out on 48 hours' written notice so the tenant can cure issues
questions.explanation: GOL § 7-108 requires the landlord to tell the tenant of the right to request an inspection no earlier than two weeks and no later than one week before the tenancy ends, on at least 48 hours' written notice. The tenant may then cure the noted conditions before vacating.

questions.q: A tenant's monthly rent is $1,400. Rent due on the 1st is paid on the 9th. What is the maximum late fee the landlord may charge?
questions.explanation: RPL § 238-a limits late fees to $50 or 5% of monthly rent, whichever is less. 5% × $1,400 = $70, so the $50 cap controls. Payment more than five days late allows a fee.

questions.q: A tenant's $900 rent is due on the 1st and is paid on the 4th. The lease provides a late fee. What may the landlord charge?
options: $45, which is 5% of the monthly rent and less than the $50 statutory cap
No late fee, because the rent was paid within five days of the due date
$50, the statutory maximum, because the lease expressly provides a late fee
$9 per day for each day late, as long as the total stays under $50
questions.explanation: Under RPL § 238-a, no late fee may be charged unless rent remains unpaid more than five days after it was due. Paid on the 4th, the rent is within the grace period, so no fee is allowed even though the lease provides one.

questions.q: A landlord of an ordinary rental tells an approved applicant to pay a $300 non-refundable 'move-in processing fee' in addition to first month's rent and a one-month security deposit. Is this lawful?
options: Yes, as long as the fee is disclosed in writing in the lease and on the rental application
Yes, because a processing fee under 15% of one month's rent is allowed for approved applicants
No; aside from the capped background/credit check fee, no fee may be charged before or at lease start
No, but only because the fee is non-refundable; a refundable processing fee of that amount would be allowed
questions.explanation: RPL § 238-a bars landlords from demanding any payment, fee, or charge for processing an application or before or at the beginning of a tenancy, other than the capped background/credit check fee. Labeling it refundable would not make an extra deposit lawful, because GOL § 7-108 caps deposits at one month.

questions.q: A New York City landlord hires a broker to list and fill a vacant apartment. Under the FARE Act, who pays that broker's fee?
options: The tenant, as long as the fee is clearly disclosed in the listing
The tenant and landlord split it equally
The tenant, unless the monthly rent exceeds a set luxury threshold
The landlord; the tenant cannot be charged for the landlord's agent
questions.explanation: The NYC FARE Act (effective June 11, 2025) bars charging a tenant the fee of a broker who represents or was engaged by the landlord. Disclosure does not shift the fee to the tenant.
questions.citation: NYC FARE Act (Fairness in Apartment Rental Expenses Act), eff. June 11, 2025

questions.q: In New York City, a tenant voluntarily signs an agreement hiring her own broker to find an apartment, agreeing to a fee of 12% of the first year's rent. She leases a unit at $3,000 per month. What is the result?
options: She may pay her own broker $4,320
The fee is prohibited by the FARE Act, so she owes nothing
She owes $360, since fees are based on one month's rent
The landlord must pay her broker $4,320
questions.explanation: The FARE Act stops tenants from paying the landlord's agent, but a tenant may still hire and pay her own broker. $3,000 × 12 = $36,000 annual rent; $36,000 × 12% = $4,320.

questions.q: A salesperson is showing an apartment in a three-family house to a prospective tenant on behalf of the landlord. Which agency disclosure form must the salesperson provide?
options: DOS-1736, the New York State Disclosure Form for Buyer and Seller
DOS-1735, the New York State Disclosure Form for Landlord and Tenant
The Property Condition Disclosure Statement
The FARE Act fee disclosure, which replaces the agency form
questions.explanation: For rentals of 1-4 family residential property (and condo/co-op units), RPL § 443 requires the Landlord and Tenant disclosure form, DOS-1735. DOS-1736 is the buyer/seller version used for sales.

questions.q: What is the key difference between an assignment of a lease and a sublease?
options: A sublease transfers the entire remaining term; an assignment transfers only part
An assignment requires no landlord involvement; a sublease always requires a new lease
In an assignment the tenant transfers the entire remaining interest; in a sublease the tenant transfers less and keeps an interest
An assignment ends the original tenant's liability automatically; a sublease creates a new landlord-tenant relationship with the owner
questions.explanation: An assignment transfers the tenant's whole remaining leasehold, while a sublease transfers part of it and the original tenant keeps an interest. Neither one automatically releases the original tenant from contractual liability to the landlord.

questions.q: A tenant in a 12-unit privately owned building (not rent-regulated) asks the landlord in writing for consent to sublet for six months. Under RPL § 226-b, how may the landlord respond?
options: Refuse for any reason or no reason, since the lease bars subletting
Ignore the request, since only rent-stabilized tenants may sublet
Charge a sublet fee equal to one month's rent before considering it
Withhold consent only on reasonable grounds
questions.explanation: In buildings with four or more residential units, RPL § 226-b lets a tenant sublet with the landlord's written consent, which may not be unreasonably withheld. The tenant must follow the statute's written request procedure.

questions.q: A lease clause says the tenant waives all warranty of habitability claims in exchange for a $100-per-month rent reduction. What is the effect of the clause?
options: It is void; the warranty of habitability cannot be waived
It is enforceable because the tenant received consideration
It is enforceable only for leases longer than one year
It is valid unless the landlord fails to make repairs within 30 days
questions.explanation: RPL § 235-b implies a warranty of habitability in every residential lease, and any agreement waiving it is void as against public policy. Consideration does not save the waiver.

questions.q: A tenant is two months behind on rent. While the tenant is at work, the landlord changes the locks and puts the tenant's belongings in storage. What is the best description of the landlord's action?
options: Lawful, because two months of unpaid rent allows a residential landlord to retake possession of the apartment
An unlawful eviction; the landlord must go to court, and only a marshal or sheriff may execute a warrant
Lawful, as long as the landlord first served a 14-day written rent demand and waited it out
Lawful, because the tenant's belongings were safely stored rather than thrown away
questions.explanation: New York prohibits residential self-help eviction. Removing a tenant by changing locks or removing possessions without a court order is unlawful eviction under RPAPL § 768; only a court-issued warrant executed by a marshal or sheriff can remove the tenant.

questions.q: In a New York City multiple dwelling, a landlord must install window guards in an apartment where a child of what age lives (or where the tenant requests them)?
options: Under 6
Under 18
10 years old or younger
12 years old or younger
questions.explanation: The NYC Health Code requires window guards in apartments where a child 10 or younger resides, and in any apartment whose tenant requests them. 'Under 6' is the threshold for the separate NYC lead paint rule.

questions.q: Under New York City's lead paint law, the landlord's annual notice asks tenants in older buildings whether a child of what age lives in the apartment?
options: 10 years old or younger
Under 18
Under 12
Under 6
questions.explanation: NYC Local Law 1 of 2004 targets children under 6, who are most vulnerable to lead poisoning; landlords must ask annually and perform required inspections and work where such a child resides. The 10-or-younger age belongs to the window guard rule.
questions.citation: NYC Local Law 1 of 2004 (Childhood Lead Poisoning Prevention Act)

questions.q: For a rent-stabilized apartment in New York City, who sets the maximum allowable rent increase for a renewal lease?
options: The NYC Rent Guidelines Board
The building owner, based on market rents
The NYS Department of State
The New York Attorney General
questions.explanation: The Rent Guidelines Board votes each year on the maximum increases for one- and two-year renewal leases of rent-stabilized units, and the tenant chooses the term. NYS Homes and Community Renewal administers the program; DOS and the AG do not set rents.
questions.citation: NYC Rent Stabilization Law (NYC Admin Code Title 26, Chapter 4)

questions.q: A buyer's offer on a house has just been accepted, and the office manager asks the salesperson for the deal sheet. Which set of information is essential to include?
options: The MLS photos, listing remarks, number of showings, and feedback from every buyer who toured the home
The buyer's age, marital status, number of children, and place of employment for the seller's review
Price, deposit, mortgage amount, contingencies, closing date, broker compensation split, and both attorneys' contacts
Only the accepted price and the parties' names, since the attorneys will gather and negotiate every other term themselves
questions.explanation: The deal sheet (memorandum of sale) summarizes the accepted terms so the attorneys can draft the contract: price, earnest money, financing, contingencies, closing date, listing/cooperating broker compensation, and contact details for both attorneys. Protected-class details are irrelevant and should not be recorded.
questions.citation: NY brokerage practice (memorandum of sale / deal sheet)

questions.q: A deal sheet shows an accepted price of $640,000, a mortgage of 80% of the price, and a 10% contract deposit. Excluding closing costs, what are the mortgage amount and the remaining down payment due at closing?
options: Mortgage $576,000; $64,000 due at closing
Mortgage $512,000; $128,000 due at closing
Mortgage $448,000; $64,000 due at closing
Mortgage $512,000; $64,000 due at closing
questions.explanation: Mortgage = $640,000 × 0.80 = $512,000, so the down payment is $640,000 - $512,000 = $128,000. The deposit of $640,000 × 0.10 = $64,000 counts toward the down payment, leaving $128,000 - $64,000 = $64,000 due at closing.
questions.citation: Real estate math (loan amount and down payment)

questions.q: On a $640,000 sale, the listing agreement provides a 5% commission, split 60% to the listing broker and 40% to the cooperating (selling) broker. How much does the cooperating broker receive?
questions.explanation: Total commission = $640,000 × 0.05 = $32,000. Cooperating broker's share = $32,000 × 0.40 = $12,800; the listing broker receives $32,000 × 0.60 = $19,200.

questions.q: After an accepted offer, the buyer asks whether the signed deal sheet means the seller can no longer accept another buyer. What is the best answer?
options: Yes; the deal sheet becomes the binding contract of sale as soon as the office manager signs it
No; it summarizes terms for the attorneys, and the parties generally are not bound until both sign a contract
Yes, but only after the buyer's earnest money has been deposited in the listing broker's escrow account
No, because real estate offers in New York become binding only when they are made and accepted orally
questions.explanation: In New York practice, the deal sheet is not the contract; the attorneys draft a contract of sale, and the deal is generally not binding until both parties sign it (the statute of frauds requires a signed writing for real property sales). Until then, the seller may still entertain other offers.

questions.q: Under RESPA Section 8, which payment is prohibited?
options: A title agent paying a salesperson $200 for each buyer referred to the title agent
A buyer paying the closing attorney's fee for legal services actually performed
A seller paying the listing broker's agreed commission
A lender paying an appraiser for an appraisal actually completed
questions.explanation: RESPA § 8 bans kickbacks and fees for referrals of settlement business in federally related mortgage loans. Payment for goods or services actually performed is allowed. Calling a referral fee "marketing" does not fix it.

questions.q: A brokerage owns part of a title agency and wants to refer its buyers there. Under RESPA, this affiliated business arrangement is lawful only if the brokerage:
options: Requires all its buyers to use the affiliate so it can keep closing costs low and consistent
Is paid a flat fee by the affiliate for each referral that closes, as long as the fee is disclosed
Discloses the relationship and estimated charges, does not require its use, and receives only an ownership return
Tells the buyer about its ownership interest in the title agency verbally, but only after the closing has been completed
questions.explanation: An affiliated business arrangement needs written disclosure at or before the referral, no required use (with narrow exceptions), and nothing of value to the referrer beyond a return on the ownership interest.

questions.q: A seller insists, as a condition of the sale, that the buyer purchase title insurance from a particular title company. Under RESPA, this is:
options: Allowed, as long as the requirement is clearly written into the contract of sale that both parties sign
Prohibited, because a seller may not require the buyer to use a particular title insurer
Allowed, if the seller agrees to pay half of the title insurance premium
Required, because the seller chooses the title insurer
questions.explanation: RESPA § 9 bars a seller from requiring, directly or indirectly, as a condition of sale that the buyer buy title insurance from a particular company in a federally related mortgage transaction.

questions.q: Under TRID, when must the lender deliver or mail the Loan Estimate?
options: At least 3 business days before consummation of the loan
Within 10 business days after the lender's appraisal of the property has been completed
At the closing table, along with the note and the mortgage
Within 3 business days after receiving the consumer's loan application
questions.explanation: The Loan Estimate is due within 3 business days after the creditor receives an application (the six items: name, income, SSN, property address, estimated value, loan amount). The 3-days-before-consummation rule applies to the Closing Disclosure.

questions.q: Under TRID, the borrower must receive the Closing Disclosure:
options: Within 3 business days after receiving the loan application
At least 3 business days after consummation of the loan
On the day of closing, before signing
At least 3 business days before consummation of the loan
questions.explanation: The Closing Disclosure must be received at least 3 business days before consummation so the borrower can compare it with the Loan Estimate. Mixing it up with the Loan Estimate timing is the classic trap.

questions.q: A borrower receives her Closing Disclosure on a Monday. No federal holidays fall that week. Under TRID, the earliest day the loan may be consummated is:
options: Monday
Thursday
Tuesday
the following Monday
questions.explanation: The CD must be received at least 3 business days before consummation. Counting Monday, Tuesday, and Wednesday as the three days, consummation may occur Thursday.

questions.q: After the Closing Disclosure is delivered, which change requires a corrected CD AND a new 3-business-day waiting period?
options: The seller agrees to a $1,000 credit to the buyer for a repair
The recording fee rises by $15
The loan product changes from a fixed-rate to an adjustable-rate loan
The closing time is moved from the morning to the afternoon of the same day
questions.explanation: Only three changes restart the waiting period: the APR becomes inaccurate beyond tolerance, the loan product changes, or a prepayment penalty is added. Other changes need a corrected CD at or before closing, but no new wait.

questions.q: Which statement best describes a typical residential closing in New York?
options: Buyer and seller usually each have an attorney, who attend the closing with or for their clients
A neutral escrow company closes the sale by mail, and attorneys are rarely involved
The listing salesperson prepares the deed and conducts the closing on behalf of both parties
The county clerk conducts the closing at the clerk's office and transfers title
questions.explanation: New York is an attorney-closing state: buyer's and seller's attorneys, the lender's attorney, and often a title closer attend. Salespersons may attend but cannot draft deeds or give legal advice. The county clerk only records documents afterward.
questions.citation: NY Judiciary Law § 478 (practice of law); NY RPL Article 12-A

questions.q: At closing, the buyer's $40,000 earnest money deposit held in escrow is entered on the closing statement as a:
options: Credit to the buyer only
Debit to the buyer only
Credit to the seller and debit to the buyer
Debit to the seller only
questions.explanation: The deposit is money the buyer already paid toward the price, so the buyer is credited. It is not a seller credit because the purchase price (seller credit) already includes it.

questions.q: On a closing statement, the purchase price is shown as:
options: A credit to the buyer and a debit to the seller
A debit to both the buyer and the seller
A debit to the buyer and a credit to the seller
A credit to both the buyer and the seller
questions.explanation: The buyer owes the price (debit), and the seller receives it (credit). Most items are double entries like this; the buyer's new loan and the seller's loan payoff are single entries.

questions.q: At closing, the seller's existing mortgage balance of $210,000 is paid off. On the closing statement this is a:
options: Credit to the seller only
Debit to the seller only
Debit to the buyer only
Debit to the seller and credit to the buyer
questions.explanation: The payoff is the seller's obligation, paid out of the seller's proceeds, so it is a seller debit. The buyer is not involved, so it is a single entry. The buyer's new loan, by contrast, is a buyer credit only.

questions.q: Annual property taxes of $7,300 are paid in arrears and have not been paid for the current calendar year. Closing is May 1; the buyer owns the closing day. Using a 365-day year, what is the proration?
options: $2,400 credit to the seller, debit to the buyer
$4,900 debit to the seller, credit to the buyer
$2,420 debit to the seller, credit to the buyer
$2,400 debit to the seller, credit to the buyer
questions.explanation: $7,300 ÷ 365 = $20 per day. Seller's days: Jan 1–Apr 30 = 31 + 28 + 31 + 30 = 120. $20 × 120 = $2,400. The seller used those days but has not paid, and the buyer will pay the bill later, so seller debit/buyer credit.

questions.q: The seller paid the full $3,650 calendar-year tax bill in advance. Closing is October 1; the buyer owns the closing day. Using a 365-day year, what is the proration?
options: $920 debit to the seller, credit to the buyer
$2,730 credit to the seller, debit to the buyer
$910 credit to the seller, debit to the buyer
$920 credit to the seller, debit to the buyer
questions.explanation: $3,650 ÷ 365 = $10 per day. Buyer's days: Oct 1–Dec 31 = 31 + 30 + 31 = 92. $10 × 92 = $920. The seller prepaid the buyer's share, so the buyer reimburses: seller credit/buyer debit.

questions.q: A house outside New York City sells for $425,000. What is the New York State real estate transfer tax, and who normally pays it?
options: $1,700, paid by the buyer
$1,700, paid by the seller
$4,250, paid by the seller
$850, paid by the seller
questions.explanation: The rate is $2 for each $500 (or fraction) of consideration: $425,000 ÷ 500 = 850 units × $2 = $1,700. The grantor (seller) normally pays; the buyer is secondarily liable if the seller does not pay.

questions.q: A buyer purchases a single-family home for $1,200,000. The additional 1% ("mansion") tax is:
options: $2,000, paid by the buyer
$12,000, paid by the seller
$12,000, paid by the buyer
$2,000, paid by the seller
questions.explanation: The mansion tax is 1% of the full consideration when residential consideration is $1 million or more, and the grantee (buyer) pays: $1,200,000 × 1% = $12,000. Taxing only the $200,000 above $1 million is the trap.

questions.q: Who customarily pays New York's mortgage recording tax on a buyer's new purchase-money mortgage?
options: The borrower (buyer), based on the amount of the mortgage debt
The seller, based on the full purchase price of the property
The broker, out of the commission
The county clerk, as an expense of recording the mortgage
questions.explanation: The mortgage recording tax is calculated on the secured debt, not the sale price, and is generally paid by the borrower. On some residential loans the lender pays a portion, but the borrower bears the main charge.

questions.q: A title search shows an old, unpaid judgment against the seller. Before closing, the seller's attorney should generally:
options: Have the judgment paid or otherwise cleared so the title company removes the exception
Ignore it, since a judgment lien is automatically released when the property is sold
Ask the buyer to take title subject to the judgment as part of the purchase price
Have the listing salesperson sign an affidavit stating that the judgment is invalid
questions.explanation: Title exceptions such as judgments, open mortgages, and liens must be cleared (paid at closing, satisfied, or bonded) to deliver the marketable, insurable title the contract requires. A sale does not wipe out a recorded judgment lien.
questions.citation: NY CPLR § 5203 (judgment liens); title insurance practice

questions.q: A new survey shows the neighbor's garage extends two feet onto the seller's lot. This finding is an example of:
options: A special assessment the buyer must pay
An easement in gross held by the utility company
An encroachment that may affect marketable title
A defect that title insurance always covers without exception
questions.explanation: A survey shows boundaries, improvements, and encroachments. An encroachment can make title unmarketable, and title policies often take a survey exception unless a survey is provided.
questions.citation: NY RPL (marketable title); title insurance practice

questions.q: The buyer's final walk-through just before closing is mainly meant to:
options: Start a new inspection period that allows the buyer to cancel the contract for any reason before closing
Confirm the property is in the agreed condition and that required repairs or vacancy are complete
Measure the home's rooms so the lender's appraiser can finish the appraisal report
Let the salesperson and the buyer renegotiate the final purchase price before signing
questions.explanation: The walk-through checks that the property is in the condition the contract requires (repairs done, fixtures left, broom-clean, vacant) as of closing. It does not create a new contingency.

questions.q: After a New York closing outside NYC, the deed is recorded with the county clerk along with the transfer tax return (TP-584) and the real property transfer report (RP-5217). Recording the deed primarily:
options: Transfers title, since a New York deed is void until it is recorded
Lets the buyer avoid the transfer tax
Replaces the need for title insurance
Gives constructive notice of the buyer's ownership to everyone
questions.explanation: Title passes on delivery and acceptance of the deed. Recording protects the buyer by giving public (constructive) notice and priority under New York's race-notice recording act.
questions.citation: NY RPL § 291 (recording act); NY Tax Law § 1409 (TP-584)

questions.q: Who is generally responsible for filing IRS Form 1099-S to report the gross proceeds of a real estate sale?
options: The buyer's homeowners insurance company, which insures the property
The listing salesperson personally, as the licensee who procured the buyer and earned the commission
The local assessor, which records the sale on the assessment roll
The person responsible for closing, such as the settlement or closing attorney
questions.explanation: IRC § 6045(e) requires the "real estate reporting person", usually the person responsible for closing, to report the seller's gross proceeds on Form 1099-S. Some main-home sales are exempt when the seller certifies they qualify.

questions.q: A foreign seller sells a New York investment property for $1,500,000. No reduced rate or exemption applies. Under FIRPTA, how much must the buyer withhold?
options: $0, because the seller's broker handles the tax
questions.explanation: FIRPTA makes the buyer the withholding agent. The standard rate is 15% of the amount realized: $1,500,000 × 15% = $225,000. The buyer can be liable if it fails to withhold.
